concepts.hook: Perceiving meaningful connections between unrelated things. It also covers gamblers who find patterns in random results.
The inability to voluntarily visualize mental images. Its opposite, hyperphantasia, is having extremely vivid mental imagery.
The inability to imagine sounds in the mind, such as a voice or a tune.
People shown nonsense words tend to link soft sounds like bouba with rounded shapes and hard sounds like kiki with spiky ones. Studies across many cultures confirm it.
A delusion that a friend or family member has been replaced by an identical impostor. It most commonly occurs in people with schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder.
Believing that different people are really one person who keeps changing appearance or wearing a disguise. The sufferer often feels persecuted by that person.
The belief that one is dead, does not exist, is rotting, or has lost blood or internal organs. Others instead hold delusions of immortality.
A rare psychiatric syndrome in which a delusional belief is transmitted from one person to another. DSM-5 does not list it as a separate disorder.
A short, pointed saying that states a general truth or practical rule.
Joy at the happiness of a partner who is romantically or sexually involved with someone else.
A catchy piece of music or saying that keeps occupying a person's mind after it is no longer being played or spoken about.
A brief, sudden twitch of the body as a person begins to fall asleep. It often makes the person jump awake for a moment, and sometimes brings a falling sensation.
Hearing loud noises that are not there, such as explosions or thunder, while falling asleep or waking up. There is typically no pain, and it is considered harmless.
Strong anger or disgust at specific sounds, most often the mouth and throat noises of eating and drinking. Loudness does not seem to set it off.
Hearing a ringing or other sounds when no matching sound is present outside. Hearing damage is its most common cause.
A phenomenon in which activating a concept evokes a perception-like sensory experience. What matters is the linguistic meaning of the stimulus, not its sensory properties.
After damage to one half of the brain, for example a stroke, attention and awareness toward the opposite side of space are impaired.
A condition in which a person's limbs seem to act on their own, without conscious control. The other hand may have to restrain the alien one.
Speech made of unrelated or barely related ideas, with the topic changing from one sentence to the next.
Daydreaming so extensive that it interferes with daily life. It is a proposed diagnosis that no major medical or psychological criteria recognize.
Pleasure taken in another person's troubles, failures or humiliation. It has been detected in very young children.
Being unable to communicate certain ideas because the language has no words for them.
Symptoms of varying severity in people who took part in or left an authoritarian religious group. The DSM-5 does not list it as a diagnosable condition.
The hypothesis that snakes helped shape primate vision. Early primates that could best spot snakes survived more often and passed that skill to their offspring.
A mental shortcut in which a current emotion, such as fear or pleasure, drives a decision. Positive feelings about an activity lead people to judge its risks as low.
Automatically repeating the vocalizations of another person, either right away or later. It occurs in many cases of autism.
A language developed by twins that only the two children can understand. Most linguists associate it with idioglossia, any language used by only one or very few people.
Fast, frenetic speech with few pauses. It is mainly a symptom of mental disorders such as bipolar disorder.
A communication disorder of excessive wordiness and repetition that can make speech incoherent. It is often reported in Wernicke's aphasia.
The variety of speech in a creole continuum that is closest to the standard, prestige language.
A poem in which the first letter of each line spells out a word or message. Medieval poets often used one to highlight their own name.
The loss of taste, especially the inability to detect basic tastes such as sweetness and bitterness. Complete loss is rarer than partial loss.
Acting against one's better judgment while believing that a different course of action would be better. It is sometimes translated as weakness of will.
A biological phenomenon in which an organism produces chemicals that influence the germination, growth, survival and reproduction of others. Often it means plants inhibiting their neighbors.
A sentence that can be read in more than one way because of its grammar. The ambiguity comes from the relations among words and clauses, not from individual words.
The union of the genetic material of two parents in sexual reproduction.
A Christian who withdraws from secular society for a life of asceticism and prayer. Unlike cenobites, who live apart in a group, an anchorite lives alone.
A connection between two things that normally branch apart, such as blood vessels, leaf veins or streams.
A reconstruction technique that re-erects a ruined building using its original pieces, with modern materials where necessary. The new material should be unobtrusive but clearly recognizable.
A grammatical feature that expresses how alive or sentient the thing a noun names is. Many languages rank humans above animals, then plants, then objects.
The inability to smell one or more odors. It may be temporary or permanent, and can follow an upper respiratory infection or head trauma.
Indifference toward whether any god exists. An apatheist does not reject the existence of gods, but may treat the question as irrelevant.
The defense of religious doctrines through systematic argument. Early Christian writers who defended their faith against critics are known as its first examples.
A certification that lets a document issued in one country be used legally in another. It removes the need for further certification by the destination country.
Protective magic meant to turn away harm or evil. Amulets, and gestures like crossed fingers or knocking on wood, are everyday examples.
The scientific study of the surface, crust and interior of Mars. The word is a neologism that sometimes stands in for Mars's geology in popular media.
The study of how past peoples understood and used the sky. It looks at the symbolically rich meanings other cultures gave to events in the sky.
A non-profit whose goal is to keep multiple redundant copies of human knowledge at sites on Earth and around the Solar System.
A state of listlessness, of not caring about one's place in the world. Early Christian monks used it for spiritual listlessness, and modern writers tie it to depression.
Body fat, the tissue that stores energy and also cushions and insulates the body. It is also a major endocrine organ that makes hormones.
Communication that carries a concealed meaning for informed members of an underground movement while appearing innocent to outsiders.
A movement disorder marked by inner restlessness, mental distress and often an inability to sit still. Antipsychotic drugs, especially first-generation ones, are a leading cause.
The fraction of sunlight that a surface reflects. Snow reflects most of it and looks bright, while trees absorb most and look dark.
A personality trait of centering attention and action on other people, the individual counterpart of collectivism. Allocentric people define themselves by their group.
Pain triggered by a stimulus that does not normally cause pain. After a sunburn, even clothing or running water on the skin can hurt.
Reduced vision in an eye that looks normal, because the brain fails to fully process its input and favors the other eye. Also called lazy eye.
A spiritual way of reading scripture for allusions to the afterlife. Dante said the allegorical meaning of his Divine Comedy has a moral and an anagogical side.
The Buddhist doctrine of non-self, that no unchanging, permanent self exists. Often read as denying the self, it is better described as a strategy for non-attachment.
Programmed cell death, a tightly regulated process in which a cell kills itself. It is how fingers and toes separate in a developing human embryo.
Writing without words or specific meaning, so readers interpret it for themselves. It can be read in a similar way whatever the reader's language.
Divination with dice marked with letters or numbers, which were historically often knucklebones. The diviner reads a cast by set rules, which are usually tied to a religion.
Hiding the sponsors of an orchestrated message so it looks like spontaneous grassroots support. It can sway opinion by flooding review sites and blogs with manipulated content.
Discrimination against deaf people, as described by deaf activists. It first meant individual attitudes and practices, then was broadened to include oppression.
A concept from the Polish psychiatrist and philosopher Antoni Kępiński, who also originated the idea of information metabolism.
A witch of Slavic folklore who eats children in some tales and helps the hero in others. She lives in a forest hut with chicken legs.
A religion that teaches the essential worth of all religions and the unity of all people. It holds that one God reveals religion progressively.
The first emanation of God in several Gnostic accounts of creation, often depicted as a supreme female principle.
A novel that follows the psychological and moral growth of its protagonist from childhood to adulthood.
Blending elements from two previously unrelated ways of thinking into a new meaning. Koestler held that discovery, invention and humor all follow this pattern.
Covert disinformation deliberately attributed to a false source, often the group it aims to discredit. Its audience is not aware that anyone is influencing them.
A kind of modality that expresses a speaker's wishes or desires, as in the adverb "hopefully".
A group of theories in particle physics and cosmology that are related to string theory, superstring theory and M-theory.
A theoretical limit on the maximum rate of computation a self-contained physical system can achieve. It follows from mass-energy equivalence and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.
A Vietnamese monotheistic religion that combines traditions, taking karma and rebirth from Buddhism and its hierarchy from Catholicism.
A special kind of geometric space called a manifold, with applications in theoretical physics. Superstring theory sometimes proposes that spacetime's extra dimensions take this form.
A dark box or room in which a small hole projects an upside-down image of the outside scene. Artists used it to trace accurate drawings.
A material made of layers of linen or papyrus covered with plaster, used in ancient Egyptian funerary masks.
A word used in a way that departs significantly from normal usage, like militate for mitigate. In rhetoric, it can mean an implausible metaphor.
A deliberate and sustained effort to damage a person's reputation or credibility.
A legal strategy in which a defense lawyer tries to confuse the jury with distractions. Named after a South Park episode satirizing a real murder trial.
In Buddhist cosmology, a vast cluster of world-systems grouped together as one unit.
An urban planning idea in which most daily needs are within a short walk, bike ride or transit ride from anywhere in the city.
The study of how a culture perceives and communicates time. It covers things like punctuality and willingness to wait.
The capacity to mentally reconstruct personal past events and imagine possible future scenarios. Tulving's term for what is usually called mental time travel.
The part of biology that studies timing and cycles in living things, such as their adaptation to rhythms linked to the sun and moon.
Classifying organisms into groups based on their most recent common ancestor. A group holds an ancestor and all its descendants, so strictly speaking fishes include humans.
A form of divination in which lots are cast, as with rolling dice, and the random result is sometimes believed to reveal the will of a deity.
A description of where a cell or substance comes from. Monoclonal means derived from one clone, and polyclonal from many.
A teaching approach designed to develop students' thinking ability.
A model of how gene variants sampled from a population trace back to a common ancestor, merging into a single ancestral copy.
An ardent longing, typically a sensual one. In Catholic and Lutheran theology, it is the human tendency to sin.
The production and study of comprehensive maps of the connections in an organism's nervous system. In small animals like worms, the entire nervous system can be reconstructed.
Merging two or more ideas, texts or opinions into one, often by mistake. It is also used to mean treating two similar but different concepts as the same.
A word with two opposite meanings. Clip, for example, can mean to attach, as in paperclip, or to cut off, as in clip the hedges.
A theory that space expanded exponentially in the very early universe. Many physicists think it explains why the universe looks the same in all directions.
The number of protons in the observable universe, named for the astrophysicist who first proposed a value for it.
A cosmological model of the early universe that explains the origin of the large-scale structure of the cosmos. It is also part of a cyclic universe theory.
The highest heaven in ancient cosmologies inspired by Aristotle, supposed to be occupied by the element of fire. Christian cosmology later adopted it to describe heaven.
A region just outside a rotating black hole. In theory, energy and mass can be extracted from it.
The hypothesis that life could not exist if the constants of nature were even slightly different, so the universe must be tuned for life.
An extremely energetic event in a distant galaxy and the brightest class of explosion in the universe. A flash of gamma rays comes first, then a longer-lived afterglow.
The large discrepancy between aspects of the weak force and gravity. Physicists have no agreed explanation for why the weak force is so much stronger.
A hypothetical field conjectured to have driven cosmic inflation, the rapid expansion of the very early universe.
The idea that physical constants, such as the gravitational constant, might change over time. Experiments have so far set upper bounds on any such change.
When an orbiting body takes as long to rotate once as to circle its partner. The same side of the Moon always faces Earth for this reason.
A short-lived change in light, color or appearance on the Moon's surface. Most reports are irreproducible, and the dispute is over how often such events occur.
A model of computation in which every step can be run backward, so the input can be perfectly reconstructed from the output.
A sequence of six consecutive nines in the decimal digits of pi has become famous as a mathematical coincidence. Reciting pi that far invites the joke that it is rational.
A natural number composed of the same digit repeated. All of them are palindromes, numbers that read the same in both directions.
An irrational number that displays certain characteristics of rational numbers. It is also called a mock rational number.
Two expressions with no direct relationship come out nearly equal, and no theoretical explanation is apparent. Engineers sometimes use one as an approximation of the other.
A number of protons or neutrons that fills complete shells in an atomic nucleus. Nuclei with such a number are much more stable than others.
Martin Rees's term for the allegedly erroneous assumption that normal matter, such as atoms and electrons, is the basis of matter in the universe.
A state with no physical counterpart, added to some quantum theories of forces so the mathematics stays consistent.
A state of matter, often reached from a gas, in which a significant portion of the particles are charged. Stars are almost pure balls of plasma.
A molecule that contains an equal number of positively and negatively charged groups. Some amino acids exist as this kind of molecule, in balance with an uncharged form.
A fundamental physical constant that measures the strength of the electromagnetic interaction between elementary charged particles. Also called the fine-structure constant.
A triangle of points laid out in rows that grow by one each time. Pythagoreans used it as a mystical symbol.
The deep part of a lake or ocean where little or no sunlight reaches. Most food there comes from dead organisms sinking from above.
A buildup of nutrients in a body of water that feeds algae and plants until they use up its oxygen. Fertilizer runoff and sewage are common human causes.
A hypothetical way to settle other worlds by modifying humans, for example with genetic engineering, so they thrive in the environment as it is. Terraforming is its alternative.
A form of reproduction in which an embryo develops from an egg without being fertilized. It occurs naturally in some plants and animals.
Describes wild animals and plants that adapted to live near people and benefit from human settlements, many of them regarded as pests or weeds.
A trait shared by a group of species and presumed to have evolved in their most recent common ancestor. Fur is one for mammals.
An infectious disease that passes from animals to people. Ebola and salmonellosis are examples.
The science of fermentation and its practical uses, from brewing and wine making to fermented milk.
A microbe that can grow in the cold but does best at moderate temperatures, unlike a psychrophile, which prefers the cold.
Feeding on plants, as herbivores do, with mouthparts and digestive enzymes adapted to break down plant material.
A virus of rabbits and hares that causes horn-like cancerous growths, usually on or near the head. Its discovery was a breakthrough in studying cancer-causing viruses.
A grammatical category with no overt marking that still shapes how words combine. In English, a noun's gender shows only when a singular pronoun must be chosen.
The indigenous religion of Tibet, sharing many similarities with Tibetan Buddhism. Scholars debate how far it is a separate tradition.
A spiritual retreat spent in a space with no light at all, practiced in Tibetan Buddhism and Bön.
The philosophical search for a single first principle, tracing the variety of existing things back to one substance.
In Neoplatonism, mystical union with the One, the fundamental source of reality. Later thinkers developed it in Christian theology and Islamic mysticism.
Worship of one supreme god while allowing that other gods may exist and be worshipped. The term was applied to Hindu scriptures that praise many deities as one divine essence.
A tradition of Eastern Christian monks who seek inner stillness through uninterrupted repetition of the Jesus prayer.
Ancient Egyptian magic and medicine, personified as a god. The same word also named the practice of magical rituals.
A Chinese political doctrine that Heaven grants the right to rule to a virtuous ruler. Famine, flood or a successful revolt signaled that Heaven had withdrawn it.
A meditative state in Tibetan Buddhism that occurs after clinical death, in which the body shows minimal signs of decomposition for days or even weeks.
In Tibetan Buddhism, a meditation deity that the practitioner visualizes in intricate detail to internalize its qualities.
In Eastern Orthodox teaching, a transformation whose aim is likeness to or union with God. It requires cooperation between human effort and God's energies.
The self-emptying of Jesus, who set aside his desires to obey God to the point of death. Theologians disagree on whether it also means he limited his divine powers.
The study of religious doctrines of salvation. Scholars often compare what different religions say salvation is and how it is obtained.
The presence of God dwelling in the world, for example among people who study Torah.
Using words such as then, here and you to refer to a time, place or person relative to the situation of speaking.
Describes a word that refers ahead to a more specific expression, as a pronoun does when it comes before the noun it stands for.
A reference to something outside the text, such as the setting of a conversation. Pronouns such as this and there are often used this way.
Something a speaker suggests without saying it outright. Telling a driver out of gas that a station is around the corner implies it is open.
A pattern of sounds that is regularly paired with a meaning. In English, sl- appears in words for low-friction motion, such as slide, slick and sled.
The addition of sounds to a word, at either end or in the middle.
In anthropology, the process by which social divisions and differences form.
In psychiatry, speech made of unrelated or barely related ideas, where the topic often changes from one sentence to another.
A grammatical case that marks the agent of a transitive verb. In languages that have it, the subject of an intransitive verb takes the absolutive case instead.
A verb with a subject and both a direct and an indirect object, one naming the theme and the other the recipient.
The inability to form grammatically correct sentences that is characteristic of fluent aphasia.
A grammatical aspect that views an action as a simple whole, with no attention to its internal structure. It is not a tense.
The way an event is structured in time, as part of a verb's meaning. Arrive has a natural endpoint, while run does not.
A verb for a very brief event that returns to its starting state, so it can be repeated. Blink and sneeze are examples.
A verb that names one particular manner of doing what another verb names. To nibble and to gorge are two ways of eating.
A concept in Indian grammatical theory about how speakers order sounds and words into coherent discourse and meaning. Bhartṛhari, who developed it, treated language and cognition as one.
The reference point, usually the current speaker, that words like this, now and my depend on. In "This is now my fish," the speaker is the origo.
A way language describes entities interacting through force, whether physical, as in leaning on or dragging, or psychological, as in wanting or being urged.
A constructed language with a tiny vocabulary, designed to be simple and to focus its speakers on basic things. Context and word combinations carry more specific meanings.
A constructed human language based on logic and designed to be syntactically unambiguous. It is proposed for communication between people of different language backgrounds.
An experimental constructed language that tries to minimize the vagueness of natural languages. Its creator deems it too complex to have developed naturally.
A programming language built to test the limits of language design, as software art, or as a joke. Its creators usually do not intend it for mainstream programming.
A writing system where each symbol stands for a concept rather than a word, aiming to be readable by people of all languages. Blissymbols is one example.
Being unable to understand or express any signs or symbols, most often after a stroke damages the brain's language areas. Recovery is common but often incomplete.
A personal name that is aptly or peculiarly suited to its owner, for instance to their occupation.
A word that is funny without context, often because of its sound more than its meaning.
The design of signs that warn people in the far future away from nuclear waste sites. Proposals layer forbidding structures, pictures and written explanations.
The jargon or language of a group, often used to exclude or mislead outsiders. Cant and argot name nearly the same thing, and their uses are inconsistent.
Writing that avoids a particular letter or group of letters. Skipping Z is easy, but skipping E means omitting many ordinary words.
The view that some statements are both true and false. Dialetheists can use paraconsistent logics, which tolerate contradictions without making every statement true.
A theory in logic and metaphysics that holds some things do not exist. Also called modal Meinongianism, after Alexius Meinong.
An attempt to cover non-being, whatever may remain outside ontology, the study of what exists. Jean-Luc Nancy distinguishes nothingness from nothing.
A branch of metaphysics about abstract objects, expanding mathematical Platonism, the view that mathematical objects exist independently of us.
Using computer software to formalize metaphysical arguments in logic and check whether they are valid.
The Christian idea that Adam's fall was fortunate, because it brought the redemption of Christ.
The belief that a god is not wholly good and can even be considered evil. Gnostic traditions, for example, treat the creator god of Abrahamic religions as evil.
Hatred of God or of the gods. In monotheism it may arise from the problem of evil, or from rejecting particular depictions of God.
The belief that many gods exist, combined with worshipping only one chosen deity. Monotheism differs by holding that only one god exists.
The transforming effect of divine grace on a person, who literally becomes divine. Most Christian denominations do not read it as erasing the difference between God and humanity.
The theory that economic growth comes mainly from within an economy, through innovation and knowledge. In some models, research subsidies raise the growth rate.
A biography of a saint or church leader. Today the word is often a criticism of any biography that is uncritical or overly reverential.
A reported supernatural appearance of the Virgin Mary. In the Catholic Church, the seers must claim to see her in their surroundings, as hearing her alone does not count.
A depiction of Christ in glory, in his glorified body rather than suffering on the cross. Byzantine art shows him from the chest up with the Scriptures in his hand.
Small leather boxes holding scrolls inscribed with verses from the Torah. Jewish men traditionally wear them during weekday morning prayer.
In Catholic teaching, the special honor given to the Virgin Mary, greater than the veneration of other saints and less than the worship of God.
An animation device in which pictures around the inside of a spinning cylinder are seen in a ring of mirrors, which produces the illusion of motion.
A Japanese idiom for appreciating the impermanence of things, together with a gentle sadness at their passing. It is also translated as an empathy toward things.
A Japanese aesthetic that centers on accepting transience and imperfection. Wabi is read as subdued, austere beauty and sabi as rustic patina.
A Japanese education policy that reduces the hours and content of the primary school curriculum. Japanese media have used the term to criticize drops in scholastic ability.
A method of running an organization that spreads authority and decision-making across self-organizing teams instead of a management hierarchy.
A theory of governance that seeks psychologically safe, productive organizations. Decisions are made by people who share a goal or work process, using consent rather than majority voting.
A perceived global upper class whose power rests on technological advantage and networking skills. Its theorists set it against an underclass called the consumtariat.
The empirical study of systems in transformation, focused on whole-system behaviors that their parts do not predict in isolation. Buckminster Fuller named and pioneered the field.
Estimates one divided by a square root quickly, by reading the number's bits as an integer and refining with Newton's method. Best known from Quake III Arena.
A programming competition in which participants try to write the shortest possible source code that solves a given problem.
A small programming exercise that a developer repeats on purpose to build skill, as a martial artist drills a form.
Writing software so it behaves predictably despite unexpected inputs or user actions. Overdone, it guards against errors that never occur and adds run-time and maintenance costs.
An agile software method that takes good practices to the extreme, so code is reviewed continuously by programming in pairs. It favors frequent releases in short cycles.
A mechanism in a process that keeps operators from making mistakes, by preventing errors, correcting them or flagging them as they happen.
The scientific study of dreams, which measures how the brain works during dreaming and leaves aside what dreams mean.
A drug that induces a dream-like state of consciousness.
A hallucinatory, dream-like state caused by prolonged sleep deprivation, sensory deprivation or drugs. It is often confused with an acute case of schizophrenia.

In traditions inspired by Tibetan Buddhism, a materialized being or thought-form created through spiritual practice and intense concentration. Modern practitioners describe it as a willed imaginary friend.
The Genesis story in which God orders Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac. An angel stops him, and a ram is slaughtered in Isaac's place.
Another name for lead poisoning, the illness caused by lead in the body. Symptoms include abdominal pain, headaches and memory problems.
The practice of attributing mystical or esoteric significance to coincidences. Two scholars describe it as part artistic practice and part conspiracy culture.
A snake-like creature from Japanese folklore, called a cryptid because its existence is unproven.
A legendary Persian creature with a human face, a lion's body and a scorpion's tail. Some accounts say its spines can be launched like arrows.
A supernatural double of a living person, especially one who haunts the person it copies. A literary example is the protagonist's evil twin.
A malevolent god in various Gnostic sects, the creator of the material world. He is a false god who keeps souls trapped in physical bodies.
In Jewish mysticism, the representation of evil or impure spiritual forces. Their realm is called Sitra Achra in Kabbalistic texts.
A set of righteous people whose existence on earth is said to guarantee the world's survival, an idea rooted in Jewish mysticism.
In the Hebrew Bible, the underworld where spirits of the dead go. It may be a metaphor for the grave or an actual afterlife.
A title in Judaism for people considered righteous, such as biblical figures and later spiritual masters. In Hasidic Judaism, the tzadik is a divine channel.
In Kabbalah, God as understood before any self-manifestation, who has no desire, thought, word or action.
The principal God and sky deity of Zoroastrianism.
A Hindu deity that represents Vishnu and Shiva together. It can also express their unity as aspects of the same ultimate reality, Brahman.
An abstract representation of the Hindu god Shiva, usually a short cylindrical pillar of stone or metal. It is typically the main devotional image in Shiva temples.
A humorous paradox claiming that all natural numbers are interesting. If some were not, the smallest dull one would be both dull and interesting for being the smallest.
A theorem that a solid ball can be cut into finitely many pieces and reassembled into two identical balls. The pieces are infinite scatterings of points.
An extension of the real numbers that adds infinitely large and infinitely small numbers. Their use in analysis is called nonstandard analysis, which defines the derivative and integral directly.
A number system that includes the real numbers plus infinitely large and infinitely small ones. John Conway's research on the endgame of Go led to its definition.
The conjecture that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function all lie on one line of complex numbers. It implies results about how primes are distributed.
An operation based on repeated exponentiation, in the way exponentiation is repeated multiplication. It is used to write very large numbers.
An integer that equals an expression built from all of its own digits and arithmetic operations. At least one operation besides joining digits together must be used.
A sequence where each term describes the one before it, by reading off its digits and counting groups of the same digit. The idea resembles run-length encoding.
A family of rapidly increasing functions on the natural numbers, indexed by ordinals. It classifies computable functions by their rate of growth and computational complexity.
Radiation released outside a black hole's event horizon through quantum effects. Black holes that gain no mass are expected to shrink and eventually vanish.
A physical force on the boundaries of a confined space that comes from quantum fluctuations of a field. Any medium that supports oscillations has an analogue.
A proposed way to extract energy from a rotating black hole. A body fires a propellant backward near the hole, and its remains escape with extra energy.
A thought experiment in which one observer watches a second observer perform a quantum measurement. In the Copenhagen interpretation, their statements about the system contradict each other.
The possible decay of a false vacuum, which is stable only locally, into a more stable state. One suggested mechanism is a spreading bubble.
A particle can pass through an energy barrier that classical physics says it cannot cross. This limits how small transistors can be.
An upper limit on the information that a region of space with a limited amount of energy can hold.
A state in which an organism's metabolism stops entirely, letting it survive drying, freezing or lack of oxygen. When conditions improve, it resumes life as before.
One organism living inside the body or cells of another, usually to the benefit of both. Mitochondria began this way, from a bacterium a larger cell absorbed.
Large, soft-bodied organisms shaped like tubes and fronds, the earliest known complex multicellular life. Whether most were animals is still unsettled.
The hypothesis that Earth's surface was once nearly entirely frozen. Whether a thin band of open water remained at the equator is still unanswered.
The open water of the ocean, from surface to seafloor and away from the shore. Pressure rises with depth while light and temperature fall.
A medieval technique in which a melody is shared between voices, one sounding while the other rests.
A wailing song or poem of mourning, composed as a memorial to someone who has died.
The beat in a line of verse, the syllable that carries the metrical stress.
A vocal technique between singing and speaking, usually called speak-singing in English. It stays closer to speech because it does not emphasize any particular pitches.
Music that uses intervals smaller than a semitone, notes that fall between the keys of a piano.
A minimalist genre built on sustained notes called drones, in long pieces where the harmony changes only slightly.
A thought experiment on sacrificing one person to save more. A runaway trolley will kill several people unless someone diverts it to a track where one dies.
Being morally blamed or praised for an action or its results, even though the person did not fully control them.
An objection to utilitarianism that it requires acts we would normally treat as optional, such as giving to charity instead of spending on ourselves.
Criteria for judging when an act is permissible although it also causes harm. The agent must intend the good effect and not the bad one.
Answering an argument by attacking the speaker's own behavior, so that they appear hypocritical. It is a kind of ad hominem attack.
The shared world of what people take as self-evident and given. Husserl treated it as the ground of all knowledge in lived experience.
Setting aside one's assumptions about what things really are, in order to describe experience as it appears.
Heidegger's term for the way of being particular to humans, who are aware of their own existence and must face issues such as mortality.
Heidegger's term for human existence as being thrown into the world.
Springing into the air with all four feet off the ground at once, as gazelles do. Biologists think it warns predators the animal would be hard to catch.
A social system with shared care of young, overlapping generations and a split between breeding and non-breeding groups. It is most widespread among ants and termites.
A fairly rapid learning process during one phase of development. An animal may learn the characteristics of something it perceives, such as a dangerous predator.
Leaving others to raise one's young, often with eggs that mimic the host's. Hosts may respond by recognizing and ejecting the parasite's eggs.
Behavior that harms another individual at a cost to the one who acts.
Luc Ciompi's theory that feeling and thinking continually interact in all mental activity. It began with schizophrenia and grew to cover politics.
Secure psychiatric hospitals in China run by the police, where people judged mentally ill and dangerous are held.
Applying scientific techniques to the analysis of archaeological materials and sites.
A ruler, often as the title of a specific public office.
An alternative treatment based on the idea that the outer ear reflects the whole body. It is considered a pseudoscience.
The study of history, especially economic and social history, through the systematic use of economic theory and statistical methods.
A geopolitical concept meant to define American, and later Western, policy toward the Muslim world. Brzezinski first developed it, and later thinkers reworked it.
The theory that words have a natural connection to the things they name.
A Surrealist collage technique in which an image is cut into squares and reassembled at random to create something new.
Radiation therapy that places a sealed radioactive source inside or right next to the tumor, so only a small area is irradiated.
The art or practice of hunting, especially with dogs.
A mood disorder with many periods of depressive symptoms and periods of elevated mood, none severe enough to count as a major depressive or manic episode.
A decorative technique for transferring engravings and prints to pottery or other materials. The shortened word decal names a mass-produced transfer or label.
A way of imitating stained glass by sticking painted translucent paper to window glass.
The world of a story as its characters experience it. Music is diegetic when the characters can hear it too.
An economic system in which the state actively steers the economy through planning, investment and subsidies, but within a market economy, not a command economy.
A North American literary movement whose writers show the seamier or more mundane parts of ordinary life in spare, plain language.
The idea that the huge, similar ratios of cosmic sizes to force strengths are no coincidence. If so, constants such as gravity's strength change as the universe ages.
A phrase that sounds ordinary to most listeners but carries a coded meaning for a particular group.
A short hymn of praise to God, often added to the end of psalms and hymns in Christian worship.
Trying to find groundwater, ores or other buried things with a forked twig or rods, whose movement is said to reveal them. It works no better than chance.
A written description of a real or imagined work of art that is used especially in poetry.
An atypical brain inflammation that left some victims speechless and motionless, as if turned to statues. It once spread around the world in an epidemic.
The brief, efficient speech of a child at the two-word stage of learning a language.
A word that occurs only once within a context, such as the works of an author or a single text. Such words are quite common.
A long dispute among American linguists over whether meaning comes from an underlying syntax, as Chomsky held, or syntax is shaped by underlying meaning, as his critics argued.
Visual effects that come from inside the eye, as when light makes objects within the eye visible.
The part of an explanation that does the explaining. Asked why there is smoke, the answer, fire, is the explanans, and the smoke is the explanandum.
German literature written abroad by refugee authors who fled Nazi Germany, Nazi Austria and the territories they occupied.
The study of theological questions raised by extraterrestrial intelligence, such as what beliefs aliens might hold or how evidence of them might change human theologies.
In Sufism, the passing away of the self, or dying before one dies. Sufis disagree on whether it means annihilating the ego or recognizing God's unity with creation.
Lacan's term for the defense mechanism he held to cause psychosis, in which a basic element of the person's symbolic world, the Name-of-the-Father, is rejected.
Sooty, or dark and murky like soot.
Confused, meaningless talk or writing, nonsense that still sounds as if it should mean something.
A method for forming metal parts that exactly reproduce a model. Printers used it to make plates, and some sculptures that look bronze are electrotyped copper.
A poetic form that borrows lines from a more famous poem. It opens with a borrowed stanza, then new stanzas end by repeating one of its lines.
A fashion trend of wearing outdoor gear, such as puffer jackets, hiking boots and fleeces, as streetwear.
Writing that is excessively wordy, rambling or full of digressions. It is most often linked to schizophrenia, though the grammar can be correct.
Retraining a person's handwriting through exercises to correct writing difficulties.
A grotesque or monstrous figure in ancient art, shown on many kinds of objects.
Ancient Indian philosophers whose asceticism went so far that they treated food and clothing as harmful to purity of thought.
A person trained in ancient Rome to practice divination by inspecting the entrails, especially the livers, of sacrificed animals.
Describes the disorganized subtype of schizophrenia, now obsolete and no longer diagnosed as a separate condition.
Weakness of one entire side of the body. Stroke is one cause, and complete paralysis of that side is called hemiplegia.
In Christian theology, the originator of a heretical doctrine or the founder of a sect that holds one.
A martyr who was a bishop or priest, in the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches. Hieromartyrs hold no special rank of saint.
A school of Japanese Zen calligraphy, believed to be a way to reach meditative absorption. Writing is not rated by whether it pleases the eye.
The space of possible movement, shaped by preferred paths rather than straight lines. Such paths balance shortest distance, security, minimal work and maximum experience.
A Christian term, used in the Nicene Creed, meaning that Jesus is of the same being as God the Father. It is also applied to the Holy Spirit.
A persistent low droning noise that many people in an area hear and others do not. It may not be a single phenomenon.
Matter, which in Aristotle's hylomorphism combines with form to make up a physical thing.
The state of consciousness leading out of sleep. Hallucinations often occur in it, along with sleep paralysis, being aware of one's surroundings but unable to move or speak.
The shift from wakefulness into sleep, during which hallucinations and lucid dreaming can occur.
Growing confusion and restlessness that begin in the late afternoon and early evening in people with dementia. It seems more frequent in the middle stages of Alzheimer's disease.
An old psychiatric term for a mood illness in which episodes of mania and depression alternate in a cycle.
A condition in which a sudden shock leads a person, mostly in Southeast Asia, to scream, curse, or imitate others' speech and behavior. Its cause remains undetermined.
Said of a disease with an unknown cause. For some conditions, such as ankylosing spondylitis, the cause of a large share of cases has not been established.
One person's own way of using language, including vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation. A dialect, by contrast, is a set of features shared among a group of people.
A pseudo-medicine that claims each sector of the iris matches an organ and that anomalies there reveal a disorder. Clinical studies have found no efficacy.
Harm caused by medical care, whether through treatment or error. Some cases are obvious, like amputating the wrong limb, while others, like drug interactions, can go unrecognized.
A mystical movement in Russian Orthodoxy that held the name of God to be inseparable from God himself. The Most Holy Synod condemned its teaching as heretical.
The symptoms and effects of starvation, a severe shortage of calories below the level needed to keep an organism alive. Prolonged starvation can cause permanent organ damage.
An insertion or deletion of bases in an organism's genome. A point mutation, by contrast, replaces one base with another without changing the total number.
The greatest lower bound of a set, meaning the largest value at or below each of its elements. Positive real numbers have no smallest member, yet have an infimum.
A psychological theory of the interaction between living organisms and their environment, developed by the Polish psychiatrist Antoni Kępiński.
Lost social and life skills after a long stay in a mental hospital, prison or other remote institution. Residents deprived of independence often cannot manage life outside.
Experimental musical instruments invented and built by the Italian futurist Luigi Russolo, in many varieties with different names.
Unconsciously adopting the thoughts, memories or personality traits of others. A child taking on parental values and attitudes is a normal example.
A map between two abelian varieties, in algebraic geometry, that is surjective and has a finite kernel, so it preserves their group structure.
A language with no demonstrable genealogical relationship to any other language, so it is a family of one. Basque is an example.
A way of showing social, technological, biological and historical connections in pictures. It uses standardized symbols, with identical figures repeated in series.
The recurrence of the same meaning feature across a text, which gives it coherence.
An inhalant made from fermented human waste and reported as a street drug among Zambian youth. An American scare over it is described as a moral panic.
A phrase that can be heard in several ways that sound alike, giving a different meaning. It can be deliberate, like a pun, or accidental.
A detailed, choreographed pattern of martial arts movements, practiced to memorize and perfect them. Kata also appear in Japanese arts such as kabuki theater and tea ceremony.
The proclamation at the core of the early church's teaching about Jesus. One Catholic formulation is "Jesus loves us, died for us, is alive and near us."
A scenario in which low Earth orbit becomes so crowded that collisions between objects cascade, producing ever more debris. It could make some orbital regions unusable.
A traditional Japanese technique for joining pieces of wood. Wooden buildings, especially temples, have used it for centuries.
A style of minimalist American short fiction that is also called low-rent tragedies.
A story, dialogue, question or statement from Chan Buddhist lore that is used in Zen practice. Meditating on one aims to let a student see their own buddha-nature.
The Japanese martial art of archery. The archer grips the asymmetrical bow in its lower third, and the art began with the samurai class.
A manufacturing process that thins material such as metal or paper by passing it between two cylinders turning in opposite directions.
A person who scientifically studies moths and butterflies, as part of entomology, the study of insects.
A probability distribution whose tails decay more slowly than a normal one, so it produces more outliers. The Laplace distribution is an example.
A divine saying, especially one spoken by Jesus, as opposed to narrative. The plural, logia, names a collection of such sayings, as in the Gospel of Thomas.
The field of recreational linguistics, which takes in word games and wordplay of many kinds.
A quarrel over words or their meanings, rather than over the facts.
The time between two successive new moons or two successive full moons, which lunar calendars use as a month. Exactly where a lunation begins varies.
A restrictive diet drawn from Zen Buddhism, balancing foods classed as yin and yang. No high-quality clinical evidence shows it helps against disease, and it may be harmful.
In Zen practice, visions and other sensory illusions that can arise during deep meditation, usually treated as distractions to be ignored.
The branch of zoology that studies mollusks, a group that includes snails, slugs and clams. Applied work also studies mollusks as carriers of diseases such as schistosomiasis.
Using a word that sounds like the intended one but means something else, often with a humorous result. Yogi Berra reportedly called switch hitters amphibious instead of ambidextrous.
An almond-shaped frame around a whole figure, often Jesus or the Virgin Mary in Christian art. Unlike a halo, it surrounds the entire body.
Explaining social life only through the decisions of individuals, each moved by their own motives. It rejects explanations that give causes to whole groups.
The interdisciplinary study of how living beings, and humans in particular, relate to the milieu they live in.
Fiction that keeps reminding readers they are reading a made-up work, by drawing attention to its own language and storytelling. It is often used for parody.
The study of the environments in which living things and human societies exist, and of how they relate to them.
The ocean's twilight zone is a layer defined by light. It begins where sunlight has mostly faded and ends where none is left.
The chemical addition of a methyl group to a molecule. In cells, enzymes carry it out, and it can help regulate genes.
The evolved resemblance of an organism to something else, often another species. Birds hunt by sight, so they avoid a harmless hoverfly that looks like a wasp.
A learning technique that aids memory, often by linking the information to something easier to remember. Short poems and acronyms are common examples.
Computers easily match adults at intelligence tests and checkers, yet struggle with the perception and movement of a one-year-old. Walking took evolution far longer to build than mathematics.
A hill or small mountain, a word used in the Caribbean.
A therapy in which patients accept life as it is. It treats emotions as part of nature and aims to lessen the damage anxiety does.
A traditional Chinese medicine therapy that burns dried mugwort on particular points of the body. It is promoted for many conditions, but good evidence does not back it.
A circle of writers and intellectuals in Munich, founded by the esotericist Alfred Schuler, the philosopher Ludwig Klages and the poet Karl Wolfskehl.
Nearsighted. Distant objects look blurry while close ones look normal, because light from far away focuses in front of the retina instead of on it.
A basic unit of narrative structure from which myths are thought to be built. Related myths share these units and reassemble them in different ways.
A country whose legitimate institutions are penetrated by the power and wealth of the illegal drug trade. Critics call the term ambiguous.
A state of wakefulness, watchfulness and sobriety in Orthodox Christian theology. One saint describes it as fixing and halting thought at the entrance to the heart.
A diagnosis for fatigue, anxiety and headache, first used for a supposed weakness of the nerves. The American diagnostic manual no longer includes it.
An abnormal, excessive growth of tissue that keeps growing even after its original trigger is removed. Malignant ones are also known as cancers.
How the sensory nervous system detects harmful stimuli and carries the signal to the brain. It usually results in the experience of pain.
A Church of Scientology tactic of telling a target's friends, neighbors and co-workers that the target is under investigation for crimes. Its aim is intimidation.
The belief in a mystical relationship between numbers and ideas. It also covers working out the numerical value of the letters in names, as in gematria.
A word or expression that comes from a proper name. The French word poubelle, from prefect Eugène Poubelle, is the classic example.
The branch of taxonomy based on the shape and structure of eggs. Used mostly with insects, it can work from a whole egg or from fragments.
The process that builds mountains where plates converge. Plate motion compresses the margin, and the crumpled plate is uplifted into one or more ranges.
The claim that UFO sightings fall along straight lines on a map, proposed by the French writer Aimé Michel.
The rearing and education of the ideal citizen of an ancient Greek city-state. It trained body, mind and soul, from rhetoric and philosophy to wrestling.
Continuing to hear a sound after the physical noise has stopped. It is often associated with damage to the temporal lobe of the brain.
A manuscript page whose text was scraped off for reuse. The word also describes an object made for one purpose and later reused for another.
The study of pollen, spores and other microscopic organic remains found in sediments and rocks. It helps date rock layers and reconstruct ancient climates.
A detailed imaginary world, usually invented in childhood, that may have its own geography, history and language. Few people ever learn of it.
Fiction that explores the subjective nature of reality and how powerful forces can manipulate it. Those forces may be a totalitarian government or a character's mental illness.
A style that favors short, simple sentences without conjunctions. In poetry it also means placing two dissimilar images side by side with no clear connection.
Focusing on small parts of an issue without considering its wider context. Used as a criticism, it is contrasted with cosmopolitanism.
In Christian theology, the second coming of Christ at the end of time. The word first also meant his invisible presence in the world.
A historians' term for periods when China's dominance in the Far East brought peace and stability. The first came under the Han dynasty, alongside the Pax Romana.
The study of the punishment of crime and prison management. It also covers theories of the purposes of punishment, such as deterrence and rehabilitation.
A model in which the Christian Church is governed by the patriarchs of the five major bishoprics of the Roman Empire. The Roman Catholic Church rejected it.
In Vygotsky's work, the way a person emotionally lives through a situation, which shapes how that situation affects their development.
Charles Sanders Peirce's name for the study of the phaneron, the total of all that the mind perceives and knows, whether it corresponds to reality or not.
Hospitality toward strangers, valued in Christian teaching as a duty.
The now discredited practice of predicting mental traits by measuring bumps on the skull. Brain areas do have specific functions, but skull shape does not reflect them.
The study of the Holy Spirit within Christian theology, covering the Spirit's person and works, along with spiritual gifts and sanctification.
Economic and social policy made by consensus in the Dutch way, with groups cooperating despite their differences.
A device that records blood pressure, pulse, breathing and skin conductivity while someone answers questions, in an attempt to detect lies. The scientific community considers it pseudoscience.
Any space more general than a metric space, because distance need not be symmetric, tell points apart or obey the triangle inequality.
Spiritual state of false holiness in Eastern Orthodox Christianity, in which a person wrongly believes in their own spiritual superiority. Humility is said to cure it.
The knowledge needed before studying a discipline, though not enough to master it. In medicine, it is the preliminary collection of data about a patient by observation.
Any newly coined word that has been repeated but has not gained acceptance beyond its original users. It becomes a neologism once someone else publishes it.
A divine voice that speaks in the first person in the Gnostic text Trimorphic Protennoia and describes its descents. The voice is the source of life and knowledge.
Romanian term for the supposed pioneering character of Romanian culture. It is sometimes used for Dacianism, a tendency to idealize the Dacian past.
The study of how people use space and how population density affects behavior, communication and social interaction.
The sound of wind rustling through leaves.
A former psychological disorder marked by phobias, obsessions, compulsions or excessive anxiety. It survives as one scale of the MMPI personality inventory.
The origin of a symptom or illness in psychological causes rather than physical ones.
Pseudoscience claiming that the traumas and conflicts of a person's ancestors cause that person's mental troubles and illnesses. It has shown neither effectiveness nor scientific basis.
A claimed psychic ability to produce written words without consciously writing, with the hand supposedly guided by spirits.
Ceiling painting technique that uses perspective to make a flat ceiling look like open sky or an architectural space above the viewer.
Social phenomenon in China in which qigong became hugely popular, with claims of telepathy and other paranormal abilities that were never scientifically substantiated.
A narrative structure in which an opening story introduces a second story given more emphasis, or a set of shorter tales. The Decameron is a notable example.
A long sequence of novels following the same characters, often a family.
Treatment of disease with X-rays. It is an early form of radiotherapy.
The role, in many religions, of a person chosen to serve a deity, perform rites and look after the relation between the community and the sacred.
A Ba'athist ideology based on the thinking of Saddam Hussein. It combines Arab nationalism and socialism and treats political disputes as battles.
An umbrella term for women who love women, covering any woman attracted to women or in a relationship with one regardless of sexual orientation.
Confused, repetitive speech linked to many mental disorders, including schizophrenia, and treated as a symptom of disordered thinking.
Poetry inspired by Japanese haiku that takes science and science fiction as its subjects. Its length is even more flexible than haiku's.
Divination by gazing into a surface such as a crystal ball or a mirror, hoping to see visions that offer guidance. It lacks empirical support.
The smallest unit of meaning recognized in semantics, a single characteristic that helps set meanings apart.
A word repeated over and over loses its meaning for a while and sounds like noise. Staring at it for a long time has the same effect.
Sending visual signals over a distance with flags, lights or moving arms. It is also used for railway signals and traffic lights.
The sabbatical year of the agricultural cycle mandated by the Torah, when the land lies fallow and farming is forbidden. Debts were to be canceled too.
A custom, usually a choice of phrasing or a single word, that distinguishes one group from another. Groups have used it as a password.
Resembling the sayings of a sibyl, an ancient woman prophet. Used of statements that are prophetic or cryptic.
An older name for electroconvulsive therapy, in which an electric current applied to the scalp under general anesthesia triggers a seizure to treat some psychiatric illnesses.
A word that is hard to use because its meaning is shifting from one sense to another, or because controversy surrounds it.
In drama, a speech in which a character alone speaks their thoughts and feelings aloud to the audience. It differs from the monologue and the aside.
A phrase that breaks the rules of grammar. It can also describe wording that is not idiomatic.
Sound produced from within the inner ear without any external stimulation. Otoacoustic emissions in general are used to measure inner ear health.
Bomber designed to avoid detection by radar and other sensors, through its shape and radiation-absorbent material. None is completely invisible to radar.
Advertising that hides the fact that it is advertising, such as a paid person praising a product to strangers as if they were an ordinary fan.
A family tree of the surviving copies of a text, showing which manuscript was copied from which.
The study and treatment of mouth disorders, such as oral cancer and salivary gland disorders, in a field between medicine and dentistry.
Relating to the Styx, one of the rivers of the Greek Underworld.
A popular or wealthy pairing that the public follows with intense interest. The term began with fictional soap opera couples and was later applied to real celebrity pairs.
The Christian doctrine that the Church has replaced the Jewish people as God's covenanted people. Rabbinic Judaism rejects it as offensive to Jewish history.
A group of computer hackers that surfaced online to support the Syrian government. It defaced websites and attacked opposition groups and Western news outlets.
John Gall's treatise arguing that large complex systems are extremely hard to build correctly. It advises smaller systems, grown step by step in close touch with users.
Magic that works through technology, found mainly in fiction and games.
Any measurable property or effect that provides scientific evidence of past or present technology, such as radiation leaking from huge engineered structures.
A theory that explains what a thought or word is about by the function it was selected to perform, a selection that usually comes about through evolution.
A composition in which the last letter of each line forms a word. Combined with an acrostic in the same composition, it makes a double acrostic.
People have a survival instinct and know that death is inevitable. The theory says cultural beliefs, such as an afterlife, ease that terror by giving life lasting meaning.
A quality in Michelangelo's art that provokes terror, awe, or a sense of the sublime in the viewer. The word also described his difficult character.
A decentralized network of far-right Telegram channels that share instructions and targets for mass shootings. Several governments have banned it as a terrorist organization.
A combination of four unlike elements in one unit. In Christian art, it is usually the lion, ox, angel and eagle that stand for the four Evangelists.
A battle between gods in Greek mythology. Such myths stress the gap between mortals and the immortals who govern them.
Faith, hope and charity, the virtues that Christian theology ties to salvation by God's grace and that have God as their object.
The claimed ability to imprint images from the mind onto surfaces such as photographic film by psychic means.
A medieval Christian scheme that splits history into an era of the Father, then of the Son, then of the Holy Spirit.
Keeping money out of the economy. The money piles up without growing or taking part in economic activity.
A sentence that presents a whole event or situation at once, with no split into topic and comment, such as "The phone is ringing."
A set of verb forms sharing all verb-specific features, such as tense, mood and voice, whatever the person, number or gender. School grammar calls it a verb tense.
The war in Greek mythology in which the older gods, the Titans, fought the younger Olympians for rule of the universe. The Olympians won.
Essence and function in Chinese philosophy. Essence is the absolute source of all things, function its concrete manifestations, and both are aspects of one process.
A problem that would take more information processing than a computer the size of the Earth could do in the age of the Earth.
Telling one story across many platforms and formats, such as film and social media. Each platform gets its own material, and the pieces stay in narrative synchronization.
A person who lives in a cave. In everyday speech it also insults someone seen as primitive or backward.
Using a web address close to a real one to catch users who mistype it. Copied content can make visitors think they are on the real site.
Savoriness, one of the basic tastes, typical of broths and cooked meats. It has its own receptors, which respond to glutamates and nucleotides.
A spontaneous oscillation in the tone of blood vessel walls, independent of the heartbeat or breathing. Its mechanisms and importance are not yet fully understood.
A form of Reichian psychotherapy that works with the physical manifestations of emotions.
A wish in principle that usually leads to no action. It sits between desire and will.
In Catholic and Lutheran teaching, a lesser sin that injures a person's friendship with God without separating the person from God completely.
The study of the history, symbolism and use of flags. Someone who studies flags is a vexillologist, and someone who designs them is a vexillographer.
The process by which a person decides on a course of action and commits to it. It can be conscious or become automatic as a habit.
A popular movement of German youth groups who hiked in the country to protest industrialization and commune with nature. Historians credit it with reviving folk songs.
A word or phrase that gives the impression something specific has been said when the claim is vague. The speaker can later deny any specific meaning.
A non-medical condition in which a writer cannot produce new work or slows down creatively. Its severity ranges from trouble finding ideas to years without output.
A color vision deficiency in which everything looks tinted yellow. The most common causes are the heart drug digoxin and cataracts.
The supposed ability to speak or understand a foreign language one could not have learned by natural means. No scientifically admissible evidence supports any alleged case.
A figure in the Church of Scientology's confidential upper-level teachings. In its account he was an extraterrestrial ruler who killed beings with hydrogen bombs.
The art of carving an image into a block of wood for printing. English rarely uses the word for images alone, but it appears with block books.
Experiments in sound and invented language by Russian Cubo-Futurist poets. Its words are neologisms that mean nothing, organized by sound and rhythm.
A Neopagan movement in Romania that rebuilds an ethnic religion from ancient Dacian and Thracian roots. It is named for Zalmoxis, a god of Paleo-Balkan mythology.
The delusion of being able to turn into an animal, or having already done so. It was commonly used for animals other than wolves, which lycanthropy names.
The scientific management of domestic or captive animals, including handling, breeding and keeping. It draws on genetics, nutrition and economics.
A position in chess or another turn-based game where a player must move and any legal move worsens their position. Passing would be best if it were allowed.
Approaching God by negation, speaking only of what may not be said about God. Its counterpart, cataphatic theology, makes positive statements about what God is.
Theology that uses positive terms to say what God is. Apophatic theology does the opposite, saying only what the divine is not.
An assembly or community. In Buddhism it means the monastic communities of monks and nuns, and also Buddhists, monastic or not, who have reached enlightenment.
In some schools of Buddhism, the state between death and rebirth. In Tibetan tradition it moves from the clearest experiences of reality to terrifying hallucinations.
Beliefs about the end of the present age, human history or the world. Abrahamic religions hold a linear cosmology, while Indian religions tend toward cycles.
The end of the world or the end times, which several religions foretell. Eschatology is the study of these expectations.
The restoration of creation to perfection. In Christianity, the belief, often linked to Origen, that everyone, even the Devil, is finally saved. Its status is disputed.
A concept in Buddhism, Jainism and Hinduism meaning suffering, unease or dissatisfaction. It can name the unease of craving for and grasping after things that do not last.
The Buddhist doctrine of impermanence, which holds that all conditioned existence, without exception, is transient. Together with suffering, it is one of the marks of existence.
Dependent origination, the Buddhist teaching that conditioned phenomena arise in dependence on other phenomena. Traditionally it is read as a chain of links explaining rebirth and suffering.
The journey of the prophet Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina. The year it took place marks the starting point of the Hijri calendars.
A conundrum or state of puzzlement. In rhetoric, it is a declaration of doubt, often feigned, made for rhetorical effect.
Movements among Melanesians after colonization that foretold an abundance of goods, the cargo, brought by ancestors. Use of the term has declined among anthropologists as too pejorative.
Turning expressions of the capitalist system and its media culture against the system. The Situationists used it for subversive political pranks.
The easing of strained political relations through dialogue. It often names the period of lower tensions between the Soviet Union and the United States during the Cold War.
A play that is meant to be read by a solitary reader, not performed onstage.
A method of making multicolor prints in lithography, using a separate stone for each color. Fewer colors and less detail made cheaper prints.
A perceptual phenomenon in which stimulating one sense or cognitive pathway triggers involuntary experiences in another. In one common form, letters or numbers are perceived as inherently colored.
A name that is incorrectly or unsuitably applied. Many arise because something was named long before its nature was known.
Two places on opposite sides of the Earth, joined by a straight line through its center.
The steady change in the orientation of Earth's axis of rotation, also called the precession of the equinoxes.
A social condition in which moral values, standards and guidance for individuals break down. For Durkheim it arises from a mismatch between personal and wider social standards.
Cultural and institutional spaces that are somehow other, similar to their surroundings yet upsetting them. Foucault's examples include ships and cemeteries.
The change in the frequency of an existing gene variant in a population due to chance. It can make variants vanish and reduce genetic variation.
The stationary part of a sundial that casts a shadow. The word is also used in mathematics and other fields, typically to measure directions, position or time.
A pattern of five points, four forming a square with a fifth at its center. It is the five-spot on dice and dominoes.
The distinctive, often elaborate swarming behavior of starlings.
A gathering of male animals that compete in displays and court visiting females. It is most common among birds such as black grouse.
Advertising by an animal to predators that it is not worth attacking or eating. The signal can be conspicuous coloration that is backed by toxicity or spines.
An organism that has both female and male traits, because cells across its body differ in their sex chromosomes. It is most often documented in insects.
The changes in an organism's behavior, form and physiology in response to its environment. It matters more for plants than for animals, which can often move away.
An underground network of fungi joining the roots of forest plants. Claims that trees share resources and warn each other through it are not strongly supported by evidence.
A year in a long but regular cycle when forest trees produce acorns and other nuts in very large quantities. Researchers hypothesize several causes, such as weather patterns.
A correlation between a population's size or density and the average fitness of its individuals, often measured as growth rate per individual.
The glow in many animals' eyes when light hits them, from a layer behind the retina that reflects light back. It improves night vision. Humans lack it.
Presenting ordinary things in an unfamiliar way so audiences can gain new perspectives. Russian formalists, who coined the term, considered it central to art and poetry.
The surname of W. G. Sebald, a German writer whose books mix fiction, memoir and photographs.
The German tradition of self-cultivation, in which a person's mind develops through education and cultural maturation. It aims to harmonize mind and heart within society.
The conflict between the Catholic Church and Prussia over control of education and church appointments. Now it also means culture wars between groups with opposing values.
A full-time functionary of the Soviet Communist Party or government, below the top ranks of management. The word is often derogatory, suggesting doubtful competence and attitude.
The bureaucratic machine of a Soviet-style party or state, made up of its full-time officials.
The Eastern Bloc practice of copying censored writings by hand and passing them from reader to reader. Printed texts could be traced back to their source.
The idea that elements of a culture's past return or persist, as if to haunt the present. Derrida coined it, and writers define it in different ways.
The intellectual, cultural, ethical and political climate of an era. It can also mean the fashions that set what is considered acceptable or tasteful.
A technique credited to Bertolt Brecht that stops the audience from simply identifying with the characters in a play. Viewers are meant to judge their actions consciously.
A work of art that draws on, or tries to draw on, all or many art forms.
A German word for longing or yearning. Some psychologists use it for feelings about what is unfinished or imperfect in life, paired with a yearning for something ideal.
A strong desire to wander, travel and explore the world.
A melancholic, nostalgic longing for a loved person or thing that is absent. It is often tied to a sense that the loss may be permanent.
A Welsh word for an especially nostalgic longing or homesickness for Wales.
A Russian word for a deep, restless melancholy that sometimes has no particular cause.
A Danish and Norwegian word for a cozy, contented mood evoked by comfort and conviviality. Treating it as a core part of Danish culture is a recent development.
A Swedish word for just the right amount, neither too much nor too little. It suggests appropriateness without necessarily implying perfection.
A Japanese concept of what gives a person's life meaning, such as a sense of purpose or a source of motivation. It comes from activities a person takes up willingly.
A Nguni philosophy of shared humanity, translated roughly as "humanity to others" or "I am what I am because of who we all are".
A Navajo (Diné) idea of living in balance, harmony and beauty with other people and the natural world.
The highest virtue in Confucian thought, often translated as humaneness. According to Confucius, it has no single definition and includes benevolence and compassion.
A concept from ancient Chinese philosophy meaning not-acting, or effortless action. Taoists aim to live in alignment with the natural order and to avoid force or haste.
The source and fundamental principle of the universe in East Asian philosophy and religions. Taoist texts describe it as formless, invisible and omnipresent.
In Vedanta, a description of the experience of ultimate unchanging reality, called Brahman, as existence, consciousness and bliss.
A Buddhist practice that cultivates compassion by breathing in the suffering of others and breathing out peace and healing.
Seated meditation, typically the main practice of Zen Buddhism. Practitioners may follow the breath or repeat a phrase.
Benevolence or loving-kindness toward others, including friendliness, good will and active interest in them. In Buddhism it is cultivated through a popular form of meditation.
An Indian principle of cause and effect in which a person's intent and actions shape their future. Good deeds bring happier rebirths, bad deeds worse ones.
The ongoing cycle of death, life and rebirth that beings experience in Indian religions. Escaping it is the core of the spiritual quest in those traditions.
In Indian religions, the ultimate state of release from suffering and from rebirth, reached when a person's passions are extinguished. Traditions describe it differently.
Liberation from the cycle of death and rebirth, in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism. In Hindu traditions it is the utmost aim of human life.
Another name for moksha, the liberation from the cycle of death and rebirth sought in Indian religions.
The final life stage in Hinduism, spent renouncing material desires and pursuing spiritual goals. Traditionally for the last years of life, though young students may skip ahead.
A key concept in Indian religions that has no single translation. Most often it means a person's moral duties, which differ between a farmer and a soldier.
The opposite of dharma, meaning whatever is not in accord with it, such as discord and wrongness. It is a flexible term whose sense depends on circumstances and context.
Enslaved people escaping from slavery to live in free communities of their own, often in remote forests or mountains.
A word naming the people of a place, such as Indian for someone from India. It covers residents whatever their ethnic or religious background.
The study of place names, including where they come from and what they mean. It is one branch of onomastics, the study of names of all kinds.
The proper name of a body of water, such as a river, lake or sea.
A person who hoards books.
The unpredictable swerve of atoms in Epicurus's atomism. Without it, Lucretius says, atoms would all fall straight down, never collide, and nature would produce nothing.
In Spinoza's philosophy, the inclination of a thing to continue to exist and enhance itself. It can mean the instinctive will to live of living organisms.
The Greek god of love and sex, known to the Romans as Cupid. He is winged and carries a bow and arrows, which make people fall in love.
The highest form of love in Christian thought, God's love for humans and theirs for God. It contrasts with brotherly love and self-love.
The kind of wisdom concerned with practical action. It implies good judgment and excellence of character, and Aristotle set it apart from other kinds of wisdom.
An ancient Greek ideal of excellence of character and soundness of mind. In a well-balanced person it leads to other qualities, such as temperance and moderation.
In Stoic philosophy, a state of mind in which one is not disturbed by the passions. The word is better translated as equanimity than as indifference.
A steady calm marked by ongoing freedom from distress and worry. Pyrrhonism, Epicureanism and Stoicism all seek it, though its role differs in each.
A Greek word for a state of good spirit, commonly translated as happiness or welfare. In Aristotle it names the highest human good.
A relatively stable disposition, such as a person's health, knowledge or character. It is a Greek word important in Aristotle's philosophy.
The creation of an invented mythology by a writer, a subgenre of speculative fiction. Tolkien popularised the idea, though it long predates him.
A sudden turn of events in a story that saves the protagonist from terrible, impending doom. Tolkien created the concept in his essay on fairy stories.
Tolkien's term for an author's making of a secondary world.
The puzzle of how people can feel strong emotions about fictional things. It rests on premises that seem true but, on inspection, produce a contradiction.
Deliberately setting aside critical thinking and real-life expectations to enjoy a work of fiction. Coleridge coined the phrase.
