Describes events that both the characters in a story and its audience experience. In music, it means sound the characters can hear.
A music teaching method created by Shinichi Suzuki. It claims anyone who can learn a native language can learn music well in the right environment.
A system that gives each note of the scale a syllable, such as do, re and mi. Teachers use it to train the ear and sight-reading.
A glide from one pitch to another. On a piano it is stepped across the notes, while in other contexts it is a continuous, seamless slide.
Music and other art whose result comes partly from chance. In some pieces the order of the measures is left to be decided by throwing dice.
Scottish Highland art music of long compositions built on a melodic theme with elaborate variations. It is set apart from popular dances and marches.
A string instrument that sounds when a hand-cranked wheel rubs the strings. Most have drone strings that give a bagpipe-like steady pitch under the melody.
An electronic instrument played without touching it. One hand near an antenna controls pitch, and the other hand controls volume.
The herald's staff carried by Hermes, a short rod entwined by serpents and sometimes topped with wings. It also symbolizes commerce and negotiation.
The name of God in the Hebrew Bible, written YHWH. Observant Jews do not pronounce it and use a different term instead.
A Hebrew word meaning gods or godhood. Plural in form, it most often takes singular verbs in the Hebrew Bible and refers to a single deity.
One of the sacred names of God in Judaism, meaning my Lord.
A title Jews use to refer to God outside prayer, to avoid pronouncing God's name casually. Baruch HaShem is a popular expression meaning thank God.
The name of several Jewish prayers that recite verses from Isaiah and Ezekiel, taken from visions in which angels sing praises to God.
The principle in Jewish law that saving a life overrides almost any other religious rule. Most commandments yield when they would hinder rescue.
Repair, as in tikkun olam, the repairing of the world through acts of kindness and justice.
Loving kindness, whether between people or from God toward humanity. In Kabbalah it is also an attribute on the Tree of Life, tied to kindness and love.
Righteousness, fairness or justice.
A Hebrew word for righteousness, commonly used to mean charity. It is an ethical obligation that helps empower poor people to support themselves.
The body of Jewish religious law, derived from the Written and Oral Torah. It guides many aspects of daily life as well as worship.
Rabbinic teaching outside of law, found in the Talmud and Midrash. It gathers folklore, anecdotes and practical advice, and conveys moral or theological truths through allegory.

A method of studying the Talmud through intense textual analysis, used to explain differences between legal rulings or reconcile apparent contradictions. In English it can mean casuistic hairsplitting.
A Jewish ethical and educational movement from Lithuania, centered on educating oneself to act properly. It produced Musar literature on ethical and spiritual paths.
A Jewish concept of closeness to God. It can mean a deep, trance-like meditative state reached during prayer or Torah study, and is especially associated with Jewish mysticism.
A tune sung in groups in Ashkenazi Jewish tradition, often built on repeated syllables such as "bim-bim-bam" instead of formal lyrics. Some are prayers of lament, others joyful.
A commandment from God, to be performed as a religious duty. The word also means an individual act of human kindness in keeping with the law.
An accepted tradition or group of traditions in Judaism. A related concept, nusach, is the traditional ordering and forms of Jewish prayer.
The Hebrew name for the Holocaust, the genocide of European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators. Most murders were committed by mass shootings and in gas chambers.
A small town in Eastern Europe with a large Ashkenazi Jewish population, of a kind that existed before the Holocaust. Today the term also describes some Hasidic communities.
A Jewish way of life, especially of the Yiddish-speaking Jews of Eastern and Central Europe. It can also refer broadly to Judaism or specifically to Orthodox Judaism.
Gentiles, or non-Jews, a word used mainly by Jews and sometimes pejorative. How derogatory it is in modern English is a point of discussion in the Jewish community.
A population scattered outside its place of origin that still identifies with a homeland. It covers communities formed by voluntary migration and by forced displacement.
Immigration of Jews to the Land of Israel from the diaspora, the communities outside it. Making aliyah is one of the most basic tenets of Zionism.
Exile, the condition of Jews who live outside the Land of Israel. In the Hebrew Bible it names the fate of the tribes of Israel after conquest.
A Haredi Jewish anti-Zionist organization. Its members believe the exile must last until the Messiah comes, so they oppose Israel's existence. Even other Haredim consider its views fringe.
A rabbinical court, found in Israel and in many Jewish diaspora communities. Its rulings are based on Jewish law, but secular courts do not always recognize them.
A document in Jewish religious law that effects a divorce between a Jewish couple. It releases the woman from the marriage and lets her marry another.
A Jewish woman stuck in her marriage under Jewish law, classically because her husband went missing. It is used for a woman whose husband refuses her a divorce.
A group of Holocaust survivors who sought revenge for the murder of Jews. It failed to poison water mains, then poisoned bread for German prisoners of war.
A Buddhist practice for gaining insight. In the Theravada tradition it seeks insight into the true nature of reality, defined as impermanence, suffering and non-self.
Mindfulness, an essential part of Buddhist practice. It means keeping a lucid awareness of bodily and mental phenomena, to counter unwholesome states and develop wholesome ones.
Hindu texts of the remembered, written tradition, inspired by the Vedas. They generally have a named author and are considered less authoritative than śruti, the Vedic texts.
A large body of religious texts from ancient India, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism. Hindus regard them as revelations heard by ancient sages after intense meditation.
Sanskrit texts that move from the ritualism of the Veda to new religious ideas. The most recent addition to the Vedas, they deal with meditation and philosophy.
In Hindu metaphysics, the highest universal principle and ultimate reality of the universe. In the Upanishads it is the origin and cause of all that exists.
In Hinduism, the innermost essence of a living being, conceived as eternal and unchanging. Vedanta schools disagree on whether it is the same as Brahman, the ultimate reality.
A Hindu path to liberation through knowledge. A guru often helps the practitioner study, meditate and reflect on the nature of the Self.
Loving devotion in Indian religions, whether to a personal God or to an enlightened being such as a guru. The devotion is often deeply emotional.
In Hinduism, the appearance of a powerful deity or spirit on Earth, including in human form. The idea is most often associated with the god Vishnu.
In Mahayana Buddhism, the mind aimed at awakening through wisdom and compassion. Giving rise to it is what makes someone a bodhisattva, a being striving toward Buddhahood.
A rite of passage in some Native American cultures. A young person fasts alone in nature and prays for a vision that will help them find their purpose.
A low hut of natural materials, and the ceremony of prayer and healing held inside it. The ceremony is traditional to some Indigenous peoples of the Americas.
A gathering with dances held by Native American and First Nations communities to socialize and honor their cultures. Some Native Americans find its use for any meeting offensive.
The annual Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca. It is a one-time religious duty for Muslims who are physically and financially capable of making the journey.
An Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca that can be made at any time of year, unlike the Hajj, which falls on specific dates.
A customary Jewish atonement ritual that Ashkenazi Jews perform on Rosh Hashanah during the High Holy Days.
A customary atonement ritual practiced on the eve of Yom Kippur, in which money, or a chicken that is then slaughtered, is waved over a person's head.
A ritual purification in Islam, done by washing parts of the body in order. It is typically performed before prayer or reading the Quran.
The state of ritual purity in Islam needed before prayer.
A bath used for ritual immersion in Judaism, to achieve ritual purity. According to Jewish law, a community must build one even before a synagogue.
Shaving or cutting some of the hair on the scalp as a sign of religious devotion or humility. Many monks do it to renounce fashion.
A Christian rite of consecrated bread and wine, which Christians believe Jesus began at the Last Supper. Churches differ on how Christ is present.
A psychoactive brew made from a vine and a plant that contains the compound DMT. Indigenous cultures of the Amazon use it in traditional medicine and shamanism.
A psychoactive compound extracted from the iboga tree. It brings a visionary, dream-like phase. Its serious risks include toxicity to the heart.
A sage plant whose leaves can induce a dissociative state and hallucinations. Mazatec shamans use it for spiritual healing sessions.
Highly poisonous plants of the nightshade family with trumpet-shaped flowers. Taken internally, they can cause delirium and death.
A tree of northern South America and the Caribbean that people use in healing ceremonies and rituals. Competition between tribes over its seeds led them to cultivate it.
Echinopsis pachanoi is the species most often meant among several cacti that can contain the psychoactive compound mescaline.
A small, spineless cactus that contains the psychoactive compound mescaline. The Native American Church considers eating it a sacrament and uses it in all-night healing ceremonies.
A ritual drink of the early Vedic religion, made from the juice of a plant whose identity is now unknown and debated among scholars.
A Pacific Islands plant whose root makes a traditional ceremonial drink. Its psychoactive effects are comparable to alcohol's but without significant cognitive impairment.
A shrub of eastern and southern Africa whose leaves are chewed as a recreational stimulant. Chewing it brings greater sociability and mild euphoria.
A vine of Southeast Asia whose leaves flavor areca nut for chewing. The chew, called betel quid, is carcinogenic and contains a psychostimulant drug.
The leaf of a plant native to western South America. It contains cocaine and acts as a mild stimulant when chewed or drunk as tea.
A caffeinated tea that Native Americans of the Southeastern United States brewed from yaupon holly. They drank it in council meetings and used it in purification ceremonies.
The root-like mass of branching threads of a fungus. It absorbs nutrients from the environment and helps decompose plant material.
An association between a fungus and a plant, in which fungal threads and plant roots interconnect. Usually both partners benefit, but sometimes the fungus is a parasite.
A genus of fungi, most of them parasitic mainly on insects and other arthropods. Several kinds have long been used in Chinese medicine.
A hybrid colony of algae or cyanobacteria living among fungal filaments. It can look like a plant but is not one.
Small organisms from different groups whose single cells come together to form fruiting bodies that produce spores. Some have been used to simulate traffic networks.
An organism that lives inside a rock, in the pores between its mineral grains. Many live in places long considered inhospitable to life.
An organism that can live or even thrive in extreme environments, such as very high pressure or radiation. Most are microorganisms, mainly bacteria and archaea.
A layered rock formation built mainly by photosynthetic microorganisms. They produce adhesive compounds that cement sand into mats, which grow layer by layer.
The community of microorganisms that live together in a habitat. In mammals, the gut microbiome helps regulate the host's physiology.
A large cauldron-like hollow that forms when an eruption empties a magma chamber and the ground collapses into it. It is a type of sinkhole.
When two tectonic plates meet, the heavier one dives beneath the other and sinks into the mantle. Earthquakes are common there, and released fluids trigger volcanism.
A landscape formed by water dissolving soluble rock such as limestone. Drainage runs through sinkholes and caves underground, so the surface may have few rivers or lakes.
The boundary between Earth's crust and mantle, defined by a distinct change in the speed of seismic waves passing through rock of different density.
A rapid diversification of complex life early in the Cambrian period. The fossil record first shows practically every major animal group in this interval.
A mass extinction that killed all the non-avian dinosaurs and most other large land vertebrates. It is generally thought to result from a massive asteroid impact.
Sedimentary rock made of alternating layers of iron oxides and iron-poor chert. It is thought to record the oxygenation of Earth's oceans.
A fossil record of what an organism did, not of its body. Footprints and root cavities are examples.
An ancient group of lobe-finned fish that were thought extinct until living ones were fished off South Africa.
A living species that resembles relatives known only from the fossil record. Scientists deprecate the term because such species still evolve.
A situation in a game where no player could gain more by changing their own strategy while all the others keep theirs fixed.
An outcome where no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
A solution people tend to choose by default when they cannot communicate, in order to avoid coordination failure. It works because it stands out from its surroundings.
A strategy of cooperating first, then copying the opponent's previous move. In everyday English the phrase means equivalent retaliation.
A game where two hunters do better catching a stag together, but each can safely take a hare alone. People often compare it to climate agreements.
A game where each player can pay a small cost that helps everyone or wait for someone else to. If nobody does, everyone gets the worst outcome.
A player chooses one box or both, after a near-perfect predictor has already decided what they contain. It is still much debated in decision theory.
A prisoner or student is told that a hanging or test will come at an unexpected time. There is no consensus on its precise nature.
A coin-flipping game with an infinite expected payoff that still seems worth little. Expected value alone recommends a bet no real person would take.
A thought experiment showing a problem in expected utility maximization. An agent that weighs outcomes by probability ends up chasing vastly improbable rewards and falling into incoherence.
A choice problem where people's real choices contradict what expected utility theory predicts. People rarely decide consistently and rationally when they must decide at once.
A proof that no ranked voting rule meets the requirements of rational choice. One is that a choice between two options should not depend on a third.
Majority rule can go in circles. A majority may prefer A to B, B to C and C to A, even when no voter's own preferences contradict themselves.
Designing rules that produce good outcomes even when the designer does not know what players truly want. It works backward from the result to a game that delivers it.
A contract whose terms depend on an uncertain event outside the parties' control. Insurance and gambling are common examples.
A way to gain legal ownership of property by occupying it continuously without the owner's permission. It is sometimes called squatter's rights.
A legal procedure that asks a court to decide whether a detention or imprisonment is lawful. It protects people against arbitrary arrest.
A rule that lets a court stop someone from going back on their word, or from bringing a particular claim.
A contract clause that frees both parties when an extraordinary event beyond their control prevents performance. Most clauses only pause the duty while the event lasts.
A doctrine that lets a court infer negligence from an injury that does not ordinarily occur without negligence, with no direct evidence of what the defendant did.
The mental state of a defendant accused of a crime. In common law jurisdictions, most crimes require proof of it and of a guilty act before conviction.
A law that retroactively changes the legal consequences of actions committed before it was passed. It may criminalize something that was legal when done.
The common law principle that courts follow past decisions when deciding similar cases, which promotes consistency and predictability.
Reasoning about an ethical dilemma by drawing rules from one particular case and applying them to others. As a criticism, it means clever but unsound reasoning.
A model of evolution in which most new species form through slow, uniform change, so no clear line separates an ancestral species from its descendant.
A figure of speech that moves one word out of its natural place in a sentence.
Deliberately leaving the conjunctions out of a series of related clauses to quicken the rhythm.
A sentence in which conjunctions are repeated on purpose, usually to slow the pace and lend a solemn note.
Ending one sentence with a word and often building a climax by starting the next with the same word.
Reversing a grammatical structure in successive phrases or clauses without repeating words. Its close relative antimetabole repeats the words.
Repeating a sequence of words at the start of neighboring clauses to give them emphasis. Repeating words at the clauses' ends is called epistrophe.
A figure of speech in which successive phrases or sentences end with the same word or words. It is very emphatic because the emphasis falls on the last word.
Repeating words in successive clauses but in reverse order, as in "I know what I like, and I like what I know."
Making a point by stating a negative to affirm a positive. The phrase "not bad" can mean either mediocre or excellent, depending on intonation.
A figure of speech that uses a part of something to refer to the whole, or the reverse, as when boots stand for soldiers.
Referring to a concept by the name of something associated with it. A suit can stand for a business executive, since executives commonly wear business attire.
Describing one sense in terms of another, as in "a bright sound". It is a figure of speech, separate from the neuropsychological condition.
A figure of speech in which other words are inserted to split a phrase. More broadly, the term covers any change to a sentence's natural word order.
Repeating a word or phrase in different senses. It is a common type of pun and is often found in slogans.
Word play that exploits a word's multiple meanings, or similar-sounding words, for humorous or rhetorical effect. Puns are usually specific to a language or its culture.
Dividing a word into parts and inserting another word between them. More broadly, words slipped into the middle of a set phrase, such as a phrasal verb.
A sentence deliberately broken off and left unfinished, as in the threat "Get out, or else". The ending is left to the listener's imagination.
Candid speech, speaking freely. Even at personal risk, it carries an obligation to speak the truth for the common good.
A speech or piece of writing in praise of a person or thing. The word also names a smaller figure of speech that praises someone or something.
A formal defense of an opinion, position or action. An apology expresses regret, but an apologia sets out the rational grounds for a position.
Attacking the character or motives of the person making an argument instead of answering its substance.
Using an authority's opinion as evidence for a claim. It is not valid logical proof, yet sources disagree on how fallible the method is.
The obligation on one party in a dispute to give enough support for its position. Traditionally it rests on whoever makes the claim.
A scientific claim is falsifiable if some possible observation could contradict it. One black swan refutes "all swans are white," but no count of white swans proves it.
Available evidence can be too thin to settle which belief to hold. A known total spent on apples and oranges, with known prices, does not reveal the mix.
An argument against scientific realism. Past successful theories were found false, so there is no reason to think today's successful theories are approximately true.
An observation shaped by the observer's theoretical assumptions. It troubles the confirmation of theories, since the evidence may already assume the thesis it is meant to support.
The view that no single statement can be confirmed or refuted by a test on its own. Only a whole theory, with its background hypotheses, can.
Observing objects that are neither black nor ravens can formally make it more likely that all ravens are black, though intuitively the observations are unrelated.
A puzzle about which generalizations from experience are law-like. Nelson Goodman built it on constructed predicates, grue and bleen, that depend on time.
A category that reflects the real world, not just human interests. Chemical elements are the standard example. Philosophers disagree on whether such kinds exist apart from us.
A term that refers to the same thing in every possible world where it exists. Non-rigid terms may refer to different things in different worlds.
A complete, consistent way the world is or could have been. Philosophers dispute whether other possible worlds literally exist.
What makes a person at one time the same person as someone at another time. Philosophers look for conditions necessary and sufficient for that sameness.
A thought experiment about whether a ship is the same after all its parts are replaced. A second ship built from the old parts complicates it.
A paradox that comes from vague words such as "heap." Remove grains one at a time, and it is unclear when the heap stops being one.
Someone declares "I am lying." If they are lying, they are telling the truth, and if they are telling the truth, they are lying.
A contradiction in the set of all sets that are not members of themselves. It would belong to itself only if it did not.
A self-referential paradox. Name the smallest positive integer not definable in under a given number of letters, and that very sentence has just defined it in fewer.
The problem of telling, for any program and input, whether the program will finish or run forever. Turing proved no general algorithm can do it.
The claim that whatever can be calculated by paper-and-pencil methods can be computed by a Turing machine. It is widely accepted but cannot be formally proven.
Whether every problem with a quickly checkable answer can also be solved quickly. It is widely believed that some such problems are harder to solve than to check.
The hardest problems among those whose solutions can be verified quickly. A fast algorithm for one would give a fast algorithm for all of them.
The shortest route that visits each city on a list once and returns to the start. Warehouse picking routes are often modeled as variants of it.
Whether some true-or-false assignment to a formula's variables makes the whole formula true. The formula "a AND NOT b" works, but "a AND NOT a" cannot.
A function that turns data of any size into a fixed-size value. Hash tables use these values to find stored data in nearly constant time.
Cryptography that uses pairs of related keys, one public and one private. The public key can be shared openly, while the private key must stay secret.
A way for one party to convince another that a statement is true while revealing nothing beyond the fact that it is.
A mathematical scheme for verifying that a message came from a sender the recipient knows. Unlike a handwritten signature, it is mathematically bound to the message's content.
A way of sending messages so that only the sender and the intended recipients can read them. Not even the service provider can read them.
Encryption with a random key at least as long as the message, used only once. Used correctly, it is proven unbreakable, but key distribution limits its use.
A method for two strangers to agree on a shared secret key over an insecure channel. Before it, keys had to be carried by secure physical means.
A widely used public-key cryptosystem. Its public key is the product of large primes, and its security rests on how hard that product is to factor.
Public-key cryptography built on the algebra of elliptic curves. It gives security equal to older systems like RSA with smaller keys.
Encryption that exploits quantum-mechanical properties such as entanglement. Because reading data encoded in a quantum state changes it, an eavesdropper can be detected.
Hiding information inside another message or object so that its presence goes unnoticed. A sender might adjust some pixel colors in an innocuous image to encode letters.
An algorithm for encryption or decryption, usually depending on a key. A code instead replaces words or phrases using a codebook.
A cipher that shifts each letter a fixed number of places along the alphabet. It is easily broken and gives essentially no security today.
Encrypting text by shifting each letter by an amount set by the matching letter of a key. It long resisted attempts to break it.
A cipher machine whose rotors changed the encryption key with every letter typed. Germany used it in World War II, and the Allies exploited its messages as intelligence.
An English country estate that became the main Allied code-breaking center in World War II. Its team built Colossus, the world's first programmable digital electronic computer.
In a small group, two people sharing a birthday is more likely than not. It seems wrong, yet it holds because birthdays get compared across all possible pairs.
A probability puzzle based on a game show. After a contestant picks a door and the host reveals a goat behind another, switching wins more often than staying.
A paradox about choosing between two envelopes of money, one holding twice the other. Symmetry says switching is pointless, yet a simple expected-value calculation suggests it pays.
Using Bayes' theorem to revise the probability of a hypothesis as new evidence comes in. It is especially useful for analyzing a sequence of data.
A function that scores how well each statistical model describes a given data set. The parameter value that maximizes it is used as the estimate.
A bias from how individuals or data are chosen for analysis, so the association between exposure and outcome in the sample differs from the one among everyone eligible.
A statistical error from studying only what passed a selection process and ignoring what did not. Leaving out failed companies makes performance look better.
Two traits look negatively correlated because the sample excludes people who have neither. Among celebrities, looks and talent seem opposed, since people with neither do not become celebrities.
A trend that appears in several groups of data but disappears or reverses when the groups are combined. Accounting for confounding variables and causal relations can resolve it.
Moving an item from one group to another can raise the average of both groups, while the overall average stays the same.
Reading meaning into data that is essentially random. A man shoots at a barn, then paints a target around the tightest cluster of shots.
The expected remaining life of a non-perishable thing, like a technology or an idea, is proportional to its current age. It does not apply to human lifespans.
An incentive that backfires and makes the problem worse. In the Delhi story, a bounty on dead cobras led people to breed cobras for the income.
When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. A statistical regularity tends to collapse once people pressure it for control purposes.
The more a quantitative social indicator drives decisions, the more it attracts corruption pressure and distorts the social processes it was meant to monitor.
The principle that a fence, or a rule, should not be torn down until someone knows why it was built.
A bias of searching only where it is easiest to look, like a drunk who hunts for lost keys under a streetlight because the light is better there.
A bias in which someone with specialized knowledge assumes others share it. A professor may no longer remember how hard a new subject is for students.
A mental shortcut that relies on whatever examples come to mind first. If something is quickly recalled, it is assumed to be important.
Judging how likely something is by how closely it matches a prototype. A person in eccentric clothes reading poetry seems more likely to be a poet than an accountant.
Relying too heavily on the first number or piece of information met when making a judgment, so later estimates stay close to it.
Letting a cost already spent and unrecoverable shape a decision about the future. People do this with past spending on repairing a car or house.
A preference for keeping one's existing situation, so any change from the current baseline is seen as a loss or gain. Retirement plans and health choices show it.
People demand more to give up an object they own than they would pay to acquire it. That holds even if the item was only obtained minutes ago.
The tendency to perceive the same situation as worse when it is framed as a loss than as a gain. Losses are weighed more heavily than equivalent gains.
A model in which a reward loses value quickly over short delays and slowly over long ones. It leads people to make choices that are inconsistent over time.
The belief that an independent outcome that has come up less often than expected is more likely next. A gambler expects a four because fours have been rare.
The belief that an athlete on a streak is more likely to succeed again. Researchers dismissed it, but later studies found a small effect in some players.
A bias toward recent events over older ones. A jury, for instance, may give the most weight to the last closing argument it hears.
The tendency to seek out, interpret and recall information that supports what one already believes. A detective who picks a suspect early may seek only confirming evidence.
The tendency to see past events as more predictable than they were. It shows up in historians' accounts of battles and in trials over accidents.
A bias in which people with low ability in a specific area rate their ability too positively. Several explanations compete, and one holds it is largely a statistical effect.
A positive impression of a person or product in one area tends to improve opinion of it in another. Someone attractive and well groomed may be assumed to be good.
The tendency to believe one is being noticed more than one really is. It is strongest when someone does something atypical, such as a faux pas.
People are less likely to help a victim when other people are present. In groups, responsibility feels weaker, though recent research questions how robust the effect is.
The discomfort people feel when their actions, beliefs or values conflict. It motivates them to change a belief or explain the conflict away.
A bias in which people place a disproportionately high value on products they partly made. People in one study would pay more for furniture they assembled themselves.
A false memory shared by many people, who recall an event or detail in the same way although it did not happen that way.
Failing to retrieve a word from memory while feeling the word is about to come back. People often still recall its first letter or words that sound like it.
The tendency of adults over forty to remember events from their adolescence and early adulthood especially well.
The inability of adults to retrieve episodic memories, meaning memories of events, from their earliest years. Memories from early childhood are also often scarce or fragmented.
A memory error where something is credited to the wrong source, like news heard from a friend and later recalled as coming from the local news.
A condition in which a person remembers an abnormally large number of life experiences in vivid detail. They also spend much time thinking about the past.
The alleged ability to recall an image with high precision after seeing it only once. It is reported in a few children but generally not in adults.
A cognitive system of limited capacity that holds information temporarily, used for reasoning and decision-making. Some theorists separate it from short-term memory, which only stores information.
A memory technique that ties information to places in a familiar setting, such as rooms in a house. Recall comes from mentally retracing the path.
A flashcard technique that shows harder cards often and easier cards less often. It suits learners who must acquire many items and keep them in memory.
In Roman religion, the protective spirit of a place. Many altars across the western empire were dedicated to a particular one.
An unplanned trail worn into the ground by people or animals, usually along the shortest or easiest route. Later walkers tend to follow the visible track.
A religious boundary around Rome and the cities it controlled. Legally, Rome existed only within it, and everything beyond was simply territory.
The main north-south street (cardo) and east-west street (decumanus) of a Roman city or military camp.
A scale of proportions by Le Corbusier, based on the height of a man with his arm raised. It bridges the Imperial and metric systems.
An architectural style that shows bare materials, often unpainted concrete, and angular shapes instead of decoration. Critics often describe the buildings as cold.
A planning movement that promoted satellite communities around a central city, separated by green belts. Such a town would contain proportionate areas of housing, industry and agriculture.
A group of metropolitan areas perceived as one continuous urban area through shared transport and economy. The cities keep their individual identities.
An urban design movement that builds walkable neighborhoods with a wide range of housing and job types. It aims to address the problems of urban sprawl.
A design strategy using the built environment to steer behavior and exclude people from public space. Armrests on benches that stop people lying down are one example.
An artistic technique, most often painting, that tricks the viewer into seeing painted objects or spaces as real. The term is also used for analogous illusions in literature.
A genre of painting built from still life images of transitory items, which stand for the brevity of life and the certainty of death.
An artistic symbol that reminds viewers of the inevitability of death. The most common motif is a skull, and bones often accompany it.
A distorted projection that shows a recognizable image only from a specific vantage point or through a device. Artists have used it to hide images from a casual spectator.
A painting technique that softens the transition between colors so they blend without lines or borders, as in smoke. Leonardo used it in the Mona Lisa.
The use of strong contrasts between light and dark, usually across a whole composition. Artists also use it to give figures a sense of volume.
A genre of Japanese art, mostly woodblock prints, showing kabuki actors, beautiful women and landscapes. Hokusai's The Great Wave is among the best-known works of Japanese art.
The popularity and influence of Japanese art and design among Western European artists. Woodblock prints became a source of inspiration for many of them.
Walter Benjamin's term for the unique presence of an original artwork, tied to its time and place, which he argued fades when the work is mechanically reproduced.
In Roland Barthes's writing on photography, the detail in a picture that pricks the viewer personally. It differs from the studium, the general cultural interest a photograph holds.
The claim that no set has a size strictly between that of the integers and the real numbers. Standard set theory can neither prove nor disprove it.
A proof that some infinite sets cannot be matched one-to-one with the natural numbers. Such sets are called uncountable.
A sequence of numbers that measure the sizes of infinite sets. The smallest is the size of the natural numbers.
The study of mathematical knots, which are like knotted string but with the ends joined. A fundamental problem is deciding when two descriptions show the same knot.
A one-sided surface with no distinct inside or outside. In ordinary three-dimensional space it cannot be built without intersecting itself.
A surface made by joining the ends of a paper strip with a half-twist. It has only one side and a single boundary curve.
The complex numbers c for which repeatedly squaring and adding c, starting from zero, does not diverge to infinity. Its boundary is a fractal curve.
An attractor, meaning a set of states a system tends to evolve toward, whose shape is a complicated fractal.
A regular grid of cells in states such as on and off, updated step by step by a fixed rule based on each cell's neighborhood.
A zero-player game on a grid of live and dead cells, where the starting pattern alone determines how it evolves. It has no win condition.
A measure of how fast two very close trajectories of a changing system separate. A positive maximal one usually signals a chaotic system.
A result saying that a function will have at least one point it maps to itself, as long as the function meets certain conditions.
A property that makes a space behave in many ways like a finite set. On a compact space, a continuous real-valued function reaches its maximum and minimum.
The branch of mathematics that studies which properties of a shape survive stretching, twisting and bending without any tearing or gluing.
A branch of mathematics that uses abstract algebra to study topological spaces, sorting them by algebraic quantities that do not change when a space is deformed.
A shape that, near any point, looks like ordinary flat Euclidean space. A circle and a sphere are examples.
The locally shortest path between two points on a curved surface. On a spherical Earth, it runs along a great circle.
A function defined in pieces, each piece a polynomial. In computer graphics the word usually means a curve built the same way.
A division of a plane into one region per seed point, each holding the points closer to its seed than to any other.
Joining a set of points into triangles so that no point lies inside the circle through any triangle's corners. It tends to avoid sliver triangles.
The frequency whose period is twice the interval between samples. Signals below it are sampled free of the distortion known as aliasing.
A phenomenon in which a signal rebuilt from samples contains low frequencies that the original lacked. In digital images it shows up as moiré patterns.
An operation that turns a function into another that shows how strongly different frequencies are present in it. Like splitting a chord into its pitches.
A mathematical operation on two functions that produces a third. It expresses how the shape of one is modified by the other.
The average uncertainty in the outcome of a random variable. It sets an absolute limit on how well data from a source can be compressed without loss.
The length of the shortest computer program that outputs a given object, such as a piece of text. It measures the computational resources needed to specify it.
A sequence of binary digits that appears random to any algorithm. Standard probability theory cannot call one sequence more random than another.
Results showing that quantum mechanics cannot be reproduced by any theory where particles carry hidden properties and are influenced only by their immediate surroundings.
A thought experiment arguing that quantum theory gives an incomplete description of reality. In an entangled pair, measuring one particle's position would predict the other's.
An interpretation of quantum mechanics in which the wave function never collapses. Instead, all possible outcomes of a measurement are physically realized in different worlds.
The loss of quantum coherence, generally as a system loses information to its environment. It is studied to understand how quantum systems come to behave classically.
Focusing attention on one sound and screening out the rest, as when a partygoer follows a single conversation in a noisy room.
Failing to notice a change in something seen. Observers often miss major differences added to an image as it flickers off and on.
Failing to see an unexpected object in plain sight because attention is elsewhere. One study had a person in a gorilla costume walk through a visual task.
Feeling pain or other sensations in a limb that has been amputated. It is one of the most common aftereffects of limb loss.
An impaired ability to recognize familiar faces, even one's own, while other vision stays intact. It can follow brain damage or be present from birth.
A disorder in which a patient cannot perceive motion but sees stationary objects normally. Milder cases show motion as separate frames, like a cinema reel.
A vision condition, usually present from birth, whose main symptom is monochromacy, seeing in a single shade. It also brings poor sharpness of sight.
A learning disorder that makes it hard to understand numbers and learn arithmetic. It does not reflect a general deficit in cognitive abilities.
Perceiving surfaces and objects by actively exploring them by touch. The inability to do so is called astereognosis.
The sense of the body's own movement, force and position. It relies on sensory receptors in muscles, tendons and joints.
The senses that report on the internal state of the body. The most commonly studied is the sense of the heartbeat.
Difficulty processing or describing one's own emotions. It is often associated with difficulties in attachment and in relationships with others.
Reduced motivation or ability to experience pleasure. Depressive disorders and some other conditions include it as a component.
Loss of hope and sense of meaning in the face of prolonged hardship, with a feeling of being unable to cope.
Exhaustion, distance from one's job and reduced efficacy caused by chronic workplace stress. The WHO does not recognize it as a medical or psychiatric condition.
Traumatic stress from repeated exposure to traumatized people in a helping or protecting profession. Family members caring for someone chronically ill may also experience it.
A traumatic experience that follows witnessing or taking part in an act seen as a moral transgression. It brings guilt or shame and moral disorientation.
A disputed idea from pop psychology that hostages tend to form a psychological bond with their captors. Psychologists generally consider the evidence dubious or nonexistent.
Captors developing sympathy for their hostages. It runs in the opposite direction from Stockholm syndrome, where hostages bond with captors.
A mental disorder in which a person imitates symptoms of illness to get attention, sympathy or care. The person acts deliberately but may not know why.
A caregiver makes another person, usually their child, appear ill, for example by altering test samples. It is thought to be driven by a desire for sympathy or attention.
A proposed condition in which an expectant parent who is not pregnant gets symptoms like morning nausea and weight gain. Its cause is debated between psychosomatic and hormonal explanations.
A Korean illness that arises when people cannot confront their anger over conditions they see as unfair. The name points to the cause of the illness, rather than its symptoms.
A cultural illness among Latin American peoples, often called fright sickness, in which the soul is thought to leave the body after a sudden scare.
A delusional belief that one's sex organs are retracting and will disappear, though the genitals have not really changed. Mass outbreaks have occurred in Africa, Asia and Europe.
An episode of sudden mass assault against people or objects after a period of brooding. It comes from the Malay world and gave English the phrase running amok.
A reaction described among Inuit, especially women, who may act irrationally or dangerously and then forget the event. Some recent studies question whether it exists at all.
An intense craving for human flesh and fear of becoming a cannibal, named for the wendigo, an evil spirit in Algonquian folklore.
A condition in South Asia in which men report premature ejaculation or impotence and believe they are passing semen in their urine. It has no known organic cause.
A Japanese syndrome of intense fear of displeasing or embarrassing others through one's body or appearance, such as blushing or body odor.
Adolescents or adults who withdraw from social life, shutting themselves in at home and often in one room. It is not a formal diagnosis, but it can co-occur with depression.
A person who has no job and is not in school or training, whether or not they are looking for work. The label frequently refers to young people.
A Japanese word for one's hometown or native place.
The Japanese art of mending broken pottery with lacquer mixed with powdered gold. As a philosophy, it treats breakage and repair as part of an object's history.
A Japanese aesthetic of simple, subtle and unobtrusive beauty. A shibui object looks simple overall but includes subtle details, so one does not tire of it.
A Japanese ideal of subdued style that hides the effort behind it at first glance. It is thought to have begun among Edo's merchants.
A Japanese concept of negative space, the gap or pause between things.
An ancient Japanese aesthetic ideal of profound grace and subtlety. It belongs to a set with wabi and sabi.
A noun form of shibui, the Japanese aesthetic of subdued beauty with economy of form, line and effort.
A Japanese phrase of regret over waste, also used to say one does not deserve something because it is too good.
A word meaning lack or without that is a key term in East Asian philosophical and religious traditions, such as Buddhism and Taoism.
The moral code of the samurai, covering their attitudes, behavior and lifestyle. It is loosely analogous to European chivalry but differs in some major ways.
A ritualized practice of making and serving tea in East Asia. At its simplest, it is a formal way of making tea, refined to give the best taste.
The Japanese art of flower arrangement. It is counted among the classical Japanese arts of refinement, along with incense appreciation and tea.
The Japanese art of growing and shaping miniature trees in containers. Pruning and grafting keep the tree small while it mimics the shape of a mature one.
The art of folding a flat square sheet of paper into a finished sculpture, generally without cuts or glue. The best-known model is the paper crane.
A short Japanese poem, traditionally with a cutting word and a seasonal reference. It began as the opening part of renga, a larger genre of Japanese poetry.
A short Japanese poem built like haiku but about human foibles rather than nature, and often cynical or darkly humorous. Unlike haiku, it has no cutting word.
A short poem form and one of the major genres of classical Japanese literature.
A Japanese form of collaborative poetry in which several poets take turns, each stanza linked to the one before. It later gave rise to haiku.
A poem of spiritual and romantic love, often about the pain of separation from the beloved. Its lines are relatively independent, but linked by theme, meter and rhyme.
A fixed verse form in which the words ending the lines of the first stanza return as line endings in the later stanzas, rotated in a set pattern.
A fixed poetic form with two refrains and two repeating rhymes. It has been noted as a form that frequently treats obsessions.
A poetic form derived from the Malay pantun berkait, a series of interwoven four-line stanzas.
A class of poetic forms with a five-line pattern. The word once described any five-line poem and now refers to forms with specific rules.
A rhetorical device that raises a subject by denying it, as in "I'm not going to say that I told you so."
Exaggeration used as a figure of speech, usually not meant literally, to emphasize a point or stir strong feelings.
A figure of speech that deliberately understates something, so that it seems smaller or less important than it is.
A figure of speech that stretches exaggeration so far that it implies complete impossibility, like a beard growing in the palm of a hand.
A figure of speech in which a speaker breaks off to address an absent person or an object as if it were present.
A rhetorical device in which something non-human speaks, or is spoken to, as if human. In Paradise Lost, Milton gives voice to Sin and Death.
A figure of speech where a modifier attaches grammatically to a word other than the one it describes in meaning. It often makes an inanimate noun seem personified.
Swapping a phrase and its modifier for two phrases joined by and, for emphasis. A long siege becomes length of time and siege.
Using one word to govern two or more others, as in rolling lightning and thunder, where rolling applies to both nouns.
A zeugma whose one word takes a different sense with each phrase. She opened the door and her heart to the stray kitten.
Purging thoughts and emotions by expressing them. In drama, it usually means arousing negative emotion in an audience, who then expel it and feel happier.
Representing aspects of the real world, especially human actions, in literature and art. Plato set it against diegesis, or narrative.
The moment in a play or story when a character makes a critical discovery. In tragedy, it is the hero's sudden awareness of the real situation.
A reversal of circumstances, or turning point, in a work of literature.
The weakness that leads a tragic character to a downfall. Some critics read it as only a random accident or mistake that implies no blame.
Extreme pride or dangerous overconfidence, often joined with arrogance. It tends to go with losing touch with reality and overrating one's own competence.
In ancient Greek myth, the goddess who personified retribution for hubris, which is arrogance before the gods.
An intense exchange where a Buddhist student and teacher test their understanding. It resembles a debate with questions and answers that seem illogical to outsiders.
An intensive Zen meditation retreat in which people devote themselves almost exclusively to sitting meditation, with short breaks for rest and meals.
A private meeting between a Zen student and the teacher, in which the student presents their practice and receives direction.
An Indian idea with several meanings depending on doctrine. In Mahayana Buddhism, it is the tenet that all things are empty of intrinsic existence.
A school of Buddhist philosophy founded by Nagarjuna. It holds that all phenomena lack any fixed essence, and that emptiness is itself empty.
A Buddhist tradition studying cognition, perception and consciousness through meditation and reasoning. Its main theory, mere representation, has several interpretations, including idealism.
The Buddhist doctrine that a Buddha has three bodies, or ways of being, which are modes of a single state of Buddhahood.
An esoteric yogic tradition from India that views the body as divine and uses mantras. The word also names a set of texts.
A sacred sound, syllable, word or phrase that practitioners believe holds religious or spiritual power. Repeating one in meditation is called japa.
A symbolic or ritual gesture or pose in Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism. Most are made with the hands and fingers.
A geometrical diagram from the Tantric traditions of Indian religions, used for the worship of deities and as an aid in meditation.
A geometric arrangement of symbols from Indian religions, used to focus attention and as an aid to meditation. In Buddhism it is a map of deities.
A domed Buddhist structure that holds sacred relics. People walk clockwise around it as a devotional practice and visit it on pilgrimage.
In Indian traditions, an aphorism or collection of aphorisms in the form of a manual. Buddhist sutras are canonical scriptures, many recording the Buddha's teachings.
A Buddhist scripture collection divided into three parts. Vinaya covers monastic rule, Sutra the teachings of the Buddha, and Abhidharma more systematic and scholastic works.
The Theravada school's systematic organization of its understanding of the highest Buddhist teachings. One scholar calls it a philosophy, a psychology and an ethics at once.
The five aggregates of clinging in Buddhism, from form and sensation to mental activity and consciousness. Suffering arises when one clings to them.
In Buddhism, a mental state that clouds the mind and leads to unwholesome action, such as anger or jealousy. Ignorance, attachment and aversion are the three roots.
A ruthless brigand who transforms after converting to Buddhism and becomes a monk. Buddhists see his story as a lesson that anyone can change.
In Buddhism, a person who has reached or is striving toward awakening. Often it means one who delays their own nirvana to help others reach Buddhahood.
In Buddhism, one who has gained insight into the nature of existence and is liberated from rebirth. How it is understood has changed over the centuries.
A word for a person who has attained the highest religious goal. The Buddha used it of himself, and its precise original meaning is uncertain.
The innate potential of all sentient beings to become a Buddha, or the belief that they already hold a pure Buddha-essence. Its meanings sometimes conflict.
A bodhisattva of great compassion, shown in many forms across Buddhist cultures. One female form is a divine mother in a white robe.
A type of goddess in Hinduism and Buddhism. Early Hindu texts use the word for flesh-eating demonesses, Tibetan Buddhism for fierce embodiments of enlightened energy.
A category of wrathful deities in Vajrayana Buddhism, enlightened beings who take on a fierce look to benefit others. They also appear as meditational deities in tantric practice.
A deity shared by Hinduism and Buddhism. In Buddhism he is a wrathful protector of the Dharma, in Hinduism a fierce form of Shiva.
A mentor, guide or master of a field of knowledge. In Indian traditions a guru is more than a teacher and is a figure the disciple reveres.
A chain of teachers and students through which a teaching is handed down from one generation to the next.
One of the three bodies of a Buddha in Mahayana Buddhism. It is the unmanifested aspect that Buddhas arise out of and return to.
A Buddhist term often translated as Thusness or Suchness. It is the essential nature of all existence and is free from dualistic thinking.
A Buddhist who reaches liberation alone, without teachers or guides, and does not teach others. Such a person leaves no community behind.
A practitioner of yoga and tantra who attained psychic and spiritual powers. Mahasiddhas are identified as founders of Vajrayana traditions such as Dzogchen and Mahamudra.
Teachings seen as the culmination of Tibetan Buddhist practice, centered on realizing the mind as it is.
A tradition of Tibetan teachings aimed at discovering and remaining in the ultimate ground of existence. Practice aims to integrate all experiences with awareness of one's true nature.
A tantric practice found in Hinduism and Buddhism, described as transferring consciousness at death. It is also called the practice of conscious dying.
A Tibetan text, known in the West as The Tibetan Book of the Dead, meant to guide a person through the experiences consciousness has after death.
A group of supernatural beings in Indian religions who possess magical powers. In Hinduism they attend Shiva and are considered demigods.
In Buddhism, any malicious force that hinders enlightenment. In the story of Siddhartha's awakening, Mara tries to seduce him with an army and beautiful maidens.
A class of powerful beings related to the Deva in Indian religions. In later Vedic texts the malevolent ones compete against the Deva as enemies of the gods.
A hungry ghost, a being that suffers extreme hunger and thirst in Hindu and Buddhist belief. Pretas are believed to have been deceitful or greedy people.
The realm of hell in Indian religions, a place of torment where hellish beings are said to reside.
A god or celestial being in Hinduism and Buddhism.
The realm of Brahma, the creator god in Hindu belief. Its inhabitants are described as never again knowing death.
A long period of time in Hindu and Buddhist cosmology, generally the span between the creation and recreation of a world.
An age of time in Hinduism. In later texts it usually means a cycle of world ages.
A cyclic period of time in Hindu cosmology, the age of a Manu, the progenitor of mankind.
In Hindu eschatology, the dissolution of the entire universe at the end of a vast age. The word also covers the dissolution of one's self through union with Brahman.
Deep sleep, which Indian philosophy treats as a state of consciousness. The Mandukya Upanishad counts it as the third part of consciousness.
The true self beyond the three ordinary states of consciousness, which are waking, dreaming and dreamless deep sleep. Several Upanishads postulate it.
Spontaneous, liberating knowledge in Indian Tantric and Tibetan Buddhist traditions.
Illusion, in Indian philosophies, with meanings that depend on the school. In Advaita Vedanta it is the force that makes the phenomenal world seem real.
In Hindu and Buddhist thought, ignorance or incorrect knowledge of the phenomenal world. Buddhism treats it as the root cause of suffering.
Deliberation in Indian philosophy, the faculty of telling the Real, Brahman, from the unreal.
In Theosophy, a believed compendium of all events, thoughts, words and emotions that have occurred or will occur. Some theosophists place it on a non-physical plane.
A phrase from the Chandogya Upanishad, translated 'That Thou Art' or 'You are that'. Advaita Vedanta reads it as saying the self is no different from Brahman.
A phrase from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, translated 'I am Brahman'. Advaita Vedanta reads such sayings as showing the self is no different from Brahman.
An analytical meditation from the Upanishads, 'not this, not that', that helps a person understand Brahman by negating everything that is not Brahman. The goal is non-dual awareness.
A Sanskrit mantra, 'I am that', often repeated in time with the breath in Hindu meditation.
The shift in a wave's frequency seen by an observer moving relative to its source. A passing vehicle sounds higher as it approaches and lower as it recedes.
The pulsing in volume heard when two tones of slightly different pitch sound together. Its rate equals the difference between the two frequencies.
A room built to stop echoes and reflections of sound or radio waves. A person inside hears only direct sound, as if outdoors in an open field.
Sound with a frequency too low for humans to hear. People use it to monitor earthquakes and volcanoes.
The sound pressure level at each frequency at which a listener hears pure steady tones as equally loud. The Fletcher-Munson curves are one of many sets of them.
A wave that oscillates in time but whose peaks do not move in space. The points of least amplitude are called nodes and those of greatest amplitude antinodes.
How long sound lingers in a room, as reflections off surfaces fade after its source stops. Architects design spaces to have a particular reverberation time for their use.
The resonances of a room, set off by a sound source such as a loudspeaker. They are one of the biggest obstacles to accurate sound reproduction.
The amount something must change before a difference can be noticed, at least half the time.
Air forced in and out of a cavity with a neck vibrates at a natural frequency. Blowing across the top of a bottle produces a resonant tone.
Animals send out calls and listen to the echoes to locate and identify nearby objects. Some bats and toothed whales navigate and hunt this way.
A filter that adds a delayed copy of a signal to itself. The result is a comb shaped row of evenly spaced notches and peaks.
A random signal with equal intensity across frequencies. Heard as sound, it is a hiss.
An apparent pulsing heard when each ear receives a pure tone of slightly different frequency.
A howl that builds when a loudspeaker's sound is picked up by a microphone and amplified again. Rock guitarists sometimes create it to get different sounds.
An area that sound waves fail to reach because of hills, buildings or wind currents.
Peaks in Earth's electromagnetic field at very low frequencies, excited by lightning in the cavity between the ground and the ionosphere.
When the presence of one sound changes how another sound is perceived. It can work across frequencies or across time.
A system's response to a change from its steady state. It is temporary and dies out with time.
When two waves are out of phase, their combination has lower amplitude and they weaken each other.
Designing a street so that people can be seen, which makes offenders feel a higher risk of being caught.
An urban planning model that handles floods with parks, wetlands and permeable ground that capture and absorb stormwater, not only drains.
Building and city design that adds natural features, such as sunlight, to improve people's health and well-being.
The glow after two neutron stars, or a neutron star and a black hole, collide. It is powered by radioactive decay and stays visible for weeks and months.
A brief pulse of radio waves from a high-energy process that is not yet understood. Magnetars are at least one source.
A neutron star with an extremely powerful magnetic field. The decay of that field powers high-energy radiation such as X-rays and gamma rays.
A galaxy core firing a jet of matter at nearly the speed of light almost straight at the observer. That alignment makes it look much brighter.
A star pulled apart by a supermassive black hole's tidal force when it passes too close. The debris forms a disk that fades over months or years.
A gas giant like Jupiter, but with a very short orbital period. Their large, rapid tug on their stars' motion makes them the easiest planets to detect.
An object with a planet's mass that is bound to no star. Some were ejected from the system where they formed, others formed alone.
A rare, hot star whose spectrum shows broad emission lines of ionized helium. Classic ones are massive stars that have lost their outer hydrogen.
Stars that orbit very close to the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way.
A black hole heavier than a stellar black hole but lighter than a supermassive one. Candidates have been found in the Milky Way and nearby galaxies.
A glowing shell of gas thrown off by a red giant star late in its life. The name is a misnomer, since it is unrelated to planets.
How an issue is presented shapes how people perceive it. Choosing fetus versus baby makes the same facts read differently.
Exposure to one stimulus influencing the response to a later one, without conscious intention. Many landmark studies of the effect failed to replicate.
Putting a lower value on money the later it arrives. In finance, a debtor pays a charge for the right to delay a payment.
A self-control strategy of restricting the choices available to oneself in the future. People use it when they predict that their preferences will change.
Taking a costly, visible action to show others a quality they cannot observe directly, such as a degree that signals ability to employers.
People copying the choices of the crowd, as when many investors buy the same asset because others do.
Searching through options until one is acceptable, without necessarily trying to find the best. Simon used it to explain decisions where an optimal solution cannot be determined.
Overweighting the present and neglecting long-term consequences when deciding. Saving too little is an example.
The property by which something stands out. A loud noise in an otherwise quiet environment is salient and draws attention.
The fact that resources are finite, so only limited amounts of any good can be produced. It plays a key role in economic theory.
A design of the decision environment that influences behavior, in contrast to education or enforcement. Skeptics think some nudges work well and others barely at all.
A social norm of responding to another person's action with a similar one. It typically results in rewarding positive actions and punishing negative ones.
A decision made freely to bind oneself in the future. Ulysses had himself tied to a mast so he could hear the Sirens without jumping into the sea.
A theory of how people actually judge losses and gains, which they weigh unequally. It departs from expected utility theory, which models perfectly rational agents.
How people divide money into mental accounts, such as savings or expense categories. A person may stop eating out when that budget is spent but keep buying groceries.
Mistaking money's face value for what it can actually buy. People tend to call a pay cut with stable prices unfair but a raise below inflation fair.
Adding a worse third option can change which of the other two people prefer. The decoy loses outright to one and only partly to the other.
Winnings that a gambler treats as the casino's, and so risks more freely than money from their own pocket.
A preference for known risks over unknown ones. People prefer betting on an urn with a known mix of red and black balls over one with an unknown mix.
Underestimating how long one's own tasks will take, even when similar past tasks ran long. Outside observers tend to guess too high.
A species with a far larger effect on its environment than its abundance would suggest. Remove it and the ecosystem can change dramatically.
An indirect effect that runs through a food web when one level is suppressed. Remove the top predators and their prey multiply and overexploit the plants below.
Competing species coexisting by occupying different niches, meaning different conditions and ways of using resources. If niches overlap, the better competitor should eliminate the other.
A model that predicts how an animal behaves when searching for food. It assumes natural selection favors the pattern that nets the most energy.
Differences between similar species grow larger where their ranges overlap and shrink where they do not. Competition for a limited resource, such as food, drives the change.
A set of separate populations of one species that interact. Any one may die out, yet migrants from another can recolonize the habitat it leaves empty.
The pattern that species richness rises from the poles toward the tropics, seen in many land and sea organisms. Ecologists have not agreed on why.
One species killing and sometimes eating a competitor of another species. It can run one way or both ways between the two.
Growth of an organism in response to light, most often seen in plants. Most shoots grow toward light, though some vine tips grow away and climb.
A plant's growth in response to gravity. Roots grow downward and stems upward, as a potted plant laid on its side shows.
The way leaves are arranged on a plant stem. Its spirals form a distinctive class of patterns in nature.
Dating wood by its tree rings, to the exact year each ring formed. Each ring marks one year, so rings also hold clues to past climate.
The bulk of the functional substance in an animal organ such as the brain or lungs. In botany it names some layers in the leaf's cross-section.
Plant tissue that gives the main structural support. Its cells have thick, reinforced walls and often die when mature.
Water-soluble plant pigments that shift from red to blue or black as acidity changes. Blueberries are rich in them, and they produce some colors of autumn leaves.
The plant tissue that carries water and some nutrients up from the roots to the stems and leaves.
A layer of plant tissue that supplies new cells for growth. In woody plants its divisions thicken the stem.
A runner, a horizontal connection between parts of an organism. In animals, stolons are typically external skeletons.
A naturally occurring organic compound that contains at least one nitrogen atom. Caffeine and nicotine are examples, and nearly all alkaloids taste bitter.
Seed plant with a stout trunk and a crown of stiff, feather-shaped leaves. It resembles a palm or fern but is not closely related to either.
A plant whose seeds are not enclosed in an ovary, as flowering plants' are. Conifers such as pines are the largest living group.
A salt-tolerant plant that grows in salty soils and waters such as seashores. Most other plants are damaged fairly easily by high salinity.
Holding seeds on the plant until an environmental trigger, most often fire, releases them. The word also describes flowering later in the season than related species.
A desert plant of Angola and Namibia whose leaves grow from a large woody stem throughout its life. It is one of the longest-living plants on Earth.
Compounds an organism makes that are not directly needed for its normal growth or reproduction. In plants they often play a role in defense against herbivores.
A form of photosynthesis in some plants adapted to dry conditions. They keep their pores shut by day and take in carbon dioxide at night.
A ring or arc of mushrooms that occurs naturally above a fungus growing underground. Folklore links rings to witches and the Devil, or to good fortune.
A carnivorous plant whose leaves clamp shut on insects like jaws. It closes fully only if a second hair is touched soon after the first.
A map projection that draws steady compass courses as straight lines, which made it standard for navigation. It inflates lands such as Greenland that lie far from the equator.
A rectangular map projection that shows areas in true proportion but distorts most shapes. It became the center of a controversy about the politics of map design.
An early world map that shows the Afro-Eurasian landmass as a circle divided into three parts by a T-shaped combination of seas and rivers. Its origin is contested.
Regions that have not been mapped or documented. Some English maps may show Parts Unknown.
A map that shades areas, such as countries or counties, by a summary value like population density.
A line on a map joining points of equal height above sea level or another set level. Lines close together mean a steep slope.
A line on a chart of the sea floor that joins points of equal depth. Nested closed loops can show a trench or an underwater mountain.
The northernmost circle of latitude where the Sun can be directly overhead on the June solstice. Its position drifts as Earth's tilt changes.
The geographical reference line that passes through the Royal Observatory in London. It was the international standard prime meridian, used worldwide for timekeeping and navigation.
Colors placed between a map's contour lines to show elevation, often as graduated bands of color. Water depth can be shown with a similar method.
A curve joining points that share the same value. On a topographic map, isolines of elevation show valleys and hills, and how steep slopes are.
A heart-shaped kind of map projection. The Werner projection is one, with correct distances along each parallel and the central meridian.
A world map projection that shows the entire world at once. It was made as a compromise in showing a whole globe as a flat image.
A reference frame that lets a place on Earth be given as exact coordinates. Between local datums, the same coordinates can point kilometers apart.
The circle of latitude dividing Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Noon sunlight is nearly overhead there, so daytime temperature stays stable all year.
A map projection that preserves angles locally, so small shapes keep their form but sizes may change.
A name for a place or people used mainly outside the community concerned. Germany is one, for the country whose own name is Deutschland.
A self-chosen name by which a people, place or language is known to its own community. Deutschland is the endonym of the country English calls Germany.
A line on a weather map joining points of equal atmospheric pressure.
The practice of navigating a ship or aircraft along a great circle, which gives the shortest distance between two points on the globe.
A reaction between amino acids and sugars that gives browned food its flavor. Seared steaks and toasted marshmallows owe their taste to it.
The property of some elements to exist in different forms, with atoms bonded in different ways. Diamond and graphite are both carbon.
A mixture that melts at a lower temperature than its ingredients do alone. Eutectic alloys are useful for soldering.
A substance above its critical point, where liquid and gas are no longer distinct. It dissolves materials like a liquid and seeps through porous solids like a gas.
A reaction between a conjugated diene and a substituted alkene that forms a six-membered ring. It is widely used to build complex natural products and new materials.
A reaction whose product also acts as a catalyst for that same reaction. A whole set of reactions can do this together and become self-sustaining.
Turning an optically active compound into an equal mix of its two mirror-image forms. This matters in pharmacology, where the forms can differ in effect.
A porous, ultralight solid made by replacing the liquid in a gel with gas. Silica aerogels feel like fragile styrofoam.
Rings or bands that form in a gel when two soluble substances react to make a weakly soluble salt. How they form is still unclear.
Light given off as a result of a chemical reaction. A light stick glows this way, and in living organisms it is called bioluminescence.
A structure that is ordered but not periodic. A shifted copy of its pattern never matches the original exactly.
A pyrotechnic mixture of metal powder and metal oxide that gives brief bursts of intense heat. It is used mainly to weld railway tracks together.
A method for making solid materials from small molecules. In solution they become a colloidal sol, which forms a connected network called a gel.
A magnetic state in which atomic spins freeze in place without a regular pattern. In a ferromagnet, by contrast, they all align in the same direction.
A reaction that turns aromatic rings into cyclohexadienes using an alkali metal in liquid ammonia. Unlike catalytic hydrogenation, it stops before a full cyclohexane ring.
A light absorber that alters the course of a photochemical reaction. It passes the energy to neighboring molecules and stays chemically intact.
The bonding of atoms of the same element into a chain. The chain can have free ends, or close into a ring.
Organic molecules that form spontaneously on a surface and settle into a single layer. Often the head of each molecule anchors it to the surface.
Combustion that starts by self-heating inside a material, which accelerates until it ignites. Improper storage of coal, cotton or hay is the main cause.
A class of reactions that make a nonlinear chemical oscillator. They show that chemical reactions need not be dominated by equilibrium behavior.
A film editing effect in which two shots in sequence give viewers more meaning than either does alone.
Set design, lighting, actors and everything else in front of the camera. It lets a director convey messages through what is placed in the scene.
The aesthetic pleasure of looking at an object or a person. In sexuality, it names the sexual pleasure of looking at erotic things.
The chronological sequence of events within a story's world. Its counterpart, the syuzhet, is the order in which they are presented.
An object, device or event the plot depends on, but that is unimportant in its own right. It is common in thrillers and other films.
A technique that squeezes a widescreen image horizontally with cylindrical lenses to fit narrower film. Projection uses a matching lens to expand it again.
Text edited into the midst of a film's action, more commonly known as a title card. Some carry character dialogue and others give related descriptive material.
A French art film movement that rejected traditional filmmaking conventions in favor of experimentation. Its filmmakers explored new approaches to editing, visual style, and narrative.
A documentary style that combines improvisation with the camera to reveal truth. Many see a paradox in hiding the camera while still interfering in what it records.
A film editing technique that sequences many short shots to condense time, space and information. In French, the word just means editing.
The way film editing, especially shot and reverse shot, draws viewers into a story by placing them in a character's point of view.
Everyday sound effects, like footsteps or breaking glass, recreated and added to a film after shooting. The best of it goes unnoticed by the audience.
A postwar Italian film movement about the everyday struggles of the poor and working class. Films were shot on location and often used non-professional actors.
A Danish filmmaking movement whose manifesto set rules that excluded elaborate special effects and technology. It was supposedly meant to take power back for directors.
An animation technique where animators trace over live-action footage, frame by frame, to produce realistic motion.
A single continuous take that moves through several places and often follows a character. It differs from a long take, which stays in one setting.
A German film style that uses distorted sets, harsh shadows and exaggerated acting to show inner states. The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari is the classic example.
A pre-film animation device, a cylinder that produces the illusion of motion by showing a sequence of drawings or photographs of a movement.
The study of how audiences watch, interpret and respond to films.
Showing a widescreen film on a narrower screen at its full width, with black bars above and below the picture.
Fast, narrow air currents in the atmosphere, mostly blowing from west to east around the globe. Airlines use them to shorten some flights.
A large region of cold, rotating air around each of Earth's poles. The term covers two distinct phenomena at different heights.
A climate pattern of shifting winds and sea temperatures over the tropical Pacific. Its warm phase is El Niño and its cool phase La Niña.
A tropical air loop that rises at the equator, flows poleward, sinks in the subtropics and returns along the surface. Many deserts lie beneath its sinking air.
A dry, relatively warm wind that descends the sheltered side of a mountain range after the air has dropped most of its moisture on windward slopes.
A streak of rain or snow that evaporates before reaching the ground. It is common in deserts.
A seasonal reversing wind with matching changes in rainfall. The word now usually means the rainy phase of that pattern.
A dense, towering cloud that builds upward on powerful rising air currents. When it causes a thunderstorm, it may be called a thunderhead.
A widespread, long-lived storm of straight-line winds, tied to a fast-moving cluster of severe thunderstorms. Its winds can reach hurricane force.
