A region of rotating air that radar usually spots inside a thunderstorm. Intense tornadoes form within it, though it is much larger than any tornado.
A narrow corridor of concentrated moisture in the atmosphere. The best-known kind, the Pineapple Express, carries warm vapor from near Hawaii toward western North America.
A storm cloud that forms above a heat source such as a wildfire. Its extreme winds and lightning can greatly increase how fast the fire spreads.
A bright spot beside the Sun, caused by sunlight bending through ice crystals in the air. They are most conspicuous when the Sun is near the horizon.
A pattern of lumpy pouches hanging under the base of a cloud. The cloud is usually a raincloud, and the pouches form where cold air sinks into pockets.
An intense dust storm. Cold air rushing down from a thunderstorm creates high winds at the surface that lift dust into the air.
A small, strong downward gust of wind from a storm that spreads outward in straight lines at the ground. It can endanger aircraft during landing.
Moving air and water follow curved paths across Earth because the planet rotates. They bend right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern.
A traveling pattern of heavier and lighter tropical rainfall that moves eastward over the Indian and Pacific oceans. A wet phase is followed by a dry one.
A line-shaped cloud of ice crystals that forms when an aircraft's exhaust meets very cold air. Some that persist contribute to climate change.
Faint clouds of ice crystals in the upper atmosphere, visible only in twilight, when they still catch sunlight while the ground below is in shadow.
A property of systems that tune themselves toward the critical point of a phase transition, with no need to set conditions to a precise value.
A transition zone between order and disorder that is hypothesized to exist in many kinds of systems. Ecology and business management have applied it.
A grid model where sand grains land at random and a site that grows too steep topples onto its neighbors. One grain can trigger a cascade.
A feature of objects or laws that stay the same when lengths, energies or other variables are multiplied by a common factor.
Collective behavior that emerges when many simple agents follow local rules with no central control, as in ant colonies or bird flocking.
The change of a medium from one state to another, such as a liquid becoming a gas when heated to its boiling point.
The movement and filtering of fluids through porous materials. Broader uses cover the connectivity of systems modeled as lattices or graphs.
Irregular alternation between nearly periodic behavior and bursts of chaos. It is common in turbulent fluid flows.
A small change in a deterministic system can lead to large differences later. Lorenz noticed it when rounding his weather model's starting data changed the results.
The way a system's later behavior can depend on its exact starting conditions, so that tiny differences grow into very different outcomes.
Wolfram's sorting of cellular automata, which are grids of cells that follow a fixed rule, into four classes by behavior. Class one settles into uniformity, class three looks chaotic.
A method for finding good paths through graphs, modeled on real ants, which lay down pheromones to direct each other to resources.
A measure, often not a whole number, of how a pattern's detail changes with scale. A coastline measures longer when a shorter stick is used.
A fractal shaped like a triangle that is divided into smaller triangles over and over, so the pattern looks the same at any magnification.
When a whole has properties that its parts lack alone and that appear only as they interact. Life is arguably an emergent property of chemistry and physics.
A set of entities in which each is created with the help of others in the set. Several models of life's origin are based on one.
The regular pattern of circulating cells that forms when a flat layer of fluid is heated from below and the warmer, less dense fluid rises.
Stripes or spots that arise naturally from a uniform state. They come from the interplay of chemical reactions and chemicals spreading at different rates.
Nassim Taleb's term for a property of systems that become more capable because of stress and mistakes. It differs from resiliency, the ability to recover from failure.
A way of coordinating indirectly through the environment. The trace one agent leaves prompts a later action by the same or a different agent.
A pathfinding algorithm that uses heuristics, which are rules of thumb, to guide its search for the shortest path from a start to a goal in a weighted graph.
An algorithm that finds the shortest paths from one starting point to all other points in a weighted graph, even when some edge weights are negative.
A game of finding the program of a given size that writes the most output or runs the longest before it stops. Its answers cannot be computed in general.
A method for minimizing a function by taking repeated steps in the steepest downhill direction. It is used in machine learning to minimize a loss function.
A compact data structure that tests whether an item is in a set. It can falsely say yes, but never falsely say no.
A programming model for processing big data sets across a cluster of computers. A map step filters and sorts the data, and a reduce step summarizes it.
A measure of how different two strings of text are, counted as the fewest single-character insertions, deletions or substitutions needed to turn one into the other.
A sequence of possible events in which the chance of each depends only on the state reached in the one before.
An algorithm that quickly breaks a signal into the frequencies it contains. Computing this directly from the definition is often too slow to be practical.
Choosing items, each with a weight and a value, so total weight stays within a limit and total value is as large as possible.
A sorting algorithm that picks a pivot element, splits the rest into smaller and larger ones, then sorts each part the same way.
A way to choose a random sample of k items from a population of unknown size in one pass, when it is too large to store.
An algorithm that finds the element making up more than half of a sequence, using linear time and constant memory.
A technique for adding and deleting items in a looped list whose items link both ways. It makes backtracking searches like Knuth's Algorithm X efficient.
A graph of variables in which arrows show which depend on which. Given a patient's symptoms, one can compute how likely each disease is.
A linear ordering of a directed graph's nodes in which each node comes after the ones it depends on, such as a valid order for tasks.
A program that takes no input and outputs a copy of its own source code. Programmers sometimes try to write the shortest one in a given language.
Simplifying a constraint problem by shrinking the possible values of its variables or adding constraints, without changing its solutions, so a solver has less to search.
A string-searching algorithm that uses hashing, which turns text into short numbers, to skip positions where a pattern cannot match. One use is detecting plagiarism.
A data structure that keeps track of non-overlapping sets and supports merging sets and quickly checking whether two elements are in the same set.
The first major constructed language meant for international communication, created by the priest Johann Martin Schleyer. Many speakers later switched to Esperanto.
A constructed language based on music, devised by the French music teacher Jean-François Sudre. Victor Hugo was among its sponsors.
A constructed Elvish language devised by Tolkien for his Middle-earth fiction and drawing partly on Finnish. He never created enough vocabulary to converse in it.
The Elvish language spoken by most Elves in western Middle-earth in Tolkien's fiction, with sounds and grammar based partly on Welsh.
A constructed language Suzette Haden Elgin created to test whether a language built to express the views of women would shape a culture.
The fictional language of the totalitarian state in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, with simplified grammar and restricted vocabulary designed to keep people from thinking critically.
The language of Spocania, a fictional island group invented by a Dutch linguist. Unlike Esperanto, it was never meant for international communication.
An auxiliary language made as a response to the European bias of Esperanto and Ido. Words come from joining roots, so male plus child gives boy.
An international auxiliary language whose vocabulary and grammar come from natural languages. Its supporters say the written form is understandable to speakers of Romance languages.
A logical constructed language designed for linguistic research. It was built to be so different from natural languages that learners would think differently if language shapes thought.
Voynichese, the undeciphered script of the illustrated Voynich manuscript. Its origins and purpose are still debated.
A constructed language designed to have no verbs. Four relationals link noun phrases and do the work of verbs, though whether it is truly verbless is questioned.
A fictional language used by many authors. In the stories that feature it, the language is said to have mystical powers.

Uttering words or speech-like sounds that believers often take to be a language unknown to the speaker. One linguistic definition is fluid speech-like syllables with no readily comprehensible meaning.
An a priori constructed language, meaning one whose words are built from scratch instead of taken from existing languages.
Microwave radiation that fills all space in the observable universe. It is light set free when the early universe turned transparent, and key evidence for the Big Bang.
Fluctuations in the density of normal matter in the universe, caused by sound waves in the early plasma. Their size gives cosmologists a standard ruler.
A distortion of the cosmic microwave background, whose photons gain energy by colliding with high-energy electrons in galaxy clusters. It has been used to observe dense clusters of galaxies.
How matter is distributed across the entire observable universe. It appears to be organized in a hierarchy, with no continued structure beyond a very large scale.
A roughly spherical region of space near the constellation Boötes that holds far fewer galaxies than expected. It is one of the largest known voids in the visible universe.
The process that made the electrically neutral atoms of the early universe ionized again. The formation of the first stars and galaxies drove it.
The epoch when charged electrons and protons first bound together into neutral hydrogen atoms. The name misleads, because they had not been combined before.
A disagreement between measurements of how fast the universe is expanding, made from the early universe and from nearby galaxies.
How the lightest atomic nuclei formed in the first minutes of the universe. Elements heavier than lithium were made later in stars.
A prediction of some models of cosmic inflation, in which inflation continues forever into the future and produces a hypothetically infinite multiverse.
A thought experiment in which a brain with false memories is likelier to appear by chance than a whole universe. Physicists use it to test competing theories.
A person's return to criminal behavior after a conviction. It also names the share of former prisoners rearrested for a similar offense.
Behavior that violates social norms, from written laws to unwritten customs. What counts as deviant depends on the place and the time.
A society's negative perception or disapproval of a person or group because of traits like race or health. It also shapes how stigmatized people see themselves.
The process by which people who once committed crimes stop offending.
Unlawful behavior by someone under the legal age of adulthood, acts that would be crimes if an adult did them. Most juvenile offending is non-violent.
The study of what happens to victims of crime, including the psychological effects on them and their relationship with offenders and the justice system.
A theory that studies crime as an event tied to its surroundings. It holds that prosperity raised crime by offering more cars to steal and other opportunities.
Trying to punish someone for breaking a law without having the right to do so, often summed up as taking the law into one's own hands.
Singling out a person or group for undeserved blame and bad treatment. It differs from buck passing, which shifts responsibility.
The movement to abolish prisons and punishment as the main response to crime, and to deal with harm in other ways.
Tending to produce crime or criminal behavior, as with a condition, environment or trait that raises the risk of offending.
The conduct of gangs, groups of individuals that engage in illegal and violent behavior, whose members usually glorify an aggressive and antisocial lifestyle.
The theory that visible signs of disorder, like vandalism, encourage more crime, so policing minor offenses helps create order. It has been debated by social scientists.
On this view, classifying people with a term can shape their identity and behavior, and no act is deviant in itself.
People learn the attitudes and motives for crime from others, and turn to it when what they have learned favors law-breaking over law-abiding.
The idea that a society's dominant values and social structure cause strain, which may push some people to commit crimes.
A widespread fear that some evil person or thing threatens a community's values or well-being. Sensational media coverage often arouses it, and the claims exaggerate the harm.
How crime varies with age, a pattern one theory explains with two kinds of offenders. Some offend only in adolescence, others from early childhood into adulthood.
The amount of crime that goes unreported, undetected or undiscovered, which is why official crime statistics alone are a limited guide.
A basic sauce in French cooking from which many other sauces, called daughter sauces, are made.
Diced vegetables, usually onions, carrots and celery, cooked slowly in butter without browning. In French cooking it is the flavor base for stocks, soups and sauces.
Cooking food placed in a pouch in a water bath at a precisely controlled, low temperature for hours. The inside cooks through without overcooking the outside.
A mold grown on steamed rice or another grain, used to ferment foods such as miso and soy sauce.
A reaction that turns sugars such as glucose into lactic acid without oxygen. Despite the name, milk is not required, and cooks use it to preserve food.
The cool area of a kitchen where savory cold dishes such as salads and pâtés are prepared and food is kept refrigerated. Its head is the pantry chef.
Caramelized sugar thinned with vinegar or another sour liquid, used as a sweet and sour flavoring for sauces such as the orange sauce for duck.
A knife cut that first slices food into thin sticks, then dices them into very small cubes. It is the smallest of the dice cuts.
Aromatic ingredients cut small and cooked slowly in oil, then used as the foundation of many dishes in Mediterranean and Latin American cooking.
Organizing and arranging the ingredients a cook will need before cooking starts. The idea also applies in classrooms and hospitals.
Removing and dissolving the browned food residue left in a pan so it can flavor a sauce, soup or gravy.
Food cooked slowly in fat at a much lower temperature than deep frying. It can preserve food, though many modern dishes skip that.
Cooking food by baking it in a folded pouch, which also steams it. Fish and vegetables are the usual choices.
The growing environment and farming practices that give a crop, such as a wine grape, its character. How much this matters is debated in the wine industry.
Butter heated until almost brown, which gives it a nutty scent and flavor. It is a warm sauce for foods such as fish or pasta.
A starch extracted from the root of the kudzu vine, used in Japanese cooking to thicken sauces.
Cooling melted chocolate while stirring until a little cocoa butter crystallizes, then warming it again. The chocolate sets glossy and snaps well.
Soaking and cooking corn in an alkaline solution, usually limewater, then washing and hulling it. Treated corn grinds more easily and makes a dough called masa.
A foam made from a flavored liquid, set with a gelling agent and pushed through a canister with nitrous oxide cartridges. It adds flavor without much substance.
A fermented fish sauce used as a condiment in ancient Greece and Rome. Like modern fish sauce, it gave dishes a rich umami flavor from glutamates.
A controller can manage a system only if it can respond in at least as many ways as the system can behave. This is Ashby's law.
A system that makes and maintains its own parts. Biologists Maturana and Varela introduced the term to describe the self-maintaining chemistry of living cells.
The process by which living organisms keep internal conditions such as body temperature and blood glucose relatively stable. It commonly works through negative feedback.
A model of the organizational structure of any autonomous system, built around what it takes to survive in a changing environment.
Bentham's prison design in which one guard can observe all inmates, who cannot know when they are watched and so act as though they always are.
A model of goal-directed action. It tests whether a goal is met, acts if not, tests again and exits when the goal is reached.
Cybernetics applied to cybernetics, in which the role of the observer is acknowledged. Heinz von Foerster called it the cybernetics of observing systems.
A theorem that a good regulator must contain or have access to a model of the system it regulates. The model can lose information about the system.
The butterfly-shaped, looping pattern traced by solutions to Edward Lorenz's equations for atmospheric convection. In the chaotic range, small differences at the start grow exponentially.
A sudden change in the behavior of a system, caused by a small, smooth change in one of its parameters.
Something that is a whole made of smaller parts and also a part of a larger whole, such as a cell in an organism.
A chain of cause and effect in which a system's outputs are routed back as its inputs, which makes simple causal reasoning difficult.
A system whose operations are produced only by its own other operations, though it still exchanges matter and energy with its surroundings.
A system viewed only through its inputs and outputs, without any knowledge of its internal workings. The human brain or an institution can be treated this way.
Meetings of scholars from many disciplines, held in New York, that aimed to promote communication across the sciences. The name often refers to the series on cybernetics.
A person, theory or system taking account of its own part in shaping what it studies.
Explaining why events take the course they do by naming the constraints that rule out the alternatives. Gregory Bateson described this approach.
Recurring interactions between a living system and its environment that trigger changes in the structure of both, so the two adapt together.
A system that, once a disturbance upsets its balance, rearranges its own organization by trial and error until it is stable again. Ashby introduced the idea.
Outcomes of a purposeful action that nobody intended or foresaw. Irrigation meant to supply farmers with water, for example, can also raise the prevalence of waterborne disease.
A postmodern dance practice in which dancers improvise movement through shared weight and continuous physical touch. Steve Paxton developed it.
A Japanese dance theatre, traditionally performed in white body makeup with slow, controlled motion. It resists fixity and is hard to define.
A method and language for describing and recording human movement. Dancers, actors and athletes use it, as do physical and occupational therapists and psychotherapists.
In ballet, the movement and carriage of the arms.
A ballet turn in which the dancer whips the raised leg out and in while spinning on the other leg.
A ballet movement in which the dancer bends the knees and then straightens them again.
The art of expression in Indian classical dance that leads the audience toward a sentiment. Its four aspects are body, voice, costume and scenery, and mental states.
A still scene in which costumed actors or models hold a pose, silently and often with props or scenery. Living statues and live nativity scenes are present-day examples.
A dance duet in which two dancers perform ballet steps together, most often a man and a woman. Swan Lake and Giselle both include one.
A method for comparing movement styles across cultures by coding dance and work movement on film.
A method of music teaching in which students learn rhythm, structure and expression through movement, often before they see the idea written down.
A ballet pose in which the dancer stands on one leg with the other stretched straight out behind.
A dance form in which expressing the dancer's own feelings is essential. It arose in Europe as a reaction against ballet, which was seen as austere and mechanical.
A ballet movement in which the foot slides along the floor until the leg and toes are fully stretched.
A traditional Indian classical dance from Kerala. It is a play of verses, performed in large and unique makeup and costumes.
The dancers in a ballet company who are not principals or soloists. They move as one, in synchronized steps, like the swans in Swan Lake.
German dance theatre that grew out of German Expressionist dance.
An acting technique for creating and analyzing a performance by exploring space, shape, time, emotion and how the performer's body moves.
A ballet movement in which the working leg moves side to side, usually in quick repeated succession so the foot seems to flutter.
In ballet, the positioning of the shoulders and head at an angle to the hips and legs.
The actual production of offspring in a population, which differs from fecundity, the physical capability to reproduce.
The number of deaths in a population relative to its size. Morbidity, which is how common a disease is, is a separate measure.
The rate of disease in a population, as distinct from the rate of death.
The number of live births in a population over a given period relative to its size. It is better known as the birth rate.
The movement of people from one place to another, to settle there for good or for a time. Most of it happens within a single country.
The shift of a population from rural to urban areas, as more people live and work in cities and towns.
The especially long-lived members of a population. Life expectancy is a different measure, the average number of years remaining at a given age.
A person who has reached the age of 100. Their numbers are expected to rise substantially as population and life expectancy grow.
A fall in the size of a human population. One cause is the tendency of women in wealthier countries to have fewer children.
A group of people who share a defining characteristic, typically an event such as birth or graduation in the same period of time.
The social norm of marrying outside one's own social group. Its opposite, endogamy, is marriage within the group.
A form of polygamy in which a man is married to two or more women at the same time.
The right of the firstborn legitimate child to inherit all or most of a parent's estate, or to succeed them as ruler. Usually this means the eldest son.
Population can grow exponentially while food grows only linearly, until falling living standards force it back down. Economists disagree on whether it still applies.
A boost in economic growth when more of a country's people are of working age than are dependents. It also requires that young people have quality education and health care.
A graph of a population by age group and sex. It typically forms a pyramid when the population is growing.
A period with a significant increase in births. The best known came in the aftermath of World War II, and the people born then are often called baby boomers.
A table showing, for each age, the chance of dying before the next birthday. Demographers and actuaries use it to measure how long a population survives.
A mathematical model of how death rates change with age. After early adulthood, the risk of dying in many populations rises almost exponentially.
The average number of children per woman needed for a generation to replace itself. Below it, a population shrinks unless migration makes up the difference.
A vivid dream of waking up while still asleep, often followed by a morning routine like showering or eating breakfast. Some studies link it to lucid dreaming.
Focusing on a chosen topic while falling asleep in the hope of dreaming about it. Someone might go to bed repeating that they will dream about an upcoming presentation.
A dream thought to signal an illness before its symptoms appear.
The scientific study of dreams. It looks for links between dreaming and brain function, and studies the process of dreams instead of interpreting what they mean.
A sleep disorder causing panic or dread, typically in the first hours of sleep. It usually begins in childhood and fades with age.
Getting up and doing things while asleep, such as walking to the bathroom or eating. Sleepwalkers often remember little or nothing of it afterward.
Seeing, hearing or feeling something that is not there while fully awake.
The feeling of living through a moment that one has already seen in a dream.
In Tibetan Buddhism, a kind of dream described as a spiritual vision, set apart from ordinary and lucid dreams.
A set of claims that the Senoi people of Malaysia share and shape their dreams in groups to reduce fear. Later research found they do not practice it as described.
Engaging with the ideas and images of one's own mind. In Jungian psychology, it is a way to bridge the conscious and unconscious minds.
Perceiving one's surroundings from a position outside one's own body. Neurological research classes these experiences as hallucinations, and their root cause is unclear.
A dream in which the dreamer knows they are dreaming. It is a trainable skill, and some dreamers gain control over the dream.
Being conscious but unable to move while waking up or falling asleep. The person may also see or hear things that are not there.
A complete loss of the sense of self. It is temporary in drug experiences, and some spiritual traditions describe a permanent form.
An altered state of consciousness marked by euphoria, a concept developed by Abraham Maslow. It can arise from simple activities as well as intense events.
An insect emerging from its pupal case, as a butterfly does when it leaves its chrysalis.
Passing food or fluid directly between individuals, which typically happens mouth to mouth. In social insects such as ants, it can also carry information.
When a honey bee colony raises a new queen to replace the old one, which usually happens because she is failing.
Insect development through egg, nymph and adult stages without a pupa. The nymph resembles the adult but lacks wings and functional reproductive organs.
A silk case that some insect larvae spin around themselves while they change into adults.
The act of becoming a pupa, the stage between larva and adult in many insects. During it the insect typically stays anchored in one place.
A tube-like organ that insects and some other animals use to lay eggs. In many parasitic wasps it also pierces.
Insects that live as parasites inside other insects such as bees and wasps. Females of most species never leave the host after entering it.
A small club-shaped organ on some flying insects that reports body rotation during flight. It vibrates with the wings and works like a gyroscope.
An opening in an insect's outer skeleton that lets air into its breathing tubes. It can open and close to admit air while limiting water loss.
A stage in the growth of an insect or other arthropod between one molt and the next. Instars often differ in body proportions, colors or patterns.
A delay in development that lets an animal survive predictable bad conditions, such as extreme temperatures or drought. It is seen especially in insects.
Sound made by rubbing body parts together, mostly by insects. A scraper is drawn across a finely ridged surface, like a needle across a record.
A temporary relationship in which an organism attaches itself to a host only to travel. Seeds that cling to animals are a plant example.
The separation of an arthropod's old outer covering from the tissue beneath. It comes just before the animal sheds it, and lets a new covering form.
A chemical signal released by a honey bee queen that tells the colony she is present and shapes how the workers behave.
The dances of honey bees, including the figure-eight waggle dance, by which foragers tell the colony the direction and distance of flowers, water or a nest site.
Well-defended species that share predators come to look alike. A predator that has one unpleasant encounter with any of them avoids all of them.
Fungus farming by leafcutter ants, which carry cut leaves to their nest and use them to grow the fungus they eat.
In some firefly species, many individuals flash at the same moment.
The puzzle of whether an act is good because the gods approve of it, or approved of because it is good. It applies to monotheistic religions too.
The conclusion that a much larger population whose lives are barely worth living can be better than a smaller one with very high quality of life.
Doing more than duty requires. An act is supererogatory if it is good but not morally required, unlike a duty, which is wrong not to do.
The claim that good can be defined in terms of described properties such as pleasant or desirable. British philosopher Moore introduced the term.
The question of whether what ought to be follows from what is. Hume argued it is not obvious how to get from one to the other.
The theory that moral words like "wrong" or "good" do not describe facts about the world. Moral sentences instead express an attitude toward something.
The view that moral claims rest on objective facts, but no such facts exist. Some defenders still think moral talk is worth keeping.
The leaves of a Southeast Asian tree that people chew or brew as tea. Their alkaloids bind to opioid receptors, and their safety and effectiveness are unclear.
A plant with tall spikes of tubular flowers. It yields drugs for the heart, but is very toxic to humans and other mammals.
An arrow poison made from plant extracts. It paralyzes muscles, but works only through a wound or the blood, not when swallowed.
A group of fungi that grow on rye and related plants. Their alkaloids can sicken humans and other mammals who eat contaminated grain.
A plant alkaloid found in Syrian rue that can cause hallucinations. In ayahuasca it blocks an enzyme, so DMT takes effect when swallowed.
A mixture of leaves and wood ash that Aboriginal Australians chew as a stimulant. The leaves come from native tobacco or the plant Duboisia hopwoodii.
A game in which two players can each cooperate or betray the other. Betraying is rational for each alone, yet both gain more by cooperating.
One player proposes how to divide a sum of money, and the other accepts or rejects. If rejected, neither gets anything.
A game in which one player decides how much money to send to another. Most send some, which undermines the assumption of narrow self-interest.
How to hire the best applicant when each is decided on right after the interview. Reject the early ones, then take the first who beats everyone so far.
A model of conflict between two players. Ideally one yields, but each tries to avoid being the one, and if neither does, the worst outcome follows.
Any social decision rule that can be carried out by a mechanism where players gain by lying can also be carried out by one that rewards honesty.
The principle that gene variant frequencies in a population stay constant from generation to generation when no evolutionary influence, such as selection or mutation, acts on it.
The loss of genetic variation when a small group founds a new population. By chance, it may end up distinctly different from the parent population.
A mobile genetic element that moves within a genome by turning its RNA copy back into DNA. It multiplies quickly and is abundant in human and maize genomes.
A genetically modified mouse in which researchers have switched off one gene. Differences from normal mice show what the gene probably does.
DNA sequences that can change position within a genome. Some copy and paste themselves into a new spot, while others make an enzyme they need to move.
A protein first isolated from a jellyfish that glows green under blue to ultraviolet light. Its gene is often used as a marker of gene activity.
A way new genes form. Exons, the segments of a gene, from different genes are brought together, or one exon is duplicated.
The change in the frequency of a gene variant in a population due to chance. It can make variants vanish and so reduce genetic variation.
The idea that an organism can pass on to its offspring traits acquired through use or disuse. Biology abandoned it, though interest in it has continued.
A method that estimates biological age from changes to DNA that accumulate over time. Many measure methyl groups building up on DNA.
A DNA sequence with no known biological function, which most organisms carry in some amount. Scientists disagree over which criteria identify a function.
A natural process and technology that spreads a gene through a population by making offspring more likely to inherit it. One proposed use is exterminating disease-carrying insects.
The predictable proportions in which traits appear among offspring when a single gene controls the trait. Mendel's pea crosses are an example.
Selection that keeps several versions of a gene in a population. It can occur when carrying two different versions is fitter than carrying two identical ones.
Improved function of a trait in hybrid offspring, from mixing their parents' genetic contributions. In crops it can mean higher yield or quicker maturity.
Having more than two paired sets of chromosomes in the cells of an organism. It is especially common in plants and is rare in mammals.
A condition in which one organism has more than one genetic line, all from a single fertilized egg. It can start when one cell mutates during development.
A single organism made of cells with different genotypes. It can arise when two embryos fuse, or through organ transplantation.
A stretch of repeating DNA at the end of a chromosome. It protects the ends from gradual degradation and keeps repair systems from mistaking them for breaks.
The movement of genetic material between organisms other than from parent to offspring. It is the primary way antibiotic resistance spreads in bacteria.
A volcanic region thought to be fed by unusually hot mantle. As a plate moves over one, it can leave a chain of volcanoes.
A proposed flow of rising material within the Earth's mantle that would explain unusual volcanism. It is often invoked for hotspots such as Hawaii or Iceland.
The gravitational balance between Earth's crust and mantle, in which the crust floats at a height set by its thickness and density.
A section of oceanic crust and upper mantle that is uplifted, often onto continental rock, and exposed. In mountain belts it documents former ocean basins.
A joining, along a major fault zone, of separate tectonic units with different histories. At the surface it is often a mountain range.
A mountain system on the seafloor where plates separate. Magma rises in the gap and cools into new oceanic crust.
A model of how ocean basins open and close as tectonic plates diverge and supercontinents assemble and break up. The Atlantic Ocean is a classic example.
A fragment of crust that formed on one tectonic plate and was attached to another. It keeps a geologic history different from the rock around it.
Sediment scraped off a sinking oceanic plate and piled against the plate above it. Most of Japan's geological basement consists of former wedges.
A basin that forms alongside a mountain belt when the mountains' mass bends the crust downward. It fills with sediment eroded off the mountains.
A fault where two plates slide past each other sideways along their boundary. Most are under the ocean, but the San Andreas Fault is on land.
The downward force a cooling, denser plate exerts as it sinks into the mantle. One analysis showed it the strongest of the forces driving plate motion.
A gift-giving feast of Indigenous Pacific Northwest Coast peoples, where a leader gives away or destroys wealth to show power. Canada once made it a crime.
Luxury goods that people want more as their price rises, against the usual law of demand. A high price can make them a status symbol.
An approach to world history that takes the world system, not nation states, as the main unit. It sorts countries into core, semi-periphery and periphery.
The average uncertainty in the outcomes of a random variable. It sets an absolute limit on how far data from a source can be compressed without loss.
The number of positions at which two strings of equal length differ, which is also the fewest substitutions needed to turn one into the other.
The highest rate at which information can be sent reliably over a communication channel. Modern error-correcting codes let wired and wireless systems come close to it.
A lossless compression method that gives common symbols fewer bits than rare ones. It is optimal among methods that encode symbols separately.
A measure of how much two random variables depend on each other. Unlike the correlation coefficient, it is not limited to linear dependence.
The maximum rate at which information can be sent over a noisy communications channel of a given bandwidth.
A result that ties the average information lost in a noisy channel to the probability of error. It gives a lower bound on the error of any decoder.
A test on a set of codeword lengths that says whether a prefix code, where no codeword begins another, can have exactly those lengths.
A measure of how much an approximating probability distribution differs from the true one. It is not a true distance, because it is not symmetric.
The average number of bits needed to identify an event when the code is optimized for an estimated probability distribution rather than the true one.
A quantity that generalizes Shannon entropy and several other notions of entropy. It is used in ecology and statistics as an index of diversity.
Error-correcting codes that can detect and fix several wrong symbols in a block of data. They are used in CDs and QR codes.
The first practical error-correcting codes to come close to the theoretical limit of reliable communication. Mobile networks and satellite links use them.
A theorem that sets the limit on data compression. Data compressed to fewer bits per symbol than the source's Shannon entropy will almost surely lose information.
The theory behind lossy compression. It asks how few bits per symbol are needed to rebuild a signal approximately within an allowed distortion.
Though many outcomes are possible, a random process most probably produces one from a loosely defined set whose members are all about equally likely.
A method that finds the best tradeoff between accuracy and compression when summarizing data. It has been proposed as a theoretical foundation for deep learning.
A result in distributed source coding about losslessly compressing two correlated data sources.
An algorithm that finds the shortest linear-feedback shift register, a simple bit-shifting circuit, that produces a given binary sequence. Berlekamp devised it to decode BCH error-correcting codes.
A lossless compression method that encodes an entire message as a single fraction. Frequently used characters take fewer bits than rare ones.
A language type whose words are built from many meaningful parts, often so long they work as whole sentences. Linguists have no agreed definition of it.
Grammatical marking of the kind of evidence behind a statement, such as seeing something directly or only inferring it.
A marker on a clause that usually shows whether its subject is the same as the subject of the previous clause.
A verb forms a compound with its direct object, so the noun becomes part of the verb. It is central to many languages in North America and Siberia.
The placement of question words such as what or who at or near the front of a clause, away from the position they would normally fill.
A grammatically correct sentence that starts in a way that leads readers to the wrong interpretation, so they hit a dead end or an unintended meaning.
A language where certain pronouns, usually the subject, may be left out when context makes them clear. Spanish and Italian often do this, English seldom.
Repeatedly halve an even number, or triple an odd number and add one. Whether every positive integer ends at one is still unsolved.
The first nontrivial taxicab number, a number that can be written as the sum of two positive cubes in two different ways.
The number Kaprekar's routine settles on. The routine subtracts a number's digits sorted ascending from the same digits sorted descending, and repeats.
An immense number that arose as an upper bound in a problem in Ramsey theory. Written out in ordinary digits, it would not fit in the observable universe.
A puzzle asking for a walk through the city of Königsberg that crosses each of its bridges exactly once. Euler proved it impossible, which laid the foundations of graph theory.
The claim that there are infinitely many twin primes, primes that sit two apart from another prime. It remains unproven despite substantial progress.
A metabolic disturbance that occurs when a starved or severely malnourished person starts eating again. Potassium levels can fall, and severe cases can be fatal.
People remember unfinished or interrupted tasks better than finished ones. A separate effect is the urge to go back and complete a task already started.
When several similar items are shown together, the one that stands out is the most likely to be remembered. Changing its size, color or underlining can be enough.
A vivid, long-lasting memory of a surprising or shocking event. People feel sure of it, yet its details can still be forgotten.
A technique for memorizing numbers by turning digits into consonants, then adding vowels to make words. It relies on images being easier to remember than numbers.
The way a group collectively stores and retrieves knowledge, with members learning who the experts are.
Memory works best when the conditions at recall match those present when the information was learned. Studying in the room where the exam is held is one example.
The point where a force concentrates its main effort to gain a decisive result.
A fast surprise attack in which several kinds of forces strike together with overwhelming concentration. Germany's army never adopted it as official doctrine, and historians use the word loosely.
A strategy of gradually wearing down an opponent to the point of collapse by inflicting continuous losses.
Attacking an enemy's flanks and rear instead of its front, so that its forces are destroyed and cannot withdraw. Attacking from both sides at once is called a pincer movement.
Using the threat of force to convince another party not to act. It is most likely to work when the attacker believes success is unlikely and the costs are high.
The many small difficulties and chance events in war that make even simple plans hard to carry out.
A style of command where a leader sets a clear objective and subordinates decide how to reach it. Success depends on them grasping the orders' intent.
A battle in which a force is surrounded and cut off from supplies and reinforcements, so it must break out or surrender.
In war, espionage or law enforcement, intercepting something on its way to where it will be used.
An attack that targets an enemy's leaders or command centers to disrupt the whole organization.
The Russian doctrine of military deception, from camouflage to disinformation. It helped Soviet forces achieve surprise even with very large forces massed.
A decision-making model of observing, orienting, deciding and acting, developed by Air Force Colonel John Boyd. The idea is that agility can overcome raw power against human opponents.
The uncertainty that people in a military operation have about the situation, including what the enemy can do and intends to do.
A strategy of destroying anything that lets an enemy force fight, such as crops and water supplies. A retreating army may use it to leave nothing of value worth taking.
Reaching a large goal through many small actions that would be hard to do all at once. Countries use it to pursue goals gradually without provoking escalation.
An act or event that provokes a war or is used to justify one. A declaration of war usually names it.
A group that usually works for an enemy to undermine a nation or larger group from within. Its members may, for example, commit sabotage covertly.
Using several types of warfare at once, such as conventional force and fake news, so the aggressor tries to avoid blame. Critics say the concept is vague.
A state's long-term plan for using military and nonmilitary means to advance its national interests. Success includes peacetime goals and prosperity as well as military victory.
Tuning musical intervals so they produce no beats and sound pure. The pitches relate by small whole-number ratios.
A tuning system in which all intervals are built from multiples of one basic step that is usually the semitone. Some intervals therefore deviate slightly from their pure sound.
A melodic framework for improvisation in Indian classical music that resembles a mode. It sets the notes allowed and traditionally carries associations with mood or season.
Two or more rhythms played at once that do not sound derived from one another.
A technique in which a repeating rhythmic pattern, called a talea, runs through at least one voice part of a whole composition.
A technique that treats timbre, the tone color of an instrument, as a melodic element. A single melodic line is divided among different timbres.
Music that uses the acoustic properties of sound, also called sound spectra, as the basis for composition.
A partnership in which a fungus penetrates the root cells of a plant and forms tree-like structures called arbuscules. The fungus helps the plant capture nutrients.
A partnership in which a fungus wraps plant roots in a dense sheath without entering their cells. It forms mostly on woody plants.
A community of microorganisms that stick together, and often to a surface, inside a slimy matrix they produce. Dental plaque is one example.
The movement of genetic material between organisms other than from parent to offspring. It is the main way antibiotic resistance spreads among bacteria.
The formation of spores, units that survive harsh conditions for long periods and may spread. Bacterial spores are not part of a sexual cycle.
A fungus's ability to grow as mold or yeast. Temperature usually triggers the switch. One human pathogen is a mold at room temperature and a yeast at body temperature.
A virus that infects bacteria and replicates inside them. Phages are seen as a possible therapy against multi-drug-resistant bacteria.
Cells that survive a lethal treatment by going dormant. The tolerance is usually not inherited and reverses once treatment stops, when the cells wake and multiply.
An imbalance in the microbes of a body part such as the gut. Species that normally dominate become scarce, while those normally held in check increase.
An organism that lives inside the body or cells of another, usually to the benefit of both. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the root nodules of legumes are one example.
Bacteria that use magnetic crystals inside them to orient along Earth's magnetic field lines. Even dead cells are dragged into alignment just as a compass needle is.
A network with short paths between any two nodes and many tightly knit neighborhoods. In social networks, strangers are linked by a short chain of acquaintances.
A network where the share of nodes with a number of connections follows a power law, so it has no characteristic scale. Preferential attachment is one proposed explanation.
The idea that any two people are six or fewer social links apart. A short story first imagined it as a game of reaching anyone in the world.
Google's algorithm for ranking web pages by counting the number and quality of links to them. It assumes that more important sites receive more links from other sites.
A measure of how often a node lies on shortest paths between others. In a telecom network, a high-scoring node controls more, because more information flows through it.
A process that hands out wealth or credit according to how much each already has, so the rich get richer. Under suitable circumstances it generates power law distributions.
Grouping the nodes of a network so each group is densely connected inside and sparsely connected to other groups. Groups may overlap.
The point at which long-range connectivity first forms in a random network. Below it no giant component exists, and above it one is as large as the system.
A small pattern of connections that recurs in a network more than chance would predict. Motifs may reflect structures that perform particular functions efficiently.
Looser relationships such as those with acquaintances. Close friends mostly know what one already knows, so acquaintances bring more new information.
A measure of how strongly the nodes of a graph cluster together. In social networks, nodes tend to form tightly knit groups more often than chance would give.
How well a network keeps working when some of its nodes or links fail.
The collaborative distance between mathematician Paul Erdős and another person, measured by joint authorship of mathematical papers. The same principle has been applied in other fields.
Typically, a person's friends have more friends than that person does. Sampling bias is one explanation, since people with more friends are in more friend groups.
A spread of content or behavior through a network in which each person who adopts it passes it on to others.
A score for how well a network splits into groups, comparing links inside groups with the number expected if links were placed at random.
A random graph in which either all graphs with a fixed number of edges are equally likely, or each edge is present independently with fixed probability.
A network whose nodes divide into two sets, so that every link joins nodes of different sets. Equivalently, it has no cycle of odd length.
A directed graph where each edge has a capacity and carries a flow that cannot exceed it. Fluids in pipes and currents in an electrical circuit are examples.
A suggested limit on how many people one can keep stable social relationships with. Robin Dunbar proposed it after linking primate brain size to average social group size.
A condition in which a person with a disability is unaware of having it because of brain damage. It typically follows damage to the parietal lobe.
People made blind by brain damage insist, often adamantly, that they can see. They confabulate to fill in the missing visual input.
The ability of people blinded by brain damage to respond to what they do not consciously see. Its existence is controversial, as it may be degraded conscious vision.
A delusion in which one denies owning a limb or a whole side of one's body. Shown proof, patients still invent elaborate stories about whose limb it is.
Loss of recognition or awareness of part of one's own body, often after damage to the right parietal lobe. The limb may be attributed to another person.
Seeing an image again after what produced it has been removed. It is a group of visual symptoms with many causes such as seizures and migraines.
A condition in which a person with partial or severe blindness experiences visual hallucinations. A related type, the closed-eye hallucination, also occurs when visual input is lacking.
A rare condition, usually following a stroke, in which speech comes to sound like a foreign accent. Speakers acquire neither that accent nor any extra fluency.
A rare neurological symptom of making puns and telling inappropriate jokes at the wrong moments. It is most common with frontal lobe damage.
The delusion that a place has been duplicated, or moved to another site. Though rare, it is most commonly associated with brain injury such as stroke.
Severe difficulty reading while writing, naming and understanding speech stay largely intact. It is also known as pure alexia.
A rare disorder of seeing only one object at a time. Someone may see the details of a complex scene but miss its overall meaning.
A neurological disorder in which a person cannot correctly interpret what a mirror shows, for instance reaching into the mirror for an object reflected there.
Blindness from damage to the back of the brain in which moving objects in the blind area stay visible, but still ones do not.
Damage to the medial temporal lobe that causes compulsive eating and a need to put inappropriate objects in the mouth. Rhesus monkeys show it more often than humans.
Behavior changes seen in some people with temporal lobe epilepsy, such as excessive writing and heightened religious feeling. Whether it is a true disorder is disputed.
A form of epilepsy in which seizures are set off by listening to very specific music that carries emotional content. Most patients have temporal lobe epilepsy.
Inability to locate and orient the parts of the body, usually after damage to the left parietal lobe.
A normal response to low glucose, in which the liver burns fat and releases ketones that the body can use as fuel. Cutting carbohydrates can induce it.
Reduced sensitivity to leptin, a hormone made by fat cells. In obesity, a person cannot sense fullness despite high energy stores.
A two-phase response in which a low dose of a stressor helps and a high dose inhibits or poisons. Breathing oxygen is an example.
Proteins or fats that react with sugars and become glycated. Their buildup is linked to diabetes and Alzheimer's disease.
An enzyme in cells that regulates growth, survival and protein synthesis. It also promotes the activation of insulin receptors.
The idea that a meal must supply enough of the amino acid leucine to trigger muscle protein synthesis.
The severe, chronic form of a shortage of thiamine, a B vitamin. Wet beriberi affects the heart and blood vessels, dry beriberi the nerves.
The idea that people eat until they get enough protein, so low-protein foods lead to overeating. It is a proposed explanation of obesity.
Describes what happens in the body after a meal, such as the rise in blood sugar.
The breakdown of stored fat into glycerol and free fatty acids. The body uses it to release energy during fasting or exercise.
The making of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources such as amino acids and glycerol. It happens mainly in the liver and helps keep blood sugar up.
A cell's regulated breakdown and recycling of its own unnecessary or damaged parts. Once seen as a defense against starvation, it also matters in fed cells.
A disease caused by too little vitamin C. It brings weakness, sore limbs and poor wound healing. On long sea voyages it once killed many sailors.
A reduced-calorie eating pattern, followed for a few days at a time, designed to produce some effects of fasting while still allowing food.
Fat tissue whose main job is making heat. It is especially abundant in newborns and in hibernating mammals and still active in adult humans.
A number estimating how much a food will raise blood glucose once eaten. It reflects the amount of carbohydrate and how strongly each gram raises glucose.
A disease caused by a lack of niacin, a B vitamin, with inflamed skin and dementia among its symptoms. It is often a disease of poverty.
The extra energy above its resting rate that the body spends processing a meal. Protein takes much more to process than fat.
Starch that resists digestion in the small intestine, so gut bacteria ferment some types instead. It has effects similar to dietary fiber.
A hollow tube of ice growing downward beneath sea ice around a stream of cold, salty brine. The brine's extreme cold freezes the water around it.
An area of open water surrounded by sea ice. Coastal ones form near the poles where strong winds push the ice away from the coast.
Tiny, loose ice crystals that form when turbulent water drops below its freezing point. They are notorious for blocking water intakes.
A layer of water where saltiness changes sharply with depth. It is common where river water or melting ice meets the salty ocean.
The part of ocean circulation driven by density differences from temperature and salt content. It is often called the ocean conveyor belt.
A large circular system of ocean surface currents driven by wind.
A large swirling current in the ocean that spins off from the main flow and carries water and heat with it.
A wave that travels inside a fluid instead of on its surface. It needs fluid like that of lakes and oceans, whose density changes with depth.
A large, unpredictable surface wave that is very dangerous to ships. It can form when strong winds and currents make waves merge into one.
An underwater mountain that rises from the ocean floor without reaching the surface and is usually an extinct volcano. Seamounts attract plankton, fish and other sea life.
A wave formed by the front edge of an incoming tide as it pushes up a river or narrow bay against the current.
The breaking of ice chunks from the edge of a glacier or ice shelf. The chunks crash into the water, often with a loud crack and hazardous waves.
A lake beneath a glacier or ice sheet, where high pressure keeps the water liquid. It can stay isolated from the outside for a long time.
A continuous shower of organic debris sinking from the upper ocean into the deep sea. It is an important food source for deep-living animals.
A flat underwater plain on the deep ocean floor. It forms when fine sediment, mostly clay and silt, buries an uneven surface of oceanic crust.
A fissure in the seabed that discharges water heated by the Earth. Bacteria there live on its chemicals and support animals such as giant tube worms.
A wind that flows downhill when cooler, denser air from higher ground sinks into lighter air below. The Santa Ana winds of southern California are one.
Partial loss of pigment that leaves an animal with white, pale or patchy skin, fur or feathers. The eyes keep their color.
A sense that detects the Earth's magnetic field, mainly used for orientation and navigation. In migratory birds, a protein in the eye seems to do the detecting.
The sound-producing organ of birds, located where the windpipe splits into the two bronchi.
Males gather in one place to compete in displays and courtship, and visiting females choose a mate. It is most common in birds such as black grouse.
Behavior in which a bird rubs ants on its feathers or lets them crawl over its body.
An attack on a predator by smaller animals, usually birds, who swoop at it and call until it leaves.
Staying in one spot in the air by beating the wings fast, as hummingbirds do, or by flying into the wind, as kestrels do.
Describes species whose young are underdeveloped at birth or hatching and mature with their parents' help.
Describes species whose young are relatively mature and mobile from the moment of birth or hatching. They usually leave the nest soon after.
A parent's behavior that pulls a predator's attention away from its nest or young. It often takes the form of feigning injury.
One animal deliberately and often aggressively taking food from another. Skuas, for example, harass other seabirds until they disgorge their food.
A sudden, irregular movement of large numbers of birds into areas where they are not usually found, often when food is scarce at home.
The tendency of an animal to stay in or return to a particular area. Returning to its birthplace to breed may be the most common form.
Two birds, usually a mated pair, singing together and often taking turns in a coordinated way.
A large, nocturnal parrot of New Zealand that cannot fly. It is the world's heaviest parrot and is critically endangered.
An egg laid by a cuckoo in another bird's nest, so that the host raises the chick.
A V-shaped flight formation seen in geese, swans and ducks. It may improve energy efficiency, though the reason is debated.
The drab plumage worn by males of many duck species for some months after the breeding season, in place of a bright one.
Male bowerbirds build and decorate a structure of twigs, then display at it to attract females.
The Arctic tern's yearly journey from its Arctic breeding grounds to Antarctic waters and back, one of the longest migrations of any animal.
A group of organisms that disappears from the fossil record for a time, then reappears. The term also covers species wrongly thought extinct and later found alive.
A rock deposit in the Canadian Rockies famous for fossils that preserve the soft parts of animals.
A sedimentary deposit that preserves an unusually large amount of fossil information. Some hold fossils in great numbers, others in exceptional condition that sometimes includes soft tissues.
An extinct marine arthropod with an easily fossilized exoskeleton made of calcite. Some were predators and some fed on plankton.
A long period early in Earth's history when microbes' photosynthesis first made free oxygen build up in the atmosphere and shallow seas.
An extinct soft-bodied sea animal with a cigar-shaped body and two long stalked eyes, found only in Illinois fossil beds. Its classification has been controversial.
A Cambrian animal of the lobopodians, the group from which velvet worms and arthropods arose. Scientists first reconstructed it upside down and back to front.
Animal or plant material preserved inside amber, which is fossilized tree resin. It gets in because the resin starts out soft and sticky.
Hearing a sound while seeing a mouth form a different one can produce the perception of a third sound.
An illusion in which an unchanging object away from where a person fixates fades and vanishes. At least part of it occurs in the brain.
A figure of notched circles in which a triangle appears, with its edges perceived without any change in brightness or color.
Two identical horizontal lines between converging lines, like railway tracks, look different in length. The upper one may look longer because it seems farther away.
Parallel lines between staggered rows of dark and light bricks or tiles look sloped, though they are straight and parallel.
Another name for the size-weight illusion, in which the smaller of two equally heavy objects feels heavier.
In phenomenology, setting aside assumptions about the world so experience can be described as it appears. Ancient skeptics used the word for suspension of judgment.
Husserl's method for finding what makes something what it is, by imagining it and varying its features. Whatever can change without the thing ending is inessential.
The body's impersonal, habitual working, such as perceiving, which carries on without a person choosing it.
Leib is the body as lived and felt from the inside. Körper is the body as a physical object of the kind a doctor examines.
A group of theories on how thinking is shaped by the body's state and abilities. They challenge computationalism, the view that the mind works like a computer.
Receptors in muscles, tendons and joints carry the sense of the body's own movement, force and position.
Instances of subjective experience, such as the taste of wine or the redness of an evening sky. Philosophers still disagree about their nature and status.
A pervasive mood that shapes how the world shows up for a person. Heidegger treated it as coming before any deliberate thought.
Heidegger's term for a thing considered as a mere object with properties, for example a hammer that is inspected while it sits unused.
Heidegger's term for equipment in use, such as a hammer in a carpenter's hand, which goes unnoticed until it breaks.
The capacity to share feelings and understandings with others, which makes communication between people possible.
In Husserl's account of time, retention is the just-passed moment still held in awareness, and protention is the immediate expectation of what comes next.
Husserl's account of how experience is lived as a flow in time, which lets a listener hear a melody as a whole.
In Husserl's phenomenology, the pure subject for whom a world appears at all. It is the condition of experience, not a thing within the world.
The ability of an organism to move on its own, using energy from its metabolism.
Words that look or sound alike and mean the same but have unrelated origins. English much and Spanish mucho are one pair.
The fading of a word's concrete meaning as it comes to do a grammatical job. Let us, meaning allow us, shrank to let's, which only introduces a suggestion.
Words such as frail and fragile that come from the same older word in one language and often differ in meaning.
A word or phrase borrowed from another language by translating its parts one by one. Italian grattacielo, for example, copies English skyscraper part by part.
A pronunciation error from applying a supposed foreign-language pattern to borrowed words. English speakers say habanero as if it were spelled habañero.
A word or phrase changed by mishearing part of it, so that the new version still makes sense. One speaker said egg corn for acorn.
A word borrowed from language to language across many, often distant, cultures. Common examples name a domesticated plant or animal that was new to the speakers.
A word taken into one language from another and at least partly assimilated. The donor language loses nothing and expects nothing back.
A word printed in a dictionary that never had a meaning or use. Typos usually create such words. A few get copied and enter real use.
Redundancy in wording, as in black darkness or burning fire. Writers sometimes use it for emphasis.
A reconstructed basic part of words in Proto-Indo-European, usually meaning an action such as to eat or to run. Roots never occurred alone.
A word changed because speakers replace an unfamiliar form with a more familiar one. English dialects remade asparagus as sparrowgrass by analogy to sparrow and grass.
Filling a gap in a word's forms with a form from an unrelated word, as English go takes the past tense went.
Replacing a word that social rules discourage with a milder one, such as pass away for die.
The irreducible quality that makes a thing this particular thing. It separates the concept "a person" from the concept "Socrates".
The view that an object is nothing but its properties, such as an apple's redness and roundness, and that no substance lies underneath.
Rival accounts of how a thing lasts through time. Perdurantists see an object as a four-dimensional worm stretched across time. Endurantists see it as three-dimensional.
In metaphysics, a particular instance of a shared property, such as the redness of one apple.
A split between properties objects have on their own, like solidity and motion, and properties that produce sensations in observers, like color and taste.
Reasoning that God exists from the idea of a greatest possible being. If it existed only in the mind, a greater one would be possible.
Reasoning from observed facts about the universe to God's existence. Some versions hold that the universe might not have existed.
The claim that nature's complex workings look designed and so point to an intelligent creator. Paley's watchmaker analogy is a well-known presentation of it.
The question of how a God who is all-powerful, all-knowing and good can coexist with evil and suffering.
The idea that God is hidden, silent or even absent altogether. The theme has a long history in Judeo-Christian and Islamic theology.
An argument that tries to reconcile an all-powerful, all-good God with the existence of evil. Unlike a defense, it aims to show their coexistence is plausible.
The view that faith is independent of reason, or even better than it at reaching some truths. Strict fideists give reason no role in finding theological truths.
A wager that believing in God is the rational choice, because the believer loses little if God is absent and gains enormously if God exists.
The doctrine that God is a single, undivided being whose attributes are not distinct from one another. His essence is simply to exist.
The view that what is morally good is whatever God commands. A classic objection is that it makes morality arbitrary or leaves God irrelevant to it.
A reduced vowel made by relaxing the mouth, written ə in the International Phonetic Alphabet. English uses one in unstressed syllables.
Vowels in a word shift to match the height or another feature of a trigger vowel. They need not sit next to each other.
Sound changes at the edges of words and word parts. Sounds may fuse across a word boundary, or shift depending on the neighboring words.
Holding a consonant longer than usual, which writing often shows as a doubled letter. In some languages, such as Japanese, consonant length distinguishes words.
A sound change in which a consonant is made in a different place or manner in the mouth, or a vowel moves forward or higher.
A sound change in Proto-Germanic. Consonants such as f and s that followed an unstressed syllable became voiced, so s turned into z.
A set of sound laws describing how the stop consonants of Proto-Indo-European changed in Proto-Germanic. They give regular correspondences with other Indo-European languages.
A consonant made by blocking airflow in the throat. English speakers know it as the catch in the middle of "uh-oh".
Consonants made with two closures in the mouth, front and back, and a sucking action on the air between them. They occur in many languages of Southern Africa.
Repeating a word, or part of one, exactly or with a slight change. Languages use it to mark plurality or intensification and to create new words.
A change in a word's tone caused by the pronunciation of the words next to it. It occurs in tonal languages.
The basic repeating rhythmic unit of a line of verse. In English it is a stressed syllable with unstressed ones in a set order.
Syllables count as heavier or lighter by the number or length of their sounds. In classical verse, this distinction was basic to the meter.
The loss of a sound, especially an unstressed vowel, from the middle of a word. Its opposite, adding sounds, is epenthesis.
The loss of a sound, most often a vowel, at the end of a word. I dunno shows the t of don't dropping in speech.
The swapping of the order of sounds or syllables in a word. Calvary for cavalry is an example. Many familiar English words changed shape this way.
A gradual lowering of pitch across a sentence in a tonal language. A high tone after a low one tends to come out lower.
A stretch of speech spoken with one pitch contour and usually ending in a pause.
The quality of the blur in the out-of-focus parts of a photograph. Lens design changes it, so some lenses blur pleasingly and others distractingly.
Henri Cartier-Bresson's name for the moment a photographer should capture. He saw capturing it as the essence of the very best pictures.
An early photographic process that records the image on polished, silver-plated copper. The surface is very delicate, and even light wiping can scuff it.
A photographic image made without a camera, by placing objects on light-sensitive paper and exposing it to light. The result is usually a negative shadow image.
A photograph made directly on a thin sheet of lacquered metal. It was ready to hand to the customer a few minutes after the picture was taken.
An early color photography process that built images by adding colors together. It was one of the principal color processes before subtractive color film arrived.
An early photographic process in which the plate had to be coated, sensitized, exposed and developed while still wet. Outdoor work needed a portable darkroom.
An early photographic process that used paper coated with silver iodide. Texture from the paper limited how well it recorded fine, low-contrast detail.
A composite photograph made by cutting, gluing and overlapping photographs into a new image. Today image-editing software does the same without film.
A fading of an image's brightness toward its edges. It is often unintended but can be added to draw attention to the center.
The stretch of daytime just after sunrise or before sunset, when the light is redder and softer. It is also called the magic hour.
The focus distance beyond which all objects look acceptably sharp. Setting focus there gives the maximum depth of field.
A process for printing photographs from an etched copper plate coated with light-sensitive gelatin. It can reproduce the continuous tones of a photograph.
A printing technique that imitates continuous tones with dots of varying size or spacing. Small dots look like smooth tones to the eye.
A dye process, also called Ilfochrome, for printing film transparencies onto photographic paper. Its prints, on a polyester base, resist fading for a long time.
A style of photography in which the photographer manipulates the picture to make an image rather than simply record one. Typical results lack sharp focus.
In Roland Barthes's account, the small detail in a photograph that strikes one viewer personally. It differs from the general interest of the image.
A technique for choosing the best film exposure and development. It ties the way a photographer visualizes the subject to the final result.
The reversal of tones that appears when film is badly overexposed. In landscape photographs, the sun can turn black instead of staying the whitest spot.
Something said that does more than give information, because saying it performs an action. Saying "I resign" carries out the resignation.
What a speaker means to do with words, apart from the literal sentence. Asking whether there is any salt at dinner is really a request.
A sentence that both describes a situation and changes the social reality it describes. Austin argued against the view that utterances only describe.
Paul Grice's rules of quantity, quality, relation and manner, describing how people normally behave in conversation. Listeners assume them even when an utterance seems to break one.
Saying one thing to do another, such as asking whether someone can pass the salt when the speaker means to request it.
The knowledge, beliefs and assumptions that speakers share and know they share, which lets them leave things unsaid.
An assumption a sentence takes for granted. Asking whether someone has talked to Hans presupposes that Hans exists, and so does saying they have not.
Moving a phrase to the front of a sentence to make it the topic. Linguists also use it to test whether a phrase is a unit.
Fixing a problem in talk as it happens, such as asking someone to repeat what they said or correcting a slip of one's own.
Speakers talk one at a time, with little overlap and short silences between turns. The conventions for handing over a turn vary by culture.
A reply, such as refusing an invitation, that goes against what the previous speaker was hoping for. Speakers usually delay and soften it.
A word or phrase that softens a statement or shows the speaker is not fully sure, such as "sort of" or "I think".
An act in conversation that threatens a person's public self-image, or face. Politeness theory treats politeness as efforts to redress such affronts.
Brown and Levinson's account of politeness as efforts to repair threats to a person's public self-image, or face. Other scholars have challenged it.
Using a word that refers to something named later. In "When he arrived home, John went to sleep," the pronoun he points ahead to John.
Two utterances by two speakers, one after the other, where the first provokes a responding utterance.
The brief signals a listener gives during a conversation, such as saying uh-huh, to show they are following.
A family of views from Bohr, Heisenberg and others on what quantum mechanics means. Versions share the idea that it is intrinsically indeterministic and gives outcomes as probabilities.
A version of quantum mechanics where a particle has a definite position at all times even when unobserved. It is deterministic and matches the predictions of other versions.
An unknown quantum state cannot be copied exactly into an independent duplicate. The theorem does not forbid one system becoming entangled with another.

A theorem that limits hidden-variable theories, which try to explain quantum results with underlying definite values. Such theories cannot keep both definite values and independence from the measuring device.
A variation of the double-slit experiment. Marking which slit a photon went through destroys the interference pattern, and erasing that mark later brings the pattern back.
A charged particle is affected by electromagnetic potentials even where the magnetic and electric fields are zero. Experiments have observed the resulting shift in its wave.
A proposed symmetry in which every known particle has a partner particle with different spin. Experiments so far have failed to find evidence for it.
Clocks disagree about elapsed time when they move at different speeds or sit in different gravitational fields. Satellite navigation such as GPS must account for it.
A twin who flies at near light speed returns to find the one who stayed home has aged more. Their paths through spacetime are not symmetric.
The radius of a sphere with the same surface area as the event horizon, or boundary, of a black hole of a given mass. Any amount of mass has one.
Ripples in spacetime produced when massive objects move relative to one another, traveling outward at the speed of light. They have been detected directly by dedicated observatories.
The slight extra travel time of radar signals passing near a massive object. It is one of the classic Solar System tests of general relativity.
A small correction to how a gyroscope's axis slowly turns near a large rotating mass such as the Earth. It arises from the mass's rotation.
The slow shift of the point where Mercury's orbit comes closest to the Sun. Newtonian gravity left part of it unexplained, and general relativity accounts for it.
Light climbing out of a gravitational well loses energy, so its wavelength stretches toward the red. Light falling in gains energy instead.
The description of the spacetime geometry around a rotating, uncharged black hole. It is an exact solution of Einstein's equations, which are very hard to solve exactly.
The singularity of a rotating black hole, which is shaped like a ring. Such a black hole is also called a Kerr black hole.
The proposal that the description of a volume of space can be encoded on a boundary with fewer dimensions. It was inspired by black hole thermodynamics.
A conjectured match between a theory of quantum gravity and a quantum field theory. When one is strongly interacting, the other is weak, so hard problems become easier.
The rotation of a massive object distorts the spacetime around it, as general relativity predicts. The effect is tiny, so detecting it takes an extremely sensitive instrument.
The hypothesis that gravitational mass equals inertial mass as a fact of nature. In its weak form, masses of any composition in free fall follow the same trajectories.
