The hypothesis that absolute rotation is determined by the large-scale distribution of matter in the universe. It is imprecise, and many rival formulations exist.
A singularity with no event horizon around it, so it could be seen directly. Naked singularities are hypothetical and have not been observed.
A sudden loss of muscle tone throughout the body during REM sleep, the phase of rapid eye movements and vivid dreams.
Any outside cue that keeps an organism's biological rhythms in step, usually the Earth's cycle of light and dark.
The mismatch between a person's body clock and the schedule that work or school imposes.
Brief bursts of neural activity in non-REM sleep. Researchers still doubt whether they are tied to memory.
A body rhythm with cycles longer than an hour but shorter than a day. Sleep stages cycling through the night are one example.
A shift of the body clock to an earlier time, so that sleepiness and waking come earlier than before.
A large waveform seen on an EEG during non-REM sleep. It may keep the sleeping brain from waking to harmless stimuli and aid memory.
A small region of the hypothalamus that regulates sleep cycles. It takes in light from the eyes to keep the body's clocks in step with the day.
The time in the evening when melatonin starts to rise under dim light. Researchers use it to mark where a person's body clock sits.
The build-up of the need to sleep during waking hours. It grows the longer a person stays awake and eases during sleep.
The drowsiness, disorientation and poor coordination felt right after waking. It may take hours to fade, which matters for decisions and safety-critical tasks.
A sudden episode of sleep lasting a few seconds, in which a person loses awareness. It can show as droopy eyes and head nodding.
Deep sleep, the stage of non-REM sleep marked by slow delta waves on an EEG. It is considered important for memory and for the brain's recovery from the day.
Sleep disorders involving abnormal movements, behaviors or dreams while falling asleep, sleeping or waking. They are partial arousals between sleep states.
The cumulative effect of not getting enough sleep, which can cause mental or physical fatigue. Scientists debate its specifics, and it is not a disorder.
A body rhythm that keeps its own period when it gets no environmental time cues such as light and dark.
A person's natural tendency, from early riser to night owl, to sleep at a particular time of day. It shifts across life, with adolescents preferring later sleep.
Sleeping in several separate periods over a day instead of one block. Online groups try it to gain productivity, but there is no scientific evidence it works.
A temporary mismatch between the body clock and local time after crossing time zones quickly. Most travelers find eastward trips harder.
Two language varieties used by one community, an everyday one and a formal one kept for literature and school. Standard German beside dialects is one case.
The regard a community gives a language or dialect compared with others. Prestige varieties are generally considered the most correct or superior.
Using different pronouns to address someone depending on formality or familiarity. French, for one, uses plural forms for a single person.
A variety of speech or writing tied to the speaker's gender, in languages that have separate forms for men and women.
A language variety that marks its speakers as members of an ethnic group that originally used another language. It carries influence from the immigrant language.
The form of language used by a social class, profession or age group. Unlike a regional dialect, it is tied to social group, not place.
A person's evaluations of languages and of the people who speak them, which can be positive, negative or neutral. They influence language learning and identity.
People adjust their speech to those they talk with, such as shifting an accent to match. Listeners may read this as fitting in or as mocking.
Using words or phrases from a language one does not speak, as in mock Spanish, is commonly viewed as a form of appropriation.
A set of beliefs about languages as they are used in society. Like other ideologies, they are shaped by political and moral interests.
The ordinary, informal, spoken form of a language. It often carries less prestige than the standard, yet it has its own consistent grammar and sound system.
The high social regard in which a nonstandard dialect is held, usually only by its own speakers. One proposed reason it persists is group identity.
Labov asked staff in New York department stores where an item was and noted whether they pronounced the r. Pronunciation varied with the store's social standing.
Anxiety about one's own way of speaking, from a belief that it falls short of the expected standard. It can push speakers toward a more prestigious variety.
A nonstandard use of language that comes from applying a perceived rule too broadly, often to sound formal or educated.
A way to move a spacecraft between orbits using an elliptical transfer orbit and two engine burns. It often uses the least fuel but takes longer.
A point where two large bodies' gravity and their orbital motion balance, so a small object can stay put. Satellites there need little fuel.
A flyby in which a spacecraft usually saves propellant by using a planet's motion and gravity to change its path and speed.
An equation for the most speed a rocket can gain, set by its exhaust velocity and the ratio of its full mass to its empty mass.
A rocket burn changes a spacecraft's energy more at high speed, so burning at the lowest point of an orbit, where speed peaks, is most efficient.
Slowing a spacecraft by impact with the surface of a planet or moon. The word began as a whimsical name for a crash landing.
An orbit above the equator where a satellite circles in step with Earth's rotation, so it appears fixed in the sky. Communications and weather satellites often use it.
The minimum speed an object needs to break free of a planet or other body without further propulsion. It does not depend on direction.
The region around a planet or moon where its gravity is treated as the main pull on a spacecraft, instead of the Sun's.
Using thruster burns to keep a spacecraft in its orbit against forces such as air drag and the gravity of the Sun and Moon.
An engine that charges a gas and accelerates the ions with electricity to push a spacecraft. Its thrust is tiny, so it works only in space.
Slowing a spacecraft with a single pass through a planet's atmosphere so it settles into orbit using almost no fuel. It needs a heat shield.
A proposed way to launch things without a rocket. A row of electromagnets fires in sequence and accelerates a payload along a path.
A space station planned in orbit around the Moon, where crews would have moved between Orion and lunar landers. NASA later shifted focus to a surface base.
A theoretical spacecraft that would deflect a dangerous asteroid without touching it, using only its own gravitational pull. It must stay close for a long time.
The slow rotation of an orbit's closest point to the Sun. Mercury's shift exceeds what Newtonian gravity predicts, and general relativity accounts for the excess.
An orbit that carries a satellite over or near both poles. Launching into it takes a bigger rocket, since it gets no help from Earth's spin.
A nearly polar orbit in which the satellite passes over any given place on the planet at the same local solar time.
The total change in speed a space mission requires, summed over its maneuvers like a financial budget. It sets how much propellant a vehicle must carry.
In many real-life data sets the leading digit tends to be small, so small digits begin numbers far more often than large ones. Electricity bills fit it.
A system that evolves by fixed rules is ergodic when it cannot be split into statistically separate parts. Under suitable conditions, time averages match space averages.
When one measurement is extreme, the next one is likely to be closer to the average. So follow-up checks help avoid false conclusions.
A relationship where one quantity varies as a power of another regardless of their starting sizes. A square's area and its side length are an example.
A rule for inverting conditional probabilities, finding how likely a cause is given its effect. It gives the chance of disease after a positive test.
A way to estimate a statistic's accuracy by resampling the observed data, often with replacement. It is an alternative when a model's assumptions are in doubt.
On average, estimating three or more independent quantities together still beats estimating each alone. For one quantity alone, it does not help.
Points scattered randomly over space or time and independent of one another. It models random events such as customers arriving at a store or phone calls.
A distribution whose tail shrinks more slowly than an exponential one, so extreme values are more likely. The exact definition is debated.
An exact confidence interval for a success probability, found from the successes in a fixed number of trials. It errs on the wide side.
Testing many hypotheses on one data set and reporting only the significant results. Some will pass by chance, so the findings can be false positives.
The more statistical tests run on one data set, the likelier at least one gives a false positive. A stricter threshold for individual tests is one fix.
Reported values, such as self-reported ages, piling up at round numbers because people round their answers.
A probability puzzle from a game show. After the contestant picks a door, the host opens a losing one, and switching wins more often.
With enough independent random samples, their average converges to the true value. A casino may lose on one spin, but its earnings over many spins become predictable.
The average of many independent values approaches a normal distribution, even when the values themselves are not normal. So normal-data methods work on many other problems.
A way to draw samples from a hard-to-sample probability distribution. It proposes a new sample from the last one, then keeps or rejects it.
A statistical method that counteracts the multiple comparisons problem.
A sequence of random variables is exchangeable when shuffling their order leaves their joint probability distribution unchanged. Simple random sampling gives such sequences.
A formula for sizing a series of bets to maximize the long-term growth rate of wealth. It has been applied to gambling and to explaining diversification.
An imaginary wall between performers and audience. The audience watches the story through it, and the performers act as if they cannot see the audience.
A technique credited to Bertolt Brecht that keeps the audience from simply identifying with the characters. Instead the audience weighs their actions on a conscious level.
A systematic approach to training actors, developed by the Russian theatre practitioner Konstantin Stanislavski. In rehearsal, the actor searches for inner motives that justify actions.
A classical form of Japanese theater that mixes drama with traditional dance, known for stylized performances and elaborate makeup. Its performers are now all men.
An actor-training system devised by the Russian director Vsevolod Meyerhold, which makes the actor's body the main tool of expression through motion rather than language or illusion.
Plays and other art with an explicitly political message, first in favor of Soviet communism. The word later came to describe any highly politicized art.
An early form of professional Italian theater popular across Europe. Actors played fixed stock characters, such as a greedy old man, and improvised within a scripted plot.
Plays that show what happens when human existence lacks meaning or purpose and communication breaks down. Logic and argument give way to irrational speech and finally silence.
The study of dramatic composition and how a play's main elements are put on stage. A dramaturg assists the director and playwright.
The ambiguous middle stage of a rite of passage, when participants have left their old status but not yet begun the transition to the new one.
A form of traditional Japanese puppet theater. Puppeteers, chanters and shamisen musicians perform it together.
An acting technique from Brecht that combines physical gesture with attitude to make visible a character's social relations and what drives their behavior.
Rehearsal techniques that aim for sincere performances by having actors experience a character's inner motivation and emotions. The American version was shaped mainly by Lee Strasberg.
A speech in a play where a character, usually alone, speaks their thoughts aloud so the audience hears their inner feelings and plans directly.
The precise arrangement of actors on stage so a performance works. Where a director places performers can also change the significance of a scene.
A plot device in which a seemingly unsolvable problem is suddenly resolved by an unexpected and unlikely occurrence. Writers use it for a happy ending or comic effect.
The virtual vertical plane in a theatre, usually framed by an arch, through which the audience watches the action. The fourth wall is essentially the same idea.
In Indian arts, the emotional flavor that a writer or performer crafts into a work and a sensitive spectator relishes.
A major form of classical Japanese dance-drama, often telling of a supernatural being transformed into a human hero. Masked actors convey emotion mainly through stylized gestures.
A form of traditional Japanese comic theater that developed alongside Noh. Unlike solemn Noh, its main goal is to make the audience laugh.
A form of Islamic worship in which phrases or prayers are recited repeatedly to remember God. Sufi orders typically adopt a form with set posture, breathing and movement.
A Sufi state of life with God, through God, in God and for God. The seeker there is ready for the constant vision of God.
In Islamic law, one person conforming to another's teaching. Sunni usage means unjustified conformity, while Shia usage means following a qualified jurist and carries no negative sense.
Independent reasoning by an expert in Islamic law to find a solution to a legal question. It is contrasted with taqlid, imitation of legal precedent.
An early Islamic theological school that grounded rationalism in God's justice and human free will. It is best known for denying that the Quran is uncreated.
A Sunni school of theology that used both scripture and reason to take a middle way between the Athari and Mu'tazila schools. It later became Sunni Islam's predominant school.
A blessing power in Islam that begins with God and flows through those closest to him. Sacred places are said to hold it and ward off evil spiritual forces.
In hadith study, the list of people who passed a tradition on from its original authority. Scholars use it to judge whether the tradition is authentic.
A report in which Muhammad relates words that he attributes to God but that are not in the Quran.
A hadith transmitted by so many people that it is taken as certain, because the transmitters could not have conspired to fabricate it.
The scholastic, rational study of Islamic theology. It arose to establish and defend the tenets of Islam against philosophical doubters and non-Muslims.
Philosophy in the Islamic tradition, a term that also covers logic, mathematics and physics. Kalam, a rationalist form of theology, is traditionally named separately.
An Arabic word for love or passion. Sufi poetry uses it extensively to describe a selfless and burning love for God.
A Sufi practice of listening to music and sung poetry as a devotion to God.
In Sufism, the perfect human being who leads the saintly hierarchy and mediates between the divine and the human. He is unknown to the world.
Adjusting the space between two specific characters in a font. Tracking is different, since it adjusts spacing uniformly over a range of characters.
Two or more letters combined into a single glyph, such as f and i joined into ﬁ. The ampersand began as a ligature of the letters e and t.
The height of lowercase letters such as x above the baseline. Many display typefaces have a high one so they read clearly from a distance.
A smooth curve defined by control points, used in computer graphics and font design. In animation it can set how an object's speed changes over time.
A decorative flourish on a letter, such as an exaggerated serif, terminal or tail, inspired by the handwriting of its period.
The sequence and direction of the pen strokes used to form a letter.
Numerals drawn with varying heights, like a line of running text. Lining figures, by contrast, are the same height as capital letters.
The specific shape a character takes in a particular typeface. The abstract letter or symbol behind it is a grapheme.
A serif typeface style between old-style and Didone, with stronger contrast between thick and thin strokes than old-style. Baskerville is an example.
A group of old-style serif typefaces named for the engraver Claude Garamond and often used for book text. Many revivals actually follow a later punchcutter, Jean Jannon.
A style of serif typeface with thin, unbracketed serifs and strong contrast between thick and thin strokes. Firmin Didot and Giambattista Bodoni defined it.
A widely used sans-serif typeface designed by Max Miedinger. Its high x-height and tight letter spacing give it a dense, solid look.
The symbol & that stands for the word and. It began as a ligature of the word et.
A font in which each character occupies the same amount of horizontal space. Most code editors use one by default because it makes source code easier to read.
A cursive type style based on calligraphic handwriting, usually slanting slightly to the right. It is used to emphasize key points and to identify types of creative works.
A serif typeface with thick, block-like serifs, either blunt and angular as in Rockwell or rounded as in Courier. Many programming fonts use it.
The space between lines of type. In hand typesetting it was made with thin strips of lead inserted between the lines.
A letter at the start of a paragraph or chapter that is larger than the rest of the text and often several lines tall.
The area of a letter that is fully or partly enclosed by its strokes, such as the hole inside an O or a B.
The craft of cutting letters into steel punches, the first stage of making metal type. Each punch was stamped into copper to make a mold for casting.
A violent mudflow of volcanic debris and water that runs down a river valley from a volcano. Large flows tend to destroy anything in their path.
A volcano that has had an eruption of the largest size on the explosivity scale. Pressure builds in a growing magma pool until the crust above it ruptures.
A vent in the ground that releases hot volcanic gases, mostly steam, with no liquid or solid material. Most die down within days or weeks of an eruption's end.
A steep, cone-shaped volcano built up from alternating layers of hardened lava and volcanic fragments. It has a summit crater and erupts explosively.
Fragments thrown out by a volcanic eruption, from fine ash to large blocks. Layers of it from a single eruption help scientists date fossils and archaeological records.
A mild kind of eruption that throws glowing molten rock into the air. Large gas bubbles rise through the magma and burst near the top.
A powerful, continuous eruption that throws a column of volcanic debris and hot gases high into the stratosphere. It resembles the Vesuvius eruption that Pliny the Younger described.
An eruption that blasts a dense cloud of ash-laden gas out of the crater and high above the peak. Its explosions come at irregular intervals like cannon fire.
A broad, low crater left by an explosion when groundwater meets hot magma. It usually fills with water to form a shallow lake.
A volcanic pipe formed when rising magma meets shallow groundwater and heated vapor sets off a series of explosions. A shallow crater called a maar is left at the surface.
A volcanic rock built from the deposits of hot, fast currents of gas and particles from a volcano. It is a poorly sorted mix of ash and pumice.
Fluid lava that cools into a smooth, billowy or ropy surface.
A large, abrupt release of water from a lake under or beside a glacier. Geothermal heat or an eruption under the ice can trigger one.
Air pollution that forms when sulfur dioxide and other volcanic gases react with oxygen and moisture in sunlight. The term is in common use in Hawaii.
Clumps of thin basalt fibers formed when lava is stretched into strands as it cools. Named for Pele, the Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes.
A fast-moving current of hot gas and volcanic matter that flows along the ground away from a volcano. Of all volcanic hazards, it is the deadliest.
A natural roofed tunnel along which molten lava flows from a volcanic vent. When the lava drains out, it leaves an empty cave.
Closely spaced cracks that split cooling rock into a regular array of many-sided columns. It occurs in cooling lava flows.
An explosion that happens when magma heats ground water or surface water, which turns almost instantly to steam. Typically it throws out steam and rock fragments.
A giant eruption, or series of eruptions, that covers large stretches of land with basalt lava. Many are attributed to a hotspot reaching the surface.
Natural selection favoring a trait because it helps an organism's relatives reproduce, even at a cost to the organism's own survival. It can lead to the evolution of altruism.
A signal that social animals give in response to danger. Some use different calls for predators on the ground and from the air.
Parental care given by an individual to young that are not its own direct offspring. Among humans, grandparents and older siblings often do it.
A male that mates by stealth rather than by fighting or displaying for females.
Neighboring territorial animals become less aggressive toward each other once their borders are well established. Aggression toward unfamiliar animals stays the same.
The tendency of female rodents to end a pregnancy after smelling an unfamiliar male. In mice it can happen only before the embryo implants.
A state in which an animal goes motionless and appears dead, most often after a predator's attack. It is considered a form of deception against predators.
An instinctive sequence of behavior that is highly stereotyped and typical of a species. Once triggered by a key stimulus, it runs to completion.
An action, usually unrelated, performed when torn between two conflicting urges. A bird may peck at grass when unsure whether to attack or flee.
A gene for helping relatives spreads when the recipient's relatedness to the helper, multiplied by the benefit to the recipient, exceeds the helper's reproductive cost.
A narrator who takes part in the story as one of its characters.
A clinical guide used in China to diagnose mental disorders. It is very similar to the ICD-10 but adds culturally related diagnoses and lacks some conditions recognized elsewhere.
Poetry in which the sounds of human speech matter more than meaning or grammar. It is intended mainly for performance.
A community model that offers a space to people going through extreme emotional crises.
Removing sample cells or tissue to find out whether disease is present. Most are done to check for cancer or inflammation.
Speculative fiction that uses Christian themes and a Christian worldview. Unlike general Christian speculative fiction, its Christian nature is overt.
Statistical shape analysis that finds the rotation, and sometimes reflection, that best lines one shape up with another.
In American politics, the combination of traditionalist and social conservatism with political and economic right-libertarianism. Frank Meyer is the thinker most closely associated with it.
Genetic admixture between people of different races or ethnicities. It has sometimes been controversial or legally prohibited, typically in societies with strict racial or ethnic separation.
Strategies of social manipulation by which a dominant group keeps its place in a hierarchy. Berit Ås named five, such as making invisible and ridiculing.
A Latin phrase meaning Carthage must be destroyed. Cato the Elder is said to have closed his speeches with it to push for war.
A nonstandard word, expression or pronunciation, especially one seen as an error in word formation. The term has no accepted technical meaning in modern linguistics.
The vague or unclear concept that explication sets out to replace with a clearer, more useful one.
A ranged weapon that damages its target with highly focused energy and no solid projectile, such as a laser or microwave beam. Most are still experimental.
The process by which a cue activates a stored memory and brings it back to mind.
Filling the whole surface of an artwork with detail, so that as little empty space as possible is left.
Staring at a complex shape delays recognizing it, as it seems to break into parts. Repeating a word over and over can strip it of meaning.
Mentally taking an object apart in imagination. People can recall a kettle, for instance, and then picture its handle broken.
Too little oxygen supply at the tissue level, whether to the whole body or a region of it. It can be part of normal physiology during strenuous exercise.
A word that has the property it expresses. "Writable" is writable, and "word" is a word. Classifying "heterological" as either kind leads to a contradiction.
A full or new Moon that nearly coincides with perigee, the Moon's closest approach to Earth, so that it looks slightly larger. Also called a supermoon.
A disease event in a nonhuman animal population that is analogous to an epidemic in humans. High population density, as in fish farms, is a major contributing factor.
The branch of Christian theology that studies sin. Some scholars treat sin mainly as a legal infraction, others as a loss of love for God.
A novel's fictional language, full of metaphors that computers cannot grasp, used on a space station to avoid surveillance. "I dreamt about blue angels" means the police visited.
An affix inserted inside a word stem, unlike a prefix or suffix, which attach to the outside of it.
A violent assault in which acid or another corrosive substance is usually thrown at someone's face. Long-term consequences can include blindness and severe permanent scarring.
The generic name for several traditional sailing vessels of the Red Sea and Indian Ocean, typically long and thin-hulled and used to carry heavy goods.
Repeating number sequences that believers read as messages from guardian angels.
A diverse group of animals that includes molluscs, annelids and flatworms. Its phyla show spiral cleavage, a pattern of early development.
A disputed condition in which U.S. and Canadian government officials and their families reported symptoms linked to a perceived loud sound. No cause has been established.
An ancient Persian method of execution whose use is historically doubted. The victim is trapped between boats, smeared with milk and honey and devoured by insects.
A crystal form that can no longer be made because it turns into a more stable form. A tiny seed crystal of the new form may start it.
An instruction in a score to play as softly as possible, until the sound is almost inaudible.
Illogical or idiosyncratic reasoning that departs from the ordinary rules of logic, seen in disorganized thinking such as in schizophrenia.
A set of persecutory delusions in which people believe a large number of people are following and harassing them.
A method for removing existential quantifiers, the "there exists" parts, from logic formulas. The new formula is satisfiable exactly when the original is but is not necessarily equivalent to it.
Historians study the standards a society or group holds about emotions and how they should be expressed.
A pseudoscientific theory of information processing and personality types. It sorts people into types, called sociotypes, that it claims go unchanged throughout life.
A spiritual kingdom in Tibetan Buddhist tradition that the Kalachakra Tantra mentions. A Hindu prophecy makes it the birthplace of Kalki, the next incarnation of Vishnu.
A French research centre in Grenoble, co-founded by Gilbert Durand, that studies the imaginary, meaning images, symbols and myths.
The hypothesis that depressed people make more realistic judgments than non-depressed people, whose appraisals of the world are positively biased.
A rare inherited neurological disorder in which abnormal calcium deposits form in areas of the brain that control movement. On CT scans they show up mainly in the basal ganglia.
A sentence describing a phenomenon that is to be explained. When someone asks why there is smoke, the smoke is the explanandum and the fire the explanans.
Abnormal intolerance of light, felt as discomfort or pain in the eyes. Despite its name it is a symptom and not a morbid fear.
Crystal growth in which a new crystalline layer forms in a defined orientation to the crystal beneath it. The semiconductor industry is one of its main commercial uses.
A line of poetry whose sentence is unfinished at the line end, so the meaning runs on into the next line. Lines without it are end-stopped.
False history derived from the superstitions of occultism. The wider category, pseudohistory, attempts to distort or misrepresent the historical record.
Jacques Lacan's term for a formula that condenses psychoanalytic theory into algebra-like symbols, so that it can be taught exactly.

The economic policies of Japan's government under Shinzo Abe, combining monetary easing, government spending and structural reforms. The structural reforms proved less effective than observers had hoped.
The sense of touch, pain, temperature and body position. Signals reaching the brain keep the location of the stimulus on the body.
The branch of medical science that classifies diseases. Influenza, for example, counts as an infectious disease because a virus causes it.
Heightened sensitivity to sound, sometimes painful, with low tolerance for everyday noise. The most common cause is exposure to loud noise, and it often occurs with tinnitus.
The ancient practice of wealthy, high-status people giving part of their wealth to the community. It was part of the patron-client system of Roman society.
A phrase whose wording is fixed by convention instead of chosen freely. In kicked the bucket, the meaning has little to do with the words.
A view in process theology that a perfect God has sometimes opposing characteristics, so no single set of them can describe God.
Any expression that mixes languages. Bilingual puns are a particular example. The label is generally derogatory and applies when the mixing has a humorous or satirical effect.
A Roman emperor who took the throne as a teenager and was head priest of the sun god Elagabal. Modern scholars question the accounts of his reign.
A defense in which the accused says they acted believing they were in a simulated world like the one in The Matrix. A version of the insanity defense.
Reliving an experience in order to purge it of its emotional excesses. It is sometimes a way of becoming conscious of repressed traumatic events.
An abnormal increase in sensitivity of senses such as hearing or touch. Heightened sound sensitivity is called auditory hyperesthesia.
The philosophical view, opposite to teleology, that existence has no final cause from purposeful design.
A level of realization in Dzogchen at which the physical body turns into light and vanishes. Other Vajrayana teachings also describe such phenomena around dying.
Mathematics done for entertainment instead of as professional research or schooling. It includes games, puzzles and magic, and many topics need no advanced knowledge.
Speech in which words are chained together by sound or meaning, as in compulsive rhyming, with no relevant context. It is found mainly in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
The basic unit of narrative structure, an idea modeled on units in linguistics. Narremes have yet to be persuasively defined in practice.
A fusion genre that mixes crunk with post-hardcore and heavy metal. It often features screamed vocals and hip hop beats.
The inhabited world as known to Greek geographers. Under Rome it came to mean civilization itself. Today it often describes the Christian Church as a unified whole.
Voltaire's battle cry against religious intolerance and persecution, a phrase he often used to close his letters.
A pop subgenre that grew out of British new wave and blended jazz, soul and pop with lavish production. The name was coined only after the genre had peaked.
The relationship between DNA segments that share ancestry through a duplication event. Segments that share it through speciation are called orthologs.
A group exercise that lets members discover for themselves the dominant attitudes and opinions in the group, while respecting each person's need for privacy and safety.
A planned multi-layer U.S. missile defense system to detect and destroy ballistic, hypersonic and cruise missiles. It would rely on thousands of satellites carrying sensors and interceptors.
Sexual interest in and attraction to people who commit crimes. Popular culture also calls it the "Bonnie and Clyde syndrome."
A collection of knowledge preserved so that future generations could still reach it if all other copies were lost. It could be a traditional library or a computer database.
A figure of speech that describes a scene so vividly the listener seems to see it, as if it were happening now.
The position in psychology that studying the individual is the most effective way to understand behavior. Individual traits count for more than group norms.
The four-fold deity of divinity, light, power and goodness who is the eternal divine manifestation of good in Manichaeism. Humans carry particles of his light without knowing it.
The object in a cluster with the smallest total dissimilarity to all the others. Unlike a mean, it is always one of the data points.
A theory that a disorder results from a predisposition, the diathesis, interacting with life stress. Two people under the same stress can differ because their predispositions do.
A test where people name the ink color of words while ignoring their meaning. Emotionally charged words slow them down more than neutral ones.
Text that takes real effort from the reader to get through, beyond moving the eyes and turning pages.
A mark added to a letter, such as the accent in café, mainly used to change how the letter sounds.
The study of how materials, from liquids to soft solids, flow and deform. Ketchup gets runnier when shaken, but water does not.
Poetry about fantastic, science fictional or mythological themes. It is defined by its subject matter, not by its form.
In Eastern Orthodox theology, the real distinction between God's essence and his energies. Western Christianity has tended to reject it as dividing the Trinity.
Younger adults speaking to old people with simpler vocabulary, pet names and slower speech. It rests on the stereotype that older people think less well.
The main Zionist paramilitary force in British Mandate Palestine that formed to defend Jewish settlements. It became the new nation's military force after Israel declared independence.
A figure of speech in which the same word is used at the end of a clause as at the beginning. It can emphasize a word or an idea.
A Chinese medicine term for withdrawal-like symptoms such as chills, nausea and anxiety, believed to be caused by loss of semen. It is a Chinese culture-bound syndrome.
The battle between the Giants and the Olympian gods in Greek mythology. The defeated Giants were said to be buried under volcanoes.
Mentally undressing someone by looking at them.
A term sometimes used for the study of Earth's atmosphere. In other definitions it covers only the free atmosphere, the region above the planetary boundary layer.
The destruction of knowledge systems, as in colonialism, where the colonizer replaces the existing ones with its own.
A quarrel among French painters over whether drawing or color matters more. The Poussinists backed drawing, the Rubenists color.
A prediction market that rewards killing a person, since anyone can bet anonymously on the date of their death.
The study of the relationship between lichens and people. Lichens are most often used for dye, but also for medicine and food.
A person's name that contains a god's name or the word for god. The Greek Apollonios, for example, embeds Apollo.
A forgotten memory returns without being recognized, so the person believes the idea is new and original. It is not deliberate plagiarism.
A temporary structure that many land snails usually make from dried mucus. In a few species calcium carbonate makes it thick and rigid.
Experimental fiction that avoids the familiar conventions of the novel and sets up its own.
A proposed cat, genetically engineered to change appearance near nuclear radiation, as a long-term warning about nuclear waste. None has ever been engineered.
German economic liberalism, which says government must make sure the free market delivers results close to its theoretical potential. It underlies the post-war German social market economy.
A title some Christian churches give to martyrs after the Roman persecutions. In Greek Orthodoxy it mostly means those killed under Ottoman rule.
A generalization of a metric space in which the distance from a point to itself need not be zero.
A term for individuals and groups that combine environmentalism with fascism. They typically argue that overpopulation is the main threat to the environment.
A speech disorder caused by neurological injury, in which people lack enough control of the speech muscles to pronounce words clearly.
A liturgical book containing only the parts of the four gospels read during Mass, arranged by the liturgical year instead of in gospel order.
A substance that raises the body's temperature set point and so causes fever. Bacterial endotoxin is a common one.
A simple model of airflow over an airfoil, treated as a thin curved line, that predicts the lift from the angle of attack.
An argument whose premise goes unstated and usually passes for common sense with the audience. Its premise is only probable, so the conclusion is tentative.
Someone who builds or solves crossword puzzles.
A worldwide network of optical instruments that watches the whole sky for laser pulses from outside the Solar System, a possible sign of intelligent life.
The perception of sounds, generated inside the head, from pulsed or modulated radio waves. The cause is thought to be thermoelastic expansion of parts of the ear.
A Jewish legislative and judicial assembly in ancient Israel. The Great Sanhedrin acted as a supreme court.
Jacques Derrida's term for giving priority to the masculine in how meaning is made. It combines focus on the masculine point of view with focus on language.
The study of heresy. Early Christian scholars recorded the teachings of rival sects to separate those they accepted as orthodox from those they rejected as heretical.
Removing unnecessary characters such as whitespace and comments from source code without changing what it does. The smaller code is sent over a network more efficiently.
Removing the cells from a tissue to leave its extracellular matrix, a scaffold that can be refilled with a patient's own cells to build an organ or tissue.
Seeing two images of one object. When involuntary, it comes from impaired eye muscle function and can be an early sign of systemic disease.
The clothing a person wears influences their thoughts, feelings and behavior, because worn attire activates abstract concepts through its symbolic meaning. One experiment used white lab coats.
The phrase cellar door, often cited as an especially beautiful-sounding English phrase regardless of what it means.
The property of giving different results depending on direction. Wood, for example, is easier to split along its grain than across it.
The difference between a simulation and the real world, which makes a robot controller trained in simulation perform worse on a physical machine.
Moving around a sacred object or idol. It is an integral part of Hindu and Buddhist devotional practice.
A hypothetical city covering a whole planet. It is best known as a setting in science fiction but has also been considered in city planning.
A variant of Chinese folk religion that arose as an exorcistic movement. Its gods are shown as wooden masks or heads.
A writing technique that mixes real and invented material so the reader must decide on each page what is real. Robert Anton Wilson called it his basic technique.
A recreational designer drug that mixes three substances at fixed doses and is claimed to mimic MDMA. Despite its name, it contains no borax.
A hypothetical vertical city, a mixed-use megastructure with high population density that aims to be independent of the outside environment. Science fiction often portrays it as self-contained.
A Japanese slang term for people or fictional characters who seem out of touch with reality, often speaking in a delusional-sounding way.
A drug that mixes methamphetamine and caffeine. It is illegal but widely used in Thailand.
The study of clustering, the grouping of objects into clusters by their similarity.
Older men giving money or luxury gifts to young women, who often provide sexual favors in return. The Japanese term is often translated as compensated dating.
Fiction that blends science fiction, fantasy and literary fiction, or otherwise ignores the usual boundaries of genre. It grew out of the experiments of New Wave science fiction.
The tendency of a network's nodes to attach to others that are often similar in their number of connections. Social networks show it, biological networks typically do not.
The formation of new blood vessels from existing ones. It is vital in wound healing and also helps tumors turn malignant, so inhibitors are used against cancer.
A reasoned study of organizations, proposed to fill a gap left by economics and sociology. It analyzes how organizations choose and use resources and how they build meaning.
The coexistence of distinct varieties, styles and points of view within a single language. For Bakhtin, it guarantees the primacy of context over text.
An enclosure in which spores form, made of a single cell or many. Virtually all plants and fungi form one at some point in their life cycle.
Paralysis of the ciliary muscle of the eye, so the lens can no longer focus on nearby objects. It is usually due to eye drops such as atropine.
In Judaism, the holy spirit, understood as the divine force, quality and influence of God over the universe or God's creatures.
A loud sound reported to come from the sky, such as rumbles with no storm or a horn-like noise. Those who hear one typically have no clear explanation.
The weighing of a person's soul to judge their fate. The motif appears in medieval Christianity and ancient Egyptian mythology.
A complex system that works has evolved from a simpler system that worked. A complex system built from scratch does not work and cannot be patched into working.
A feeling of anxiety, apprehension or insecurity that is close in meaning to anguish.
Explanation after the fact. Skeptics say psychics use selective thinking to fit vague predictions to an event once it has happened.
The theory that building design can raise or reduce crime. Higher crime was found in high-rise housing, where residents felt no control over areas shared by so many.
A medieval deed giving a person land in exchange for a pledge of service. Later, landowners used it to give land to one person for another's use.
A lack of voluntary coordination of muscle movements. It can affect gait, speech and eye movements, and signals dysfunction in the nervous system.
The dependence of a system's state on its history. A magnet in a given field can be magnetized differently, depending on how the field changed before.
A fashion style of pale skin, dark circles under the eyes and emaciated features. It was partly a reaction against the healthy, vibrant look of earlier models.
A theory that traumatic events lead to PTSD when an experience cannot fit a person's cultural worldview, which normally buffers anxiety about death.
A specific phobia of machines or anything mechanical. It often arises after losing a limb or another traumatic incident involving machinery.
The East and Southeast Asian countries, such as Japan, Korea and Vietnam, that Chinese culture historically shaped. Japan adapted Chinese characters as kanji, Korea as hanja.
Gene sequences related through shared ancestry by a speciation event, as opposed to paralogs, which arose from a duplication event.
The part of logic devoted to the analysis of questions, sometimes called the logic of questions and answers.
A word that stands in for another word, phrase or sentence whose meaning is clear from context. A pronoun, which substitutes a noun or a noun phrase, is one kind.
The love of knowledge and the drive to know.
A delusion that another person is infatuated with the patient. The supposed admirer is usually unattainable because of high social or financial status, or an existing relationship.
A family of mind techniques built on one shared method, aimed at solving set tasks by drawing on distinctive properties of the mind.
The study of how an organism reacts to any kind of harm, such as a wound or surgical shock. Henri Laborit, who founded it, also called it aggressology.
A political regime in which political and corporate elites control the infrastructure of the internet, and use it to reshape the ideas and values through which a society sees politics.
The person who carries the processional cross at the head of a procession in some Christian churches, at the start and end of a service.
